# HydroModPy documentation

<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/index.html -->
# HydroModPy

A Python toolbox for automated, reproducible, catchment-scale modeling of shallow groundwater. One TOML file takes a catchment from its digital elevation model to a calibrated model: where the water table sits, where it reaches the ground, which streams it keeps flowing, and how all of it changes with the seasons.

Important

This documentation is for version 2.0.1. Install it with `pip install hydromodpy`. Projects written for version 1 should stay pinned to an exact tag such as `v1.0.0`.

Looking for one parameter? The whole file as a tree filters every key by name, value or word. You read a report made with HydroModPy and you do not run it yourself? Start with What HydroModPy does, then Reading the results.

## What’s new

Every notable change is recorded in the changelog. The keys added, removed or changed in the TOML file since the last release are listed, from the models, in What changed in the TOML.

## How to cite

If HydroModPy supports your work, please cite the companion technical note, published in Hydrology and Earth System Sciences (2026, doi:10.5194/hess-30-5571-2026), and the software, archived on Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.22141925). Cite gives BibTeX, RIS and plain-text versions; `CITATION.cff` at the root of the repository is what GitHub shows behind “Cite this repository”.

Papers that use HydroModPy and the catchments where it has been deployed are listed in Applications and papers.

# A first run

Install HydroModPy, run a first model in under a minute, then run example 04 from its file and from Python.

## Quick start

Six commands. Run them in a terminal where Python 3.11 to 3.13 is available, and in a virtual environment if you keep one (Install has the variants for Windows and conda).

```
pip install hydromodpy
hmp workspace init
cd ~/hydromodpy
hmp run projects/example/run_demo.toml
hmp example add 04
hmp run projects/04_streamflow_intermittence_in_transient/project.toml
```

What each command does, and how long it took on a clean machine (a 2-core laptop, fast connection):

| Command | What it does | Time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pip install hydromodpy` | Installs the package and its geospatial wheels, 1.3 GB in a clean environment. | about 2 min |
| `hmp workspace init` | Makes `~/hydromodpy`, with 27 data folders and the project `example`. | 8 s |
| `cd ~/hydromodpy` | Enters the workspace. `hmp example add` looks for a workspace at or above the current folder and has no default. Elsewhere, add `-w ~/hydromodpy`. | instant |
| `hmp run projects/example/run_demo.toml` | Solves a synthetic 1 km square under a steady recharge with MODFLOW-NWT. No download, except the solver itself the very first time. | 9 to 15 s |
| `hmp example add 04` | Fetches the Nançon catchment, 92 MiB, most of it a regional DEM. Cached by content: a second workspace costs nothing. | 20 s |
| `hmp run projects/04_.../project.toml` | Solves the real catchment month by month from 2000 to 2002 with MODFLOW 6, draws eight figures and writes four groups of files. | about 1.5 min |

The clock on the last line of a run, `Run completed`, is shorter than what you wait: Python starts, imports the geospatial stack and reads the configuration first. Count 15 to 30 s more than the figure. The numbers above are measured, on a machine that was sometimes busy with other work.

A run ends with this, the name and the first eight characters of the run id being yours:

```
Run completed: nancon_intermittence_mf6 [b9716f06] 86s nse=0.97
next: hmp show nancon_intermittence_mf6 | hmp publish nancon_intermittence_mf6 --to <folder> | hmp export nancon_intermittence_mf6 --list
```

The figures of that run are in `runs/nancon_intermittence_mf6/figures/`, among them the depth of the water table in October 2002 with the cells where it reaches the ground. The run prints one `WARNING` line on the way, about the outlet. Example 04 says what it means.

## Then

Concepts gives the six words that name the things on disk, in two minutes. Then Example 04 walks through the file of example 04 and the script that plays it step by step. Install has the variants of the installation and what to do when it fails.

Looking for one parameter? Go to the reference.

<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/get-started/calibrate-k.html -->
# Calibrate K on a network

**Task**: Move K until the stream network the water table sustains matches the mapped one.
**Time**: About a minute for the search, 14 steady solves.
**Needs**: The files of example 10. The network map is a file of the example, so nothing is downloaded.
**Gives**: The best K, a full run at that K with its figures, and a trace of the search.

Example 10 models the Urse catchment, an Alpine headwater with no gauge. The only thing to match is the mapped stream network. The search moves K alone until the cells where the water table reaches the ground fall on the mapped reaches. The map is a target. It scores the model and never enters it. How sure is the model? says what the result can and cannot tell.

## What can be calibrated

`hmp config targets` lists the parameters a calibration can move, with their current value, unit and the path they write to. It loads the file and solves nothing. On example 10:

```
name                    current       unit  space     draw         default bounds            physical range            path
thickness                    50          m  log       log_uniform  -                         0 .. 10000                domain.depth_model.thickness
drainage                      0       m2/s  log       log_uniform  -                         -                         flow.bc.drainage.value
K                   3.11338e-06        m/s  log       log_uniform  -                         1e-14 .. 100              flow.param.K.field.value
Ss                        1e-05        m-1  log       log_uniform  -                         1e-12 .. 0.001            flow.param.Ss.field.value
Sy                         0.01          -  log       log_uniform  -                         0.0001 .. 0.5             flow.param.Sy.field.value
"recharge.factor"             1          -  log       log_uniform  0.5 .. 2                  -                         flow.sinks_sources.recharge.factor
vka                           1          -  log       log_uniform  -                         0.001 .. 100              solver.modflow6.process_specific.vka
```

A parameter you move gets a `[calibration.parameters.<name>]` table with a pair of bounds. The search is in log space.

## The file

`run_calibration_k.toml` inherits `project.toml` and writes only the search. K goes from one to a thousand times the recharge, and a bisection closes on the K where the gap between the two networks changes sign.

examples/projects/10_coupling_with_land_surface_model_pyhelp/run_calibration_k.toml · keys link to their card

```
1# Example 10, K from the mapped stream network.
2#
3# The same catchment and the same PyHELP recharge as project.toml, which this file inherits.
4# Only the conductivity changes, and it is searched. No discharge is observed on this Alpine
5# headwater, so the search has only the mapped network to go by. The criterion is the signed
6# gap between the length of the network that the water table sustains and the length of the
7# mapped one. A K too small lets the water table reach the ground nearly everywhere. A K too
8# large keeps it deep and leaves the streams dry. The gap changes sign between the two, and
9# a bisection on K finds where it is zero. The method is the one of Abherve et al. (2023),
10# 10.5194/hess-27-3221-2023.
11#
12#   hmp check run_calibration_k.toml
13#   hmp run run_calibration_k.toml
14
15base_config = "project.toml"
16
17[workflow]
18mode = "calibration"
19
20[simulation]
21name = "urse_example_10_k"
22description = "Urse catchment, K from the mapped stream network, PyHELP recharge."
23
24[calibration]
25seed = 42
26# The best trial is replayed as a full run, with its figures and its exports.
27save_runs = "best_n"
28save_best_n = 1
29
30# K / recharge from 1 to 1000. The recharge is 2.38e-8 m/s, so K goes from 2.4e-8 to 2.4e-5 m/s.
31[calibration.parameters.K]
32bounds = [2.4e-8, 2.4e-5]
33
34# The network is scored on the cells of the catchment, at the end of the run.
35[calibration.outputs.seepage_network]
36support = "network"
37time = "last"
38
39# The polygon of the catchment, 6.17 km2, and the catchment that the flow directions of the
40# DEM give, 6.5 km2, differ by 7.7 %, because the DEM and the polygon disagree along the
41# divide. The outlet is the same, so the search goes on.
42[calibration.outputs.seepage_network.verdict]
43max_catchment_mismatch = false
44validity_length = "auto"
45
46# The mapped network, the one to match. A simulated cell within 50 m of it counts as on it.
47[calibration.outputs.seepage_network.map]
48complete = "urse_stream_network.gpkg"
49position_accuracy = "50 m"
50
51[calibration.outputs.seepage_network.model]
52seepage_threshold = 0.0001
53weighting = "area"
54
55[[calibration.objective_blocks]]
56name = "network_gap"
57metric = "distance_gap"
58uses_outputs = ["seepage_network"]
59
60# The search stops when the interval of K is narrower than 1 % of its middle.
61[[calibration.phases]]
62name = "steady_conductivity"
63method = "bisection"
64max_trials = "auto"
65parameters = ["K"]
66objective_blocks = ["network_gap"]
67
68[calibration.phases.method_options]
69rel_tol = 0.01
70sweep_points = 7
71
72# The figures of the run and the ones that only a search has: the root search, the
73# parameter against the cost, and the progress of the search.
74[display]
75on_error = "raise"
76
77[[display.figure]]
78variable = "downslope_distance"
79scale = "log"
80
81[[display.figure]]
82preset = "root_search"
83when = "session"
84
85[[display.figure]]
86variable = ["trials.parameter", "trials.cost"]
87type = "xy"
88facet = "parameter"
89when = "session"
90
91[[display.figure]]
92preset = "calibration_progress"
93when = "session"
```

An output is a simulated quantity paired with its observation. The tables of the network output carry the choices that matter.

- `map` is the mapped network. `complete` is every reach. A file that also gives `permanent`, the reaches that never dry, makes a two-bound search.
- `model` says how the model draws its own network, with the weight of each cell and the flow a reach must carry to count.
- `verdict` says when the result holds. A distance above the validity length logs a warning, or stops the run with `on_invalid = "error"`. Downslope distance between two networks gives the criterion.

A block scores outputs with one metric, and a phase moves some parameters against some blocks. A file can chain phases, K on the network then Sy on a gauged discharge, and each phase can carry a `window`. Write calibration phases shows how.

## Check it, then run it

From the folder of example 10:

```
hmp check run_calibration_k.toml
hmp calibrate run_calibration_k.toml --list-phases
hmp run run_calibration_k.toml
```

The first command lists every problem of the file at once. The second prints each phase before any solve. The third runs the search and replays the best trial as a full run, `runs/urse_example_10_k/`. Its trials are in `sessions/urse_example_10_k/`.

## Read the result

The `root_search` preset, asked with `when = "session"`, draws the search. Each point is a trial. The two curves are the mean distance from the simulated network to the mapped one, and from the mapped one to the simulated one. A K too small lets the water table reach the ground nearly everywhere, so the simulated network is far longer than the map. A K too large leaves the streams dry. The search closes on K = 3.9e-6 m/s, a bracket 0.9 % wide, where the two distances cross.

The figure comes from `hmp show sessions/urse_example_10_k --figure root_search`, and the table of targets from `hmp config targets project.toml`, both in the folder of example 10. Scoring a simulated stream network explains the network criterion. The options of each method are on Calibration methods and metrics, and the keys on [calibration].


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/get-started/cluster.html -->
# On a cluster

A project of many catchments runs on a Slurm cluster from its plan. HydroModPy writes the job scripts; you submit them with `sbatch`, as any other job. Each task of the array runs one case, the same `hmp run plan/<hash>/<case>.toml` the local launcher runs.

Warning

Nothing on this page is verified on a cluster. The scripts are tested for their content and their shell syntax, and run under stand-in `hmp` and `sacct` commands, never under a real scheduler. Read them before the first submission, and run a small plan first.

## Write the scripts

```
hmp project plan .
hmp campaign array . --scheduler slurm
```

`hmp campaign array` writes a folder `jobs/<stamp>-slurm/` with three files, frozen when they are written:

| File | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `cases.txt` | One case per line, the cases of the current plan. Task N of the array reads line N. |
| `prepare.sh` | An array that fetches the data of each case, `hmp run <case> --until load_data`, with `--set workflow.mode=simulation` for a calibration case. It is the only job that adds to the input cache of the workspace. |
| `array.sh` | The array of the solves, `hmp run <case> --frozen`, one task per case, plus `--resume <case>` on a simulation that an earlier attempt left unfinished. |

Each task finds its case with `hmp campaign case <job> <N>`, which reads the frozen `cases.txt` of its own job, and chooses the flags of `hmp run` when it starts, from the state its case is in: a resubmitted task resumes its case. `HMP_PYTHON` overrides the interpreter the scripts call. A new plan, written while an array waits in the queue, does not change what its tasks run; `hmp project plan` refuses to write one while a case of the current plan is running.

`--partition`, `--time` and `--threads-per-case` set the partition, the wall time and the threads of each case; the command reference lists the options. A task asks for `sites.run.threads_per_case` CPUs times the solves of the largest case, since a calibration solves several trials side by side, and the worker limits its own threads to that budget.

## Submit

```
sbatch jobs/20261020-143000-slurm/prepare.sh
sbatch --dependency=afterok:<id of prepare> jobs/20261020-143000-slurm/array.sh
```

Each task runs in the scratch of its node: `array.sh` sets `HMP_SCRATCH_ROOT` to `$SLURM_TMPDIR` when the node has one. The folder of the case, under `runs/`, receives the results.

A task ends with an outcome in every case. Slurm sends `SIGTERM` ten minutes before the wall time (`--signal=B:TERM@600`), and the worker writes `aborted` before it stops. When the worker dies without writing anything (a native crash, an out-of-memory kill), a `trap` in the script writes `failed` with the exit code, the signal and the end of the log, marked `written_by = "trap"`. The log of a task is written under `jobs/<stamp>-slurm/logs/`, and the trap copies it to `runs/<case>/logs/job-<id>.out`.

A task that Slurm resubmits, or a job submitted twice, never makes a `_v2`: the claim of an attempt is atomic, so the second worker on a case leaves, and a case that failed resumes in place.

## Follow and collect

```
hmp ls --plan
hmp project log . --failed
hmp catalog reindex -w . --incremental
hmp campaign collect .
```

`hmp ls --plan` reads the `outcome.json` and the heartbeat of each case. When `sacct` is on the path, it also asks Slurm which jobs ended: a task whose job ended while its outcome still says running shows as failed instead of stale. `hmp project log` rebuilds the journal of the job from the outcomes. No task opens the index of the project: rebuild it once the array is done, then write the summary.

## Limits

The layout assumes a file system where `mkdir`, `rename` and file locks behave as on a local disk. A network file system depends on its mount options, and HydroModPy does not test any: keep the input cache and the project where the cluster documents these operations as safe, and keep the solver scratch on the node.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/get-started/concepts.html -->
# Concepts

Six words name the things on disk. This page is the whole mental model you need before example 04.

```
~/hydromodpy/                          workspace
├── workspace.toml
├── data/                              inputs shared by every project
│   ├── dem/
│   ├── hydrometry/
│   ├── sites/catalog.csv              the sites you declared, optional
│   └── ...                            one folder per variable
└── projects/
    ├── example/                       a project: the synthetic demo
    │   ├── project.toml               marks the root of the project
    │   ├── run_demo.toml              a file you run
    │   ├── runs/demo/                 a run
    │   └── .hmp/index.duckdb          the catalog, rebuilt from runs/ and sessions/
    └── 04_streamflow_intermittence_in_transient/
        ├── project.toml               [site] names the catchment
        ├── py1_run_and_plot.py        plays project.toml step by step
        ├── runs/                      one folder per run
        ├── sessions/                  one folder per calibration
        └── trash/                     what you deleted, until you empty it
```

Workspace. A folder made by `hmp workspace init`, `~/hydromodpy` by default. It holds the input data in `data/`, one flat folder per variable, and your projects in `projects/`. Several projects share the same `data/`. A workspace is optional: a project folder alone also works, with its input data in a `data/` folder next to `project.toml`. HydroModPy takes the first of: `workspace.root` or `workspace.data_dir` in the file, the `HMP_WORKSPACE` environment variable, the workspace that holds the project under `projects/`, and the project folder itself.

Project. A folder that has a `project.toml`: that file marks the root. In a workspace it is a subfolder of `projects/`. The project holds the TOML files you run and everything those runs write. Create one with `hmp project new <name>`; list them with `hmp project list`. A relative path written in any file of the project is read from this root.

Site. The catchment a file models: its name, and optionally a label, the gauge at its outlet and a stable code. A file that models a real catchment declares it in `[site]`, with `site.name` required. The gauge, `site.gauge`, is the station every observed series and every score reads unless a section names another one. A project of many catchments replaces `[site]` with `[sites]` and a table, one row per site (Many catchments).

Run. One execution of one TOML file. It writes a folder `runs/<name>/`, where `<name>` is the `simulation.name` of the file, or the name of the file. The folder holds the frozen resolved config (`config.toml`), the fields (`fields.zarr`), the tables (`tables.parquet`), the inputs it read (`inputs.json`), its figures, exports and report, a generated `README.md` and, written last, `manifest.json`. These are open formats: `xarray`, `zarr` and `pandas` read a run without HydroModPy. Running an unchanged file again does nothing; an edited file, or the same file with `--set`, makes `<name>_v2`. A run that failed keeps its folder, with `outcome.json` saying why, and the next attempt resumes there.

Session. The record of one calibration, `sessions/<name>/`: its frozen configuration, one line per trial in `trials.jsonl`, and the best trial. That best trial is promoted to a run of the same name, `runs/<name>/`, which you read like any other run.

Catalog. The index of the runs and sessions of one project, a DuckDB file at `.hmp/index.duckdb`. `hmp ls` lists the runs. The disk is the truth and the catalog is derived from it: `hmp catalog reindex` rebuilds it from `runs/` and `sessions/`, and deleting `.hmp/` loses nothing. Opening a project builds a missing index, and one process writes it at a time. Its reference lists the commands. Deleting a run moves it to `trash/`; a deleted name is never given out again.

## Reading a TOML file

- The sections say what `hmp run` does: a file with `[calibration]` calibrates, a file with `[overview]` and no `[simulation]` draws the overview, any other file simulates. `workflow.mode` names the operation when you want to write it out.
- Each section is a request: what to model or produce, when, where. The parameter reference groups the sections by the question they answer, and marks each key for the user, the developer or the expert (the profiles).
- A file names a parent with `base_config` and writes only what changes. The merge rules are in the grammar.

Next: the quick start, or example 04 if you have already run the demo.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/get-started/example-04.html -->
# Example 04

Example 04 models the Nançon catchment (Ille-et-Vilaine) with MODFLOW 6, from 2000 to 2002 in monthly stress periods. As the recharge swings between wet winters and dry summers, the cells where the water table reaches the ground spread out and draw back. The example is two files. `project.toml` says the model, its figures and its exports, and `hmp run` plays it in about a minute and a half. `py1_run_and_plot.py` plays the same file one step at a time from Python, looks at what each step built, and tries three values of Sy.

## Get the example

```
hmp workspace init ~/hydromodpy
hmp example add 04 -w ~/hydromodpy
cd ~/hydromodpy/projects/04_streamflow_intermittence_in_transient
```

`hmp example add` downloads the files of the example, about 92 MiB, most of it a regional DEM. Files are cached by content, so a second workspace costs nothing. `hmp example list` shows the examples your version ships and `hmp example show 04` lists the files one by one. `hmp example add 00 07 08` installs several examples at once and `hmp example add --all` installs every one. Each becomes a project of the workspace, and the regional DEM they share is downloaded once.

## The model file

`hmp run` plays the file as one forward simulation, because it holds no `[calibration]` and no `[overview]`. The file opens with the catchment. `[site]` names it and its gauge, `NANCON`. Every series below reads that station: the discharge, and the SIM2 recharge and runoff averaged over the catchment. `[metrics]` sets the window the discharge is scored on, 2001 and 2002, so the year 2000 is spin-up.

examples/projects/04_streamflow_intermittence_in_transient/project.toml · keys link to their card

```
16# The catchment. The gauge is the station of every series below: the discharge,
17# the recharge and the runoff read station NANCON. The recharge and the runoff
18# are the SIM2 means over the catchment. The uri is the Hub'Eau code of the
19# site, a key that survives a move to another workspace.
20[site]
21name = "nancon"
22label = "Le Nançon à Lécousse"
23gauge = "NANCON"
24uri = "hubeau:J0014010"
```

...

```
26# The discharge is scored on 2001 and 2002. The year 2000 is spin-up.
27[metrics]
28window = { start = "2001-01-01", end = "2002-12-31" }
```

...

```
30[simulation]
31name = "nancon_intermittence_mf6"
32description = "Nancon catchment, monthly transient 2000-2002, seasonal seepage intermittence."
```

...

```
34# Thirty-six monthly stress periods, one time step each.
35[simulation.time]
36start_datetime = "2000-01-01"
37end_datetime = "2002-12-31"
38step_value = "1 month"
```

...

```
40[[simulation.process]]
41id = "flow_main"
42kind = "flow"
43solvers = ["modflow6"]
```

The catchment is cut out of a regional DEM of 75 m, upstream of the outlet, after the depressions of the DEM are breached. The domain is the box around the catchment, 172 by 157 cells, and the aquifer is one layer of 30 m under the ground.

examples/projects/04_streamflow_intermittence_in_transient/project.toml · keys link to their card

```
45# The catchment is cut out of a regional 75 m DEM, upstream of the outlet,
46# after the depressions of the DEM are breached. The domain is the box around
47# the catchment widened by 10 % of the square root of its area: 172 x 157 cells.
48[geographic]
49crs_project = "EPSG:2154"
50dem_correc_type = "breach"
```

...

```
52[geographic.catchment]
53kind = "from_outlet_coord"
54x_outlet = 389285.910
55y_outlet = 6816518.749
56snap_dist = "150 m"
57buff_area = "10% of sqrt(area)"
```

...

```
59# One layer, 30 m thick under the ground surface.
60[domain.depth_model]
61kind = "constant_thickness"
62thickness = "30 m"
```

`[data]` lists what the run reads, each from a file of the shared `data/` folder of the workspace, named by `workspace:` and read in the folder of its variable. The discharge, the recharge and the runoff are chronicles of the station `site.gauge` names, each read with the location file of its folder, which gives the place and the unit of the station.

examples/projects/04_streamflow_intermittence_in_transient/project.toml · keys link to their card

```
64# The DEM, the mapped streams, the gauge, and the monthly recharge and runoff of
65# station NANCON. The mapped streams are drawn and exported. The model does not
66# read them. Each name is read in the folder of its variable, data/dem/,
67# data/hydrometry/ and so on. A chronicle CSV is read with the location file of
68# its folder, here hydrometry_custom_LOC.csv, recharge_custom_LOC.csv and
69# runoff_custom_LOC.csv, which give the place and the unit of station NANCON.
70[data]
71types = ["dem", "hydrography", "hydrometry", "recharge", "runoff"]
```

...

```
73[[data.dem.sources]]
74source = "file"
75path = "workspace:DEM_armorican_massif.tif"
```

...

```
77[[data.hydrography.sources]]
78source = "file"
79path = "workspace:nancon_stream_network.gpkg"
```

...

```
81# Daily discharge of the gauge, 1982 to 2022.
82[[data.hydrometry.sources]]
83source = "file"
84path = "workspace:hydrometry_custom_NANCON_19820201_20220125_D.csv"
```

...

```
86# Monthly SIM2 recharge and runoff of the catchment, 2000 to 2002, in mm/day.
87[[data.recharge.sources]]
88source = "file"
89path = "workspace:recharge_custom_NANCON_20000101_20021231_M.csv"
```

...

```
91[[data.runoff.sources]]
92source = "file"
93path = "workspace:runoff_custom_NANCON_20000101_20021231_M.csv"
```

The flow is transient, so the heads move from one month to the next and the aquifer stores water. The aquifer has one K, one Sy and one Ss. Every cell drains at the ground, with a conductance that follows K. The first month is solved in steady state under the recharge of January 2000, so the run starts from a wet winter water table.

## Run the file

Command line

```
hmp run project.toml
```

Python

```
import hydromodpy as hmp

run = hmp.run("project.toml").open()
print(run.name)
```

A relative path is read from the folder you are in. `hmp.run` returns the Run, whose reference page lists what it reads.

The run writes its figures to `runs/nancon_intermittence_mf6/figures/` and its exports to `runs/nancon_intermittence_mf6/exports/`. The last line gives the name of the run and the NSE of the discharge at the gauge, about 0.97.

Run an unchanged file a second time and nothing is computed. The command says which run is already there, and `hmp run --force` computes it again. Edit the file, even one value, and the second run is a new one, `runs/nancon_intermittence_mf6_v2/`, then `_v3`. A name is never given out again: hmp ls lists the versions, hmp diff compares them, and a deleted run goes to the project trash.

## What can go wrong

| Message | Cause | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Outlet moved 130 m (limit 150 m) onto the flow network`, a `WARNING` line of every run | The coordinate of the file does not fall on a stream cell of the DEM, so the outlet moves to the cell with the largest flow accumulation in a window of `geographic.catchment.snap_dist`, here 150 m. | Nothing, here. A move close to the limit means the coordinate is far from the stream, so check it. |
| `Flow solver '<solver>' failed for run`, with a percent discrepancy and `did not converge` from the listing file | A very small Sy lets the water table move by metres in a month, and MODFLOW 6 does not converge in one time step. The script meets it with Sy = 0.001. | Cut each month in several time steps with `simulation.time.substeps_per_period`, as the script does with 4. |

## The script, step by step

`py1_run_and_plot.py` sits next to the file. It finds the project from its own location, so it runs from any folder, and it can be stepped through cell by cell (`# %%`) in Spyder or VS Code. It plays the model in a lab, which builds the model in memory one step at a time and writes no run until it is asked to.

After `load_data`, the forcing of the station is in memory, one value per month. The script draws it.

```

state = lab.advance("load_data")
print(state.geographic)
print(state.data)

# The recharge and the runoff over the catchment, one value per month in mm/day. The model takes
# the recharge, and the runoff is added to the drain flow to give the discharge.
forcing = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        name: getattr(state.data, name).points[0].data.set_index("datetime")["value"]
        for name in ("recharge", "runoff")
    }
)
print(forcing.describe().round(2).to_string())
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
ax.plot(forcing.index, forcing["recharge"], color="dodgerblue", lw=2, label="recharge")
ax.plot(forcing.index, forcing["runoff"], color="navy", lw=2, label="runoff")
ax.set_ylabel("mm/day")
ax.legend()
fig.savefig(FIGURES / "recharge_and_runoff.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")

```

A run stopped at `prepare_solver` already stores the ground of every cell, so it draws the mesh on the relief before anything is solved.

```

# A run stopped at `prepare_solver` stores the ground of every cell, so it draws the mesh.
state = lab.advance("prepare_solver")
print(state.model)
before = lab.run(until_step="prepare_solver")
print(
    before.figure(
        "topography",
        overlays=["mesh", "outline", "network", "outlet"],
        save=FIGURES / "mesh_on_relief.png",
    )
)

```

Then Sy takes three values, and each one is kept as a run with the figures and the files of `project.toml`. The value of the file gives the run of `project.toml`, so it is not solved twice. With Sy = 0.001 the water table moves by metres in a month, and MODFLOW 6 needs four time steps per month to converge.

```

# Sy sets how much water the aquifer stores for a metre of water table. Each run writes the
# figures and the files of project.toml. Sy = 0.05 is the value of the file, so its run is
# the run of project.toml.
SY = {"small": 0.001, "file": 0.05, "large": 0.3}
runs = {}
for label, sy in SY.items():
    # With Sy = 0.001 the water table moves by metres in a month, and MODFLOW 6 needs four
    # time steps per month to converge. That run takes about three minutes.
    steps = 4 if label == "small" else 1
    lab.set({"Sy": sy, "simulation.time.substeps_per_period": steps})
    runs[label] = lab.run(None if label == "file" else f"nancon_sy_{label}")
lab.close()

```

Each run gives the months when the catchment seeps the least and the most, and `run.figure` draws the seepage cells and the water table of these two months from the sealed run, so nothing is solved again. A small Sy lets the water table follow each month: the network swells in winter and nearly dries in summer. A large Sy smooths the year.

```

# The fields are stored by month. Each month is named by its first day, and the figures take
# the middle of the month. Only the cells of the catchment are counted.
rows = []
for label, run in runs.items():
    months = run.periods.edges[:-1]
    seeps = run.read("seepage_mask").to_numpy()[:, run.catchment_mask.ravel()] > 0
    share = pd.Series(seeps.mean(axis=1) * 100, index=months)
    scores = run.metrics.set_index("metric")["value"]
    rows.append(
        {
            "Sy": SY[label],
            "least (%)": share.min(),
            "in": share.idxmin().strftime("%Y-%m"),
            "most (%)": share.max(),
            "in ": share.idxmax().strftime("%Y-%m"),
            "NSE": scores["nse"],
            "NSE log": scores["nse_log"],
        }
    )
    for word, month in (("least", share.idxmin()), ("most", share.idxmax())):
        middle = (month + pd.Timedelta(days=14)).strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
        print(
            run.figure(
                "seepage_mask",
                time=middle,
                overlays=["outline"],
                save=FIGURES / f"seepage_sy_{label}_{word}.png",
            )
        )
        print(
            run.figure(
                "watertable_elevation",
                type="section",
                time=middle,
                line=SECTION,
                save=FIGURES / f"section_sy_{label}_{word}.png",
            )
        )
# A small Sy lets the water table follow each month, so the network swells in winter and
# nearly dries in summer. A large Sy smooths the year.
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Sy").round(2).to_string())

```

The script takes about six minutes, most of it the run with the small Sy. Its figures land in `summary/figures/`, beside the runs.

## Then

Calibrate K on a network searches K on the mapped network of another catchment. Work in the lab lists every member of the lab, and Run step by step stops a run after a given step. The reference has one card per key of the file.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/get-started/from-v1.html -->
# Coming from version 1

Version 1 was a set of Python scripts. You built a `Watershed` object, called `add_*` and `update_*` methods on it, and ran MODFLOW with `preprocessing_modflow` and `processing_modflow`. Version 2 puts the same choices in a TOML file. You run it with `hmp run`, and every run is stored in a folder you can read without HydroModPy.

The v1 scripts stay on the tag `v1.0.0`, and the branch `v1.0` is frozen. Nothing forces you to move a finished study. For a new one, start from A first run.

## What changes

- Every setting is a key in a TOML file. There are no setter calls.
- A project is a folder with a `project.toml`. A run file names it with `base_config` and states only what it changes. A loop over a parameter becomes several run files, or a calibration.
- Results go to `runs/<name>/` as Zarr, Parquet and JSON. There is no pickle file to reload.
- Units are written with the value, as in `"30 m"` or `unit = "m/s"`. Version 1 expected meters and days. Version 2 stores SI units, so a v1 `hk` in m/day must be divided by 86400 or written with its unit.
- Data come from a `[data]` table, either from a provider or from your own file.

## Keys

| Version 1 | Version 2 |
| --- | --- |
| `Watershed(from_xyv=[x, y, snap, buffer, crs])` | `[geographic.catchment]` with `kind = "from_outlet_coord"`, `x_outlet`, `y_outlet`, `snap_dist`, `buff_area`, and `crs_project` in `[geographic]` |
| `from_dem`, `from_shp` | `kind = "dem"` and `cell_size`, or `kind = "from_polyg_shp"` and `polyg_shp_path` |
| `dem_path` | `[[data.dem.sources]]` with `source = "file"` |
| `BV.add_hydrography`, `add_hydrometry`, `add_geology` | `types = [...]` and `[[data.<variable>.sources]]` in `[data]` |
| `update_simulation_state('transient')` | `flow_regime` in `[flow]`, and `[simulation.time]` for the dates |
| `update_nlay`, `update_lay_decay` | `nlay` and `lay_decay` in `[domain.layers]` |
| `update_thick(30)` | `[domain.depth_model]` with `kind = "constant_thickness"` and `thickness` |
| `update_hk`, `update_sy` | `[flow.param.K.field]` and `[flow.param.Sy.field]`, with `kind`, `unit` and `value` |
| `update_recharge` | `[flow.sinks_sources.recharge]`, and `recharge` in the `types` of `[data]` |
| `update_sink_fill` | `sink_fill` in `[solver]` |
| `update_input_particles(zone_partic=...)` | `zone_partic` in `[transport.modpath]` |
| `update_model_name` | `name` in `[simulation]` |
| `postprocessing_modflow(watertable_depth=True, ...)` | `[[display.figure]]` and `[[export]]` tables with `variable` |

A table of a process now carries `kind` where an alpha release of version 2 used `type`. If an old file does not load, `hmp doctor --fix-config` rewrites the renamed keys and says what it changed. The generated reference lists every key: TOML parameters.

## Commands

| Version 1 | Version 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Edit the paths at the top of a script | `hmp workspace init`, then `hmp example add 04` |
| `preprocessing_modflow` and `processing_modflow` | `hmp run project/step.toml` |
| `postprocessing_modflow` and `postprocessing_netcdf` | `hmp export <run> --list`, then `hmp export <run> ...` |
| Plot functions of `visualization_results` | `hmp show <run> --figure NAME`, and the `[[display.figure]]` tables |
| Reload a pickle of models | `hmp ls`, `hmp show <run>` and `run.read(...)` in Python |
| Calibration scripts | `hmp calibrate file.toml`, see hmp calibrate |
| Copy a folder of results to a colleague | `hmp publish <run> --to <folder>` |

Every command takes `-w <workspace>`, and prints JSON with `--format json`. The full list is in Command line.

## Moving a study

1. Run `hmp workspace init` and put your input files in `~/hydromodpy/data/`.
1. Write a `project.toml` with the site, the catchment, the depth and the data. Example 04 shows a whole file, section by section.
1. Run it with a steady regime first. Check the figures, then add the dates and the forcings.
1. Compare with your v1 results through `hmp diff` or a notebook.

Results are not bit for bit equal to version 1. The recharge, the drains and the meshing were rewritten, and each change is in the changelog.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/get-started/install.html -->
# Install

HydroModPy needs Python 3.11, 3.12 or 3.13. The version of this site is 2.0.1; the versions page says what each release promises. On a fast connection pip needs about two minutes, and a clean environment weighs 1.3 GB: most of it is the geospatial and scientific wheels.

Linux on x86_64 is the supported platform. macOS and Windows are best effort until their CI is green: the weekly jobs below run there, but a failure on them does not block a release. The terrain tools depend on `whitebox-workflows`, which publishes wheels for glibc 2.35 or newer on Linux x86_64, macOS arm64 and Windows x64 only, so an older cluster cannot install it.

## Install the package

Linux and macOS

```
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
pip install hydromodpy
```

Windows

In PowerShell:

```
py -3.12 -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
pip install hydromodpy
```

conda or micromamba

You do not need a clone of the repository. Save this file as `environment.yml`:

```
name: hmp
channels:
  - conda-forge
dependencies:
  - python=3.12
  - pip
  - pip:
      - hydromodpy
```

Then create and activate the environment:

```
micromamba create -f environment.yml
micromamba activate hmp
```

With conda, write `conda env create -f environment.yml` and `conda activate hmp`. If pip cannot find a wheel for one geospatial library on your platform, add that library under `dependencies:` before the `pip:` entry: conda installs it first and pip keeps it.

The package installs two commands, `hmp` and `hydromodpy`. They are the same program. Check the version:

```
hmp --version
```

To upgrade later, run `pip install --upgrade hydromodpy`.

## Get the solver binaries

MODFLOW 6, MODFLOW-NWT, MODPATH and MT3D-USGS are not part of the package. They are downloaded into the HydroModPy cache folder (`~/.cache/hydromodpy/bin/` on Linux) the first time a solver runs. To fetch them now, for example before going offline:

```
hmp install-binaries
```

`--subset mf6,mfnwt` takes only some of the programs and `--upgrade` downloads them again. Each version of HydroModPy names one MODFLOW release and the sha256 of its files, and a download that does not match is refused. The other options are in the command reference. The environment variable `HMP_BIN` points HydroModPy at a folder of your own binaries, flat, with the file names `mf6`, `mfnwt` and so on. When it is set, HydroModPy reads that folder and downloads nothing, and `hmp install-binaries` without `--to` fills it. The data still need the network once: a first run fills the cache of the workspace, and hmp run –frozen then refuses any new download.

## Check the install

```
hmp doctor
```

`hmp doctor` prints one line per check: Python, the core dependencies, the optional ones, each solver binary, and the workspace (`~/hydromodpy`, or the one you give with `--workspace`). It exits with an error code when a check is `KO`. A `WARN` does not change the exit code. On a fresh machine, the binaries and the workspace are `WARN`, because nothing exists yet:

```
WARN   solver:mf6                   not cached, not on PATH
       -> Run 'hmp install-binaries --subset mf6' (or let the first simulation trigger a lazy download).
WARN   workspace                    /home/you/hydromodpy does not exist
       -> Run 'hmp workspace init <workspace>' to scaffold one
```

Both are fixed by the next steps. The other options of the command are in the command reference. From Python:

```
import hydromodpy
print(hydromodpy.__version__)
```

## In a container

The repository builds a Docker image whose entry point is `hmp`. Run in Docker says how to pull it, run a request and start the server.

## On a Windows server

Put the projects under a short root such as `D:\hmp\`. A project writes paths up to 160 characters below its folder, and MODFLOW 6 and DuckDB open no path longer than 259 characters, so the project folder may hold 99 characters at most. A longer folder is refused when the project is created and when a run or a calibration session takes its folder, before anything is computed. A root like `D:\hmp\<organisation>\projects\<name>` with names of 40 characters is 97 characters long.

Fill `HMP_BIN` once, from the service account, with `hmp install-binaries`. The runs only read that folder, so it can be read-only for the account that starts them.

Give the server a fixed host name of 35 characters at most, and with Docker pass `docker run --hostname hmp-<code>` with a short code. A product being written carries the host name in its path, 125 characters plus the host name below the project folder, so a name of 35 characters reaches the 160 of the budget. `hmp-` and an organisation name of 40 characters would reach 169. A run that was interrupted is recognised as dead from its host name and its process id. A container that gets a new name at each start leaves every interrupted run `stale` until you use `--force`.

A delivery destination on a network share is written as a UNC path, `\\server\share\folder`, like a local one. Keep the project itself on a local disk and use the share only as a destination.

## Tested platforms

The continuous integration of the repository runs these jobs. A platform that is not listed may work; nothing checks it.

| Platform | Python | What runs there |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linux (Ubuntu) | 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 | Every push to `main` and `dev`: lint, architecture gate, fast tests. Python 3.13: unit and integration tests. Weekly: end-to-end tests and the full regression suite (3.12) |
| macOS | 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 | Weekly: unit tests, fast regression and analytical validation, on an install from a clone |
| Windows | 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 | The same weekly job as macOS |

The jobs install from a clone with `pip install -e ".[test,calibration]"`, not from PyPI, and they do not run the examples. The PETSc backend of the Boussinesq solver is Linux only, and its smoke test is the only job that installs from conda-forge. The other solvers do not need it. The workflows are in `.github/workflows/` and described in Reading a failing check.

## Install troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `hmp: command not found` | The environment that holds the command is not active, or the folder of pip scripts is not on `PATH` (a `pip install --user`). | Activate the environment. Or call the module, which is the same program: `python -m hydromodpy --version`. On Windows the command is `.venv\Scripts\hmp.exe`. |
| `ImportError: ... cannot open shared object file` when `gmsh` or `rasterio` loads, on Linux | A system library is missing. The Dockerfile of the repository installs `libglu1-mesa` for gmsh and `libexpat1` for rasterio. | On Debian or Ubuntu: `sudo apt-get install libglu1-mesa libexpat1`. |
| `Could not download the MODFLOW binaries of release <tag> from <address>: [Errno 111] Connection refused. ...` from `hmp install-binaries`, or `step 'run_solver' failed: NetworkError: Could not download ...` from the first run. Exit code 16 | The binaries are downloaded from GitHub and the machine has no direct route to it. | Behind a proxy, set `HTTPS_PROXY` (`requests` reads it). Offline, download the executables elsewhere, copy them in one flat folder and set `HMP_BIN` to it. |
| `<zip> downloaded from <address> hashes to <digest>, and HydroModPy pins sha256 <digest> for it. ...` from `hmp install-binaries` or the first run. Exit code 16 | The file that arrived is not the one this version was released with. HydroModPy keeps nothing of it. | Check the proxy and try again. If it stays, report it, and meanwhile set `HMP_BIN` to a folder of executables you trust. |
| `WARN solver:mf6 not cached, not on PATH` from `hmp doctor` | Nothing was downloaded yet. | Run `hmp install-binaries`, or run any simulation: the first one downloads. |
| Pip builds a library for a long time, or fails on `rasterio` or `pyproj` | No wheel for your Python or platform. | Use the conda tab above and let conda-forge provide that library. |

Every exit code and its category are listed in Exit codes.

## Optional extras

Add an extra between brackets: `pip install "hydromodpy[ide,mesh]"`.

- `ide`: JupyterLab, Spyder and PySide6.
- `calibration`: `cma` and `cmaes`, for the CMA-ES variants. The default `optuna` sampler is in the base install.
- `mesh`: `gmsh`.
- `mf6api`: `modflowapi` and `xmipy`.
- `viz`: `datashader` and `lttb`.
- `fair`: `pystac`. It checks the item that the STAC view of the annex writes (`hmp export --as stac`). That view and the PROV view live in the annex, so they work from a checkout of the repository only. The RO-Crate export of the package needs no extra.
- `metrics`: `psutil`.
- `sftp`: `paramiko`.
- `all`: `calibration`, `mesh`, `mf6api`, `viz`, `fair`, `metrics` and `sftp`. The extras for people who work on HydroModPy itself are not in it.

The extras `test`, `performance`, `profiling`, `docs` and `dev` are for people who work on HydroModPy itself; see Contribute. The generated list, with the packages and the version bounds, is on Optional dependencies.

## Shell completion

Optional. `hmp completion bash` prints a completion script for the shell, and `zsh` and `fish` print one for theirs. To load it in the current bash:

```
eval "$(hmp completion bash)"
```

The script asks `hmp` for its commands each time you press TAB, so it follows the commands that exist. In fish, pipe it to `source`: `hmp completion fish | source`.

<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/get-started/many-catchments.html -->
# Many catchments

A model tuned on one catchment runs on a hundred with the same project. The project keeps its configuration, swaps `[site]` for `[sites]` and a table with one row per catchment, and lists its recipes: the variants run on every site. The plan is every site crossed with every recipe, and each pair is a case named `<site>-<recipe>`, with its own folder under `runs/`.

This page walks through that project: declare the sites, check the plan, run it, follow it, rerun what failed, and read the summary. On a cluster runs the same plan on a Slurm cluster.

## Declare the sites

Start from the `project.toml` you tuned on one catchment. Remove `[site]`, then add `[sites]`: the table of sites, the recipes, and which columns of the table fill which keys.

```
# not checked: a [sites] project has no [site], so it does not load on top of example 04
[sites]
table = "sites.csv"
enabled = "enabled"
overrides = "site_overrides/"

[sites.recipes]
base = "project.toml"
k2e_5 = { file = "project.toml", set = { "flow.param.K.field.value" = 2e-5 } }
calibration = "calibration.toml"

[sites.bind]
"site.name" = "site"
"site.label" = "label"
"site.gauge" = "gauge"
"geographic.catchment.x_outlet" = "x_outlet"
"geographic.catchment.y_outlet" = "y_outlet"
```

```
site,label,gauge,x_outlet,y_outlet,enabled
J0014010,Nancon at Lecousse,J0014010,389285.910,6816518.749,true
J0170000,Couesnon at Romazy,J0170000,377120.000,6831410.000,false
```

- `sites.table` is a CSV, Parquet or GeoPackage file, read from the project root. Its columns are yours. Without a table, the plan reads `data/sites/catalog.csv` of the workspace, which `hmp site add` and `hmp site import` fill, and whose fixed columns (`site`, `label`, `gauge`, `uri`, `x_outlet`, `y_outlet`, `crs`, `tags`) need no `bind`.
- `sites.bind` maps a key of the configuration to a column. The key is written between quotes, in the grammar of `hmp run --set`; unquoted, TOML would read it as a nested table, and the file is refused. The cell is read by the type of the key it fills, and an empty cell leaves the key unbound.
- `sites.recipes` names each recipe: a file, or an inline table that changes a few keys of a file. A recipe name is letters, digits and underscores, because `-` separates the site from the recipe in the name of a case. `sites.recipes_table` reads the recipes from a CSV instead, one row per recipe.
- `sites.enabled`, `sites.include` and `sites.exclude` choose the sites of the plan without editing the table.
- `sites.overrides` is a folder of ordinary TOML files, one per site that needs a change of its own, such as a wider snapping distance for one outlet.

A key whose value depends on the catchment is marked varies by site in the reference: the outlet, the gauge, the paths of custom data. The plan refuses a project where one of these keys keeps a literal value with no `bind` and no override, and lists the keys: otherwise every catchment would run with the outlet of the first one.

The value of a key in a case comes from, the last one winning: the defaults, `project.toml`, the bound cells, `site_overrides/<site>.toml`, the keys the recipe file writes itself, then `--set` on the command line. A recipe beats the table on the keys it writes: `k2e_5` sets K on every site, which is what its name says.

A calibration is a recipe like any other. `calibration.toml` writes `base_config = "project.toml"`, its `[calibration]` and, if the bounds vary by site, its own `[sites.bind]` lines, which hold for that recipe only.

## Check the plan

```
hmp check project.toml
hmp run project.toml --dry-run
```

`hmp check` resolves every case and reports every error once, with the row and the column it comes from: `sites.csv:37 column x_outlet -> geographic.catchment.x_outlet: <message>`. The same error on many cases is one line, `100 cases: ...`. `--dry-run` writes nothing. It counts the cases, the solves and the peak of solves running together, and estimates the scratch space.

`hmp project plan .` writes the plan under `plan/<hash>/`: one resolved TOML file per case, which replays alone from any folder, and `cases.csv`, one row per case with the cells of its site. A plan is never rewritten in place: an edited table or recipe makes a new hash, and `plan/current` names the plan in force. `hmp run` writes the plan itself when the current one is out of date.

## Run it

```
hmp run project.toml
hmp run calibration.toml
```

The first command runs every case of the plan, the second the recipe file `calibration.toml` on every site. Each case runs in its own process, as `hmp run plan/<hash>/<case>.toml`. Before the solves, a `prepare` phase fetches the data of every case into the input cache of the workspace. Each file goes there with its sidecar, and one station is written at a time under a file lock, so two cases that need the same station leave one file and never compete for it.

`sites.run.parallel` is the number of solves that run side by side. A calibration case that solves five trials at once counts for five, at its widest phase, and a case wider than `sites.run.parallel` is refused without `--force`. A campaign that holds a calibration is also refused above 8 solves without `--force`. Eight solves held 6.5 GiB on a model of 21 000 cells, so about 0.8 GiB each, with no case lost and the same costs at widths 2, 4 and 8. Scale that memory to your model before you raise the width on a small machine. `sites.run.on_error` says whether a failed case stops the launch or lets the others go on.

## Follow it

```
hmp ls --plan
hmp project log . --failed
```

`hmp ls --plan` reads the `outcome.json` and the heartbeat of each case, never the index, and counts the cases by state: planned, running, completed, failed, and stale when a heartbeat is old. `hmp project log . --failed` prints the error of each failed case, one line each. The full log of a case is in `runs/<case>/logs/`.

## Rerun what failed

```
hmp run project.toml --only failed
hmp run project.toml --only failed --fresh
hmp run project.toml --only stale --force
```

A failed case keeps its folder. `--only failed` starts a new attempt in place: the earlier attempt moves under `runs/<case>/attempts/<n>/`, and the new one resumes from what the first one left. A calibration reopens its session `sessions/<case>/` and keeps its trials. `--fresh` files the whole earlier attempt away and starts over; for a calibration it opens a new session, `sessions/<case>_v2/`. A case whose heartbeat is old may still be running on another machine, so a stale case is only rerun with `--force`, when you know its process is dead. Without `--fresh`, a rerun never makes a `_v2`: a version is for a changed configuration, not for a second try.

## Read the results

```
hmp campaign collect .
hmp ls --by site --best nse
hmp diff J0014010-base J0014010-k2e_5 --to ../k_study
hmp publish . --to /srv/deliverables/my_project
```

`hmp campaign collect` writes `summary/`: `by_case` with one row per case, `by_site` with the best case of each site, a map of the sites as a GeoPackage, the cohort figures, the exports of each `[[sites.export]]` block, a report and a dated `README.md`. It is regenerated from the runs each time. `sites.summary` chooses the metrics, the parameters and the figures, and `sites.summary.best` which case of a site counts as its best: by default, a calibrated one.

The scores of a summary are those of the metric rule of each run: the gauge of the site and the window of `metrics.window`. `collect` refuses to rank cases scored on different windows unless you pass `--mixed-windows`, because their scores do not compare. Beside them, the objective of each calibration sits in its own columns, under its own name.

`hmp publish .` copies the project out of the tree, one folder per site and the summary, each with its `README.md` and its `PUBLICATION.json`.

A small project of this shape can hold two catchments of Brittany, with one simulation recipe and one short calibration.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/get-started/share-a-simulation.html -->
# Share a simulation with its data

A run, or a whole project, leaves your workspace as one archive that holds every file it read. A colleague imports it into their own workspace and runs it again. The data lands in their `data/`, next to their own files: identical bytes are not copied twice, and nothing of theirs is overwritten.

## A run, in four commands

On your machine, publish the run. A copy takes its results and its inputs by default:

```
hmp publish nancon_step5_export --to sim.tar --container tar
```

On the other machine, import it into a project, rerun it, and compare the rerun with the copy:

```
hmp catalog import sim.tar -w ~/hydromodpy/projects/lab
hmp catalog rerun nancon_step5_export -w ~/hydromodpy/projects/lab
hmp diff nancon_step5_export nancon_step5_export_v2 -w ~/hydromodpy/projects/lab
```

`hmp catalog import` prints the last two commands with the names they take in that project. On step 5 of example 04, the diff says `params: identical`, and the only metric that moves is the solve time. The heads of the two runs are the same.

The results are the stores of the run (`fields.zarr`, `tables.parquet`) and its `final_state/`, so the copy can be compared. `--without results` sends the configuration and the data only, and `--without inputs` sends the run without the files it read. The copy also holds the sealed mesh, `products.json` and a `.zenodo.json` that a Zenodo deposit reads. A replay that is not classed `bit` is not published, because a published copy states that it gives the sealed numbers: publish the source run, or a replay classed `bit`.

## What the inputs are

Every file the run read, as `inputs.json` names it, and nothing else:

| What the run read | Where it lands in the other workspace |
| --- | --- |
| A station series of your own (`hydrometry_custom_NANCON_..._D.csv`) | `data/hydrometry/`, with its row in `hydrometry_custom_LOC.csv` |
| The DEM of `[[data.dem.sources]]` (`source = "file"`), a GeoPackage of `[[data.hydrography.sources]]` | `data/dem/`, `data/hydrography/` |
| A file Hub’Eau, SIM2 or BD Topage delivered | the same folder, with its sidecar `<file>.json` and its station row |
| The `[site]` of the run | a row of `data/sites/catalog.csv` |

A declared folder is never copied whole: from `data/hydrometry/` the run takes the files of the stations it read. The archive stores each file once, under its sha256, and lists them in `INSTALL.toml`: the destination, the size, the sha256, the variable, the provider, the request, the licence and the digest of the sidecar. The examples of `hmp example add` use the same index.

A file a provider delivered is installed with its sidecar, which `INSTALL.toml` completes, so the file is a row of the data cache of the other workspace and a rerun reads it there instead of downloading it again. A run of example 04 that read Hub’Eau and BD Topage reruns with no network at all.

## The rules of an import

| What the workspace already holds | What the import does |
| --- | --- |
| Nothing at that path | Copies the file, with its sidecar |
| The same bytes at that path | Nothing: the file costs nothing |
| Other bytes at that path | Refuses, naming the path and both sha256 |
| The station with the same values | Nothing |
| The station with other values | Refuses, naming the registry and the station |
| A file of the data cache for the same station, from other bytes | Refuses, naming both files |
| A site of the same name with another outlet, or another name at the same outlet | Refuses, naming the site |

A refused import writes nothing: no file, no row, no run. Move your file aside, or import into another workspace.

## Licences

Each input carries the licence its provider states: `etalab-2.0` for Hub’Eau, SIM2 and BD Topage. A file of your own is `LicenseRef-undetermined` until you declare its licence, in the `license` key of its sidecar:

```
{"source": "file", "license": "CC-BY-4.0"}
```

`hmp publish --public` warns when the project declares no `[publication] license`, and when the copy carries its inputs it warns and names each input that has no licence. The copy is written anyway. It states `LicenseRef-undetermined` for what has no licence, and `INSTALL.toml` and the RO-Crate state the licence of each input as it stands.

## The configuration travels without your paths

The frozen `config.toml` of a run names each input with a path relative to the project root, typically under `inputs/`. Bare file names are no longer looked up in fallback workspace data folders. The record of the run, `manifest.json` and `inputs.json`, names them relative to the workspace (`data/dem/DEM_armorican_massif.tif`). No path of your machine leaves with the archive.

## A whole project

```
hmp publish nancon --package --to nancon.tar --with runs --with mesh --with fetched
hmp project import nancon.tar -w ~/hydromodpy
```

The archive holds the files you wrote at the root of the project (the TOML files, the scripts, the README, `sites.csv`, `site_overrides/`) and every data file those TOML files reference, on the same `INSTALL.toml`. On demand:

| Option | Adds |
| --- | --- |
| `--with runs` | the sealed runs, with their results and the files of your own they read |
| `--with sessions` | the calibration sessions |
| `--with mesh` | the mesh products the runs cite (`.hmp/products/`): gmsh cannot promise to draw the same mesh twice, this keeps the one the runs were computed on |
| `--with fetched` | the files the providers delivered to the runs, with their sidecars |

The project lands as `projects/<name>` of the workspace, with the same rules for its data. A name the workspace already holds is refused; `--name` gives another one. The runs keep their names.

## Without importing

`hmp replay <copy> -w <project>` replays a published copy from the bytes it carries (Replay a run).

## Check an archive

```
hmp publish --verify sim.tar
```

compares every file with the sha256 the archive lists. `hmp catalog import` and `hmp project import` run the same check before they write anything.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/how-to/deliver-exports.html -->
# Deliver exports

An `[[export]]` block that names `deliver_to` sends the files of that block once the run is sealed, and each copy is recorded in the run. I use it to hand a partner the files of a run without copying them by hand, and to keep a remote copy on an FTP server.

## Name the destination

`deliver_to` takes a list of destinations. Each one is a local or UNC path, or an `ftp://`, `ftps://` or `sftp://` address.

| Form | Example | Where the file lands |
| --- | --- | --- |
| local folder, absolute, ending in `/` | `/data/depot/` | `.../depot/head_last.tif` |
| local file, absolute | `/data/depot/head_last.tif` | at that path |
| UNC folder, Windows | `\\server\share\depot\` | under the share |
| FTP folder | `ftp://gis.example.org/depot/` | under the remote folder |
| FTP file, with a port | `ftp://gis.example.org:2121/head_last.tif` | at that name |
| FTPS folder | `ftps://gis.example.org/depot/` | under the remote folder |
| SFTP folder | `sftp://data.example.org/depot/` | under the remote folder |

```
[[export]]
variable = "head"
time = "last"
file = "head_last.tif"
deliver_to = ["/data/depot/", "ftp://gis.example.org/depot/"]
```

A folder address ends with `/`. A file address names one file, so the block writes `file = "..."`. A view that names neither `folder` nor `file` is written at the root of the run, outside `exports/`, and is refused for delivery. Give it a `folder` or a `file`.

A destination is never created. The subfolders of the file under `exports/` are, so `/data/depot/` must exist and be writable, and `/data/depot/sub/` is made when the file is `sub/head.tif`. A typo stops the run before any calculation, not after the solve.

## `credentials.toml`

A remote address takes its identity from `credentials.toml`. The file sits outside every project and every workspace, readable by its owner alone (mode 600, and a group or other read bit is refused). Its default place is `<state home>/credentials.toml`, usually `~/.local/state/hydromodpy/credentials.toml` on Linux, and `--credentials PATH` names another.

The file holds one `[[host]]` block per address prefix. The longest prefix that matches a destination gives its identity, so no user name is ever written in a project file.

```
[[host]]
prefix = "ftp://gis.example.org/"
user = "partner"
password = "the-password"

[[host]]
prefix = "ftps://gis.example.org:2121/"
user = "partner"
password_file = "/home/me/.config/gis-password"

[[host]]
prefix = "sftp://data.example.org/"
user = "me"
key_file = "/home/me/.ssh/id_ed25519"
host_fingerprint = "SHA256:the-fingerprint-the-server-shows"
```

A prefix carries the port when the address names one, so `ftps://gis.example.org:2121/` answers `ftps://gis.example.org:2121/depot/` and `ftps://gis.example.org/` does not. The password is written in clear or named by `password_file`. An `sftp://` address needs the `sftp` extra (`pip install 'hydromodpy[sftp]'`), a password or a `key_file`, and the `host_fingerprint` the server shows. The `key_file` is an ed25519, ECDSA or RSA private key, in OpenSSH or PEM form, without a passphrase. A clear `ftp://` sends its password in clear and warns once per destination, so use `ftps://` when the server offers it (explicit TLS, `PROT P`).

## The check before the run

Every destination is checked before the first step. A host is public by default, and `--allow-host HOST` names one. A call that names hosts reaches only those, which is the way to reach a private address such as `127.0.0.1`. A local folder must exist and be writable. A remote address needs its `[[host]]` block, and the server must answer and enter the folder. A refusal stops the run with one sentence, and nothing has been computed.

```
hmp run nancon_daily.toml \
  --credentials ~/.local/state/hydromodpy/credentials.toml --allow-host 127.0.0.1
```

## Read the states

Each file of a block and each destination make one pair. The run appends a `pending` line, pushes the file through `<name>.part`, renames it and compares its size, in at most three attempts, 1 s then 2 s apart. A failed attempt removes its `.part`. The last line of a pair is `delivered` or `failed`, with the sha256, the bytes and the number of attempts. A `failed` line carries the sentence that says what went wrong. A file of `exports/` that cannot be read gives a `failed` line with one attempt and no sha256 or bytes.

A delivery failure does not fail the run. The run stays sealed and completed, `hmp run` exits 0, and the log holds a `WARNING` for the file and its address. `hmp show <run>` lists the deliveries after the exports, and the library reads `run.deliveries`.

## Deliver again

```
hmp export nancon_daily --deliver --credentials ~/.local/state/hydromodpy/credentials.toml
```

It reads the sealed `config.toml` and the lines of the run, checks each destination against the hosts and folders this call allows as the run did, and warns of a clear `ftp://` password. A refused destination gives a `failed` line. It sends every pair whose last line is not `delivered`, and sends again a delivered file whose bytes changed since, because a promotion or `--regen` rewrites `exports/`. It prints one line per pair and `Delivered 2 of 3 file(s)`, and exits 1 when a line stays `failed`, 0 otherwise. `--format json` prints `{"deliveries": [...]}`. `--deliver` takes no variable, no `--list`, no `--regen` and no export option, and is refused with exit code 2. The library call is `hmp.export(run, deliver=True)`.

A run with windows delivers each window as it is sealed, so a fixed remote file keeps the last window. A calibration delivers the run it promoted for each case, and only once the session is `completed`. A session that stops early or promotes no run delivers nothing and logs a `WARNING`.

## What a published copy keeps

`hmp publish` copies the run without `deliver_to`. The key is removed from `config.toml` and `config.resolved.toml`, and `exports/index.json` never records it. A copy never delivers anything.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/how-to/long-transient-runs-in-windows.html -->
# Long transient runs in windows

A transient run over many years in daily periods can take hours. When I cut it into windows, each window is a run of its own, sealed when it ends. A stop, a crash or a power cut costs me the window in progress and nothing before it. This page says how I cut a run, how I play it, how I stop it and how I start it again.

## Cut the run

I add a length to `[simulation.time]`. The length is a calendar length written with its unit. The steady first period takes the recharge of the first period, for the reason given below.

```
[flow]
flow_regime = "transient"

[simulation.time]
start_datetime = "2000-01-01"
end_datetime = "2002-12-31"
step_value = "1 day"
window_length = "1 year"

[flow.sinks_sources.recharge]
first_clim = "first"
```

The windows start at `start_datetime` and follow one another. The last one ends with the simulation and may be shorter. If I want hydrological years, I start the simulation on the first of October.

Every edge between two windows must fall on the end of a stress period. With daily periods any length in days, months or years does. With periods of seven days, `"1 month"` is refused, and the message names the edge and the two period ends around it. I change the length or the step.

A run in windows needs a transient flow and a backend that can start from a saved state, which is MODFLOW 6 today. It cannot carry a transport process and it is not a calibration trial. A steady first period that takes the mean recharge or ETP (`first_clim = "mean"`, the default) would average window 1 only, so it is refused too. I set `first_clim` to `"first"` or a number, or I turn `flow.first_period_steady` off and start from `[flow.ic] kind = "steady_state"`, which the chain computes over the whole simulation. The file is refused with the reason when it is read.

## Play the windows

`hmp run project.toml` plays the windows one after the other. Each one is a sealed run named after the run with `_w1`, `_w2` and so on. From ten windows the numbers have two digits, so the names sort in order (`island_w01`, `island_w02`). Window 1 starts as the run in one piece would start, from its starting heads. Window `k` starts from the `final_state/` of window `k - 1`, and the run records that folder and its digest as an input.

I can play one window with `window = 2` in `[simulation.time]`. It needs window 1 sealed first. Without it the run is refused and says to play window 1 first, or to set `window = "all"`.

The heads are meant to equal the run in one piece to the last bit. The page on the groundwater flow problem gives the measure, and the one case where the difference is not zero, SFR with storage.

## Start again after a stop

`hmp run project.toml` again gives back the windows that are sealed with the same request, and says so for each one. It resumes the window that stopped and plays the ones after it. A window resumes at the step it stopped in. A stop in the solve plays the solve again from its first time step.

To stop a run on purpose I use `hmp stop`, from any terminal.

```
hmp stop island_w3
```

The command writes a flag in the run folder and returns at once. The run reads it between two steps, and MODFLOW 6 through libmf6 also between two time steps. The run ends `aborted`, and the chain stops with it. `hmp stop` works on a calibration session the same way.

`hmp run project.toml --resume island_w3` asks for the resume of that window and refuses when something changed since the stop, an input or a key of the file. The refusal says so. A plain `hmp run project.toml` starts the window over in that case. Without the file, `hmp run --resume island_w3` reads the configuration the window froze in its folder, resumes it and plays the windows after it.

The `config.toml` of a sealed window is the request of that window alone. `hmp replay island_w2` replays window 2 from the final state of the run its `inputs.json` names, so window 1 must still be in the project.

## Read the time of each window

Each run writes `profile.json`, the time and the memory of each step, solve, figure and export. `hmp show island_w2` prints the total, the start-up, the solve of each run of the plan, the three longest steps and what was reused. A run from version 2.0 has no profile, and the command says so and prints the solve time its seal holds.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/how-to/plan-and-score-experiments.html -->
# Plan experiments and score them later

A plan of experiments runs one model at many points of a box of parameters. This page shows how to draw the points, then how to score the stored runs again on any window, without a new solve.

## Draw the points

A `[sites]` project can draw its own recipes. `[sites.design]` names a method, a number of points, a seed and the parameters that move. Each point becomes a case, named `<site>-p0001`, `<site>-p0002` and so on. For `lhs` the lot is part of the name, `b1p0001`. The drawn values go to `cases.csv` of the plan.

```
# not checked: a [sites] project has no [site], so it does not load on top of example 04
[sites]
table = "sites.csv"

[sites.recipes]
base = "project.toml"

[sites.design]
method = "sobol"
n = 64
seed = 1
recipe = "base"

[sites.design.parameters.K]
path = "flow.param.K.field.value"
bounds = [1e-7, 1e-3]
sampling = "log_uniform"

[sites.design.parameters.Sy]
path = "flow.param.Sy.field.value"
bounds = [1e-4, 0.35]
sampling = "log_uniform"
```

`sampling` is always written, because a uniform default on a parameter that spans three decades would put almost every point in the top decade. `method` is `sobol`, `lhs` or `grid`. `seed` is required for `sobol` and `lhs`, so that two expansions give the same points and the same case names. Doubling a Sobol `n` keeps the first points, and a second lot of `lhs` (`n = [60, 60]`) keeps the first one. A run that finished is not run again. `hmp check` and `hmp run --dry-run` read the design like any other plan.

## Score one run

A run stores its simulated and observed series. `run.score` pairs them as the seal did and gives one row per station, variable, metric and window.

```
import hydromodpy as hmp

project = hmp.open("my_project")
run = project.runs()[0]

table = run.score(
    windows={"dry": ("2016-06-01", "2016-10-31"), "all": (None, None)},
    metrics=["nse", "kge"],
)
```

`windows` maps a name to a start and an end, either one may be `None`. Without `windows` the run is scored on the window of its own `[metrics]`, and the numbers are those of its seal. Without `metrics` every metric of a series pair is computed. `station` picks one station. The columns include `value`, `n_samples` and `n_sim_nan`, the number of periods lost to a missing simulated value.

`months` keeps the periods that fall in the given calendar months, after the pairing.

```
summer = run.score(windows={"w": ("2010-01-01", "2018-12-31")}, months=[6, 7, 8, 9])
```

A mean period counts when all its days are in the months. A metric that needs consecutive days, such as `bfi_gap`, is refused on a masked window. `nse_seasonal` needs two full cycles in what is left.

## Score a set of runs

`runs.score` takes the same arguments and stacks the rows of every run, with the parameters of each run as columns. `runs.timeseries` stacks the stored series themselves.

```
runs = project.runs()
table = runs.score(windows={"w": ("2016-01-01", "2018-12-31")}, metrics=["nse"])
series = runs.timeseries(station="J0014010", variable="discharge")
```

A run with no series at that station gives no row, with a warning.

## Score the stream network

`run.score_network` scores the stream network of a stored run as a calibration trial scores it, from the settings the run sealed or the defaults. The table has one row per quantity, bound and year. The numbers equal those of a trial when the run stored its fields with `[simulation.results.persistence] field_precision = "exact"`. With the default `compact` precision, a cell right at the seepage threshold can flip, so write `exact` in the plan when the network scores matter.

```
network = runs.score_network(window=("2001-01-01", "2010-12-31"))
```

The network metrics `distance_gap` and `distance_mean` are given here and not by `score`, as quantities such as `J_signed` and `D_so`.

## Score a whole workspace

`hmp.index` opens a workspace. Its `score` and `score_network` run the set methods on every project and add a `project` column in front.

```
workspace = hmp.index("~/hydromodpy")
table = workspace.score(windows={"w": ("2016-01-01", "2018-12-31")}, metrics=["nse"])
network = workspace.score_network()
```

## Score at collect

`hmp campaign collect` can do the same for every run of a `[sites]` project. Each `[[sites.summary.window]]` block names a window, and the collect writes `summary/scores.parquet` with the metrics of `[sites.summary]`.

```
# not checked: part of a [sites] project
[[sites.summary.window]]
name = "dry-summers"
start = "2010-01-01"
end = "2018-12-31"
months = [6, 7, 8, 9]
```

## Look at the plane of two parameters

The figure `parameter_space` draws each run as a point on log axes, coloured by one score. `variable` names the two parameters, and a third name picks the score. It is a metric of `score`, or a quantity of `score_network`. `time` gives the window. `station` picks one station, or the bound of a network quantity scored on two bounds.

```
runs.figure("parameter_space", variable=["K", "Sy", "kge"], time=["2016-01-01", "2018-12-31"])
runs.figure("parameter_space", variable=["K", "Sy", "J_signed"])
```

A ring marks a run whose simulated series has missing values in the window, because its score covers fewer periods. The months mask is not a figure option. Score with `months` and read the table.

## Read a ridge in a calibration

A calibration that runs a `lhs` or a `grid` phase writes `ridge` in the report of the phase. It takes the best fifth of the trials, at least five, and reads them in search space, each axis scaled to the width of its bounds. It gives the Spearman correlation of each pair and `axis_ratio`, the square root of the ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue of their covariance. A round cloud gives a ratio near one. A narrow cloud along a diagonal gives a large ratio and a correlation near one, which says the data fix a combination of the parameters and not each one.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/how-to/replay-a-run.html -->
# Replay a run

A replay plays a sealed run again and says whether it gives the same numbers. I use it to check a run I kept, to read a run a colleague sent me, and to see what a new version changed. The run it reads is never rewritten: the replay is a new version beside it.

## Play it

```
hmp replay runs/nancon_daily
```

The reference is a run directory inside a project, or a published copy. A copy outside a project needs the project it goes to:

```
hmp replay ~/shared/nancon_copy -w ~/projects/nancon
```

A published copy carries its own bytes. The replay reads your files under `inputs/` of the copy. It installs the files a provider delivered by their sha256 in the workspace of the project, with their sidecars and their station rows, then plays the run from the data cache. A file already at that path with other bytes refuses the replay and nothing is written, and without `-w` a copy is refused.

A run folder copied by hand carries no such bytes. The replay reads its inputs from the project `-w` names, each at the digest its seal records. Nothing is ever written in the copy.

The replay writes a new version of the same stem, `runs/nancon_daily_v2`, and seals it. It reads the configuration the run sealed and the digests of `inputs.json`, so an input whose bytes moved is refused with both digests. A URL is contacted only when the cache lacks the file. Its bytes are not pinned, so values that move with them show in the class of the replay.

I add `--strict` when a difference must stop me:

```
hmp replay runs/nancon_daily --strict
```

With `--strict` a replay that differs ends failed, its fields and tables stay readable, and no seal is written. Without it the replay is sealed whatever it found, and the class it wrote says what happened.

## Read the lineage
