The seal of the replay carries `lineage.kind = "replay"` and `parent_sim_id`, the `sim_id` of the source. Its block `lineage.replay` holds what it compared and what it found.

| field | says |
| --- | --- |
| `basis` | `float64` for a seal of this version, `stored` for a run of a pre-release, `none` when the source carries no values |
| `class` | `bit` when every value hashes the same, `deviation` otherwise, and none without a basis |
| `differs` | each key that differs, with `max_abs` and `rel_l2` of the whole field and the precision of the values it read |
| `added`, `removed` | the keys present on one side only |
| `producer` | each field of `provenance.json` that differs, with the sealed value and the value found |
| `changes` | the entries of the register of changes the source crossed |
| `strict` | whether I asked for the refusal |

On a run of this version the comparison reads the value digests of the source seal, one per field and per column of a quantity, taken in double precision. A field that is rounded for storage is hashed before the rounding, so `bit` holds the calculated value and not the stored one. On a run of a pre-release of 2.0 the comparison reads the stored values of both sides, so `bit` holds to the rounding of 2^-17 on a compact precision and to the last bit on an exact one, which is the case of most of the reference runs.

The README of the replay says the class in its lineage section, and `lineage.replay` in `runs/nancon_daily_v2/manifest.json` keeps the whole record. `hmp show` gives the summary of the run beside it.

## What a class does not refuse

A configuration that moved does not refuse a replay. The keys that differ from the sealed `config.resolved.toml` go in `lineage.drift`, and the class measures what they changed. A default this version added, absent from the sealed file and at its own default, is not a difference. A solver binary that differs goes in `lineage.replay.producer`, with a line in the log, and the replay runs. A replay classed `deviation` is sealed all the same, and `hmp publish` refuses it, because the level of publication is read in the lineage.

Two things still refuse. An input whose digest differs is refused before anything runs, because the run cannot read the bytes it sealed. A folder with no seal is refused, because there is nothing to compare with.

## Replay a run of a pre-release

A run sealed by a pre-release opens as it is and replays like any other. The comparison reads its stored values, so its `basis` is `stored`. A run sealed by a pre-release has no stable reader and is refused with its sentence; I play its `config.toml` again if I still have it.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/how-to/run-in-docker.html -->
# Run in Docker

The `Dockerfile` of the repository builds a slim image whose entry point is `hmp`, so a container runs the same program as the command line. The image holds HydroModPy with every extra, the solver binaries, which `hmp install-binaries` fetched under `/opt/hmp/bin` at the build and checked against their pinned sha256, and the HTTP server of the repository. The versions of the build are kept in `/opt/hmp/constraints.txt`. Each version tag publishes the image on the GitHub container registry, tagged with the version, and as `latest` when the version is not a pre-release. Pull it by its tag:

```
docker pull ghcr.io/hydromodpy/hydromodpy:2.0.0
docker inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' ghcr.io/hydromodpy/hydromodpy:2.0.0
```

The second command prints the image name, `@` and its digest, `sha256:` followed by 64 hex characters. Or build the image from a clone, with the tag you give it:

```
docker build --build-arg HMP_IMAGE_TAG=2.0.0 -t hydromodpy:2.0.0 .
```

A run request is one JSON file that holds the configuration under `config`. A container plays it from a project folder you mount, and `--base` names the folder its relative paths are read from:

```
docker run --rm -v "$PWD/project:/project" hydromodpy:2.0.0 run /project/request.json --base /project
```

The run folder, `request.json` included, is written under `/project/runs/`. The request itself is described in Build a frontend. An image cannot hold its own digest, so pass it with `-e HMP_IMAGE_DIGEST=sha256:<digest>`. For a pulled image, take the part after `@` of the `RepoDigests` line above. For an image built here, `docker inspect --format '{{.Id}}' hydromodpy:2.0.0` gives it. A run then writes the tag and the digest of the image in its `provenance.json`. A replay of the run with `hmp replay <run> --strict` gives the same numbers to the bit only in the same image, on the same family of processor and with the number of BLAS threads fixed, for example with `-e OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 -e OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1`. The CI plays such a replay in each image it builds. The server needs the digest to start:

```
docker run -d --hostname hmp-server -p 8765:8765 -v /srv/hmp:/project \
  -e HMP_IMAGE_DIGEST=sha256:<digest> \
  --entrypoint python hydromodpy:2.0.0 -m hydromodpy_server --root /project --host 0.0.0.0
```

Serve over HTTP describes its routes.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/how-to/run-step-by-step.html -->
# Run step by step

A run can stop after any step and continue later. This page shows how I look at the ground of a model before the solve, draw a figure at that point and then finish the run. To build a model in memory and change it, see Work in the lab.

## Stop at a step

`hmp.run(project, until_step="prepare_solver", name="demo")` plays the steps up to `prepare_solver` and stops. It gives back an outcome, and `hmp.open(outcome.run_dir)` opens the partial run. `run.steps` lists the steps done, from `validate` to `prepare_solver`, and `run_solver` is not in it. The run has no seal yet.

`run.read("topography")` then reads the ground of every cell, before any solve. This works for a backend that builds a cell column. The heads do not exist yet, so reading them is refused.

## Draw a figure at that step

A figure of the `[[display.figure]]` table says when it is drawn with `when`. The value `"after:prepare_solver"` draws it as soon as that step is done. A figure whose data comes at `extract`, such as the heads, cannot be drawn there. `hmp.check` refuses it and names the step.

```
[display]
enabled = true

[[display.figure]]
variable = "topography"
when = "after:prepare_solver"
```

## Continue and seal

`hmp.run(project, name="demo")` with the same name continues the run in place. It plays the steps that are missing and seals the run. Nothing is played twice.

Each window is one attempt on the same run folder, and the sealed run records the number of the last attempt.

## Play it again

If I play the same calls again with no change, each window gives back the run already done. No new version such as `demo_v2` appears. This holds when I do not pass `from_step`, `resume` or `force`.

## An example

The lines below come from a test that runs on every change.

```
import hydromodpy as hmp

outcome = hmp.run("island.toml", until_step="prepare_solver", name="demo")
first = hmp.open(outcome.run_dir)  # a partial run, not sealed yet
steps = first.steps
print(steps)  # the steps done so far
ground = first.read("topography")  # the ground of every cell, read before the solve
last = hmp.run("island.toml", name="demo")  # continues in place and seals
again = hmp.run("island.toml", name="demo")  # unchanged, gives the run back
```


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/how-to/use-your-own-files.html -->
# Use your own files

HydroModPy reads elevation models, hydrography, geology, structures, forcings and observation series from public APIs or from files on disk. When I bring my own data, I place the files under the `inputs/` folder of my project and declare them in the project configuration.

## Where files sit

I store local data files under `<project>/inputs/`. Paths written in the configuration are relative to the project root, so they remain valid when the project moves or when I share it with a collaborator.

For example, a digital elevation model in `inputs/elevation.tif` is declared with `path = "inputs/elevation.tif"`.

HydroModPy resolves relative paths against the project root only. A bare file name such as `path = "elevation.tif"` is not looked up in the data folders of the workspace. When a bare name is not found at the project root, the run stops, and the message gives the form to write.

## Files shared by several projects

A file that several projects of the workspace read, such as a regional elevation model or a regional stream network, sits in the data folder of the workspace, in the folder of its variable. I name it with `workspace:`, and HydroModPy reads it in that folder.

```
[[data.dem.sources]]
source = "file"
path = "workspace:regional_dem_aber.tif"        # data/dem/regional_dem_aber.tif

[[data.hydrography.sources]]
source = "file"
path = "workspace:regional_stream_network.shp"  # data/hydrography/regional_stream_network.shp
```

A station folder is the folder of the variable itself, `path = "workspace:."`. It holds `hydrometry_file_LOC.csv`, with the id, x, y, CRS and unit of each station, and one chronicle per station, `hydrometry_file_<id>_<start>_<end>_<step>.csv`. For hydrometry, recharge and runoff, a source without `station_ids` reads the gauge of `[site]`. The files a provider cached in the same folder carry the name of the provider, such as `hydrometry_hubeau_...`, and this source does not read them.

When a folder holds two chronicles of one station, a monthly and a daily series for example, the run stops and lists them. I then name the one to read, and HydroModPy reads it with the location file of its folder.

```
[[data.recharge.sources]]
source = "file"
path = "workspace:recharge_file_NANCON_20000101_20021231_M.csv"
```

A named chronicle belongs to one station, the one of `station_ids` or of the gauge of `[site]`. A file whose name says another station is refused. After the id, a chronicle name holds nothing, a step such as `_D`, or the two dates and the step, so `hydrometry_file_NANCON_REA_...` is a chronicle of station `NANCON_REA` and never of `NANCON`.

The name does not depend on where the project sits in the workspace, and it follows `[workspace] data_dir` when the data folder lives elsewhere, on a shared disk for example. A run writes the same form in its frozen configuration and in its manifest, so the index of the project lists the file under this name with its digest. The parameter reference gives the folder on the card of each key that accepts a workspace name.

A path cannot start with a URL scheme such as `https://`. When data reside on a remote server, I declare them with `source = "url"` instead.

## The `file` source

Local files are declared with `source = "file"`. This source replaces the earlier `source = "custom"` and works for rasters, vector layers, tabular data and station chronicle folders.

```
[[data.dem.sources]]
source = "file"
path = "inputs/elevation.tif"
```

The `file` source reads files directly from disk without copying them into the data cache. Before the run begins, HydroModPy calculates the SHA-256 digest of each input file to record its provenance in the run manifest and seal.

If an older configuration still writes `source = "custom"`, `hmp doctor --fix-config` rewrites it to `source = "file"`.

## The `url` source

When a file is hosted online, I can declare it directly with `source = "url"`. The `url` source applies to variables that are read from a single file, such as digital elevation models, geology rasters or vectors, stream networks, structures, and single-file climate grids.

```
[[data.dem.sources]]
source = "url"
url = "https://example.org/data/dem.tif"
sha256 = "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef"
```

The URL source downloads the remote file once into the local data cache under `data/<variable>/` and creates an accompanying JSON sidecar. The simulation run then reads the cached file in the same way as a local `file` source.

HTTPS is accepted directly. An unencrypted HTTP URL is accepted only when I pin its expected SHA-256 digest with the `sha256` parameter.

When a download is already cached, HydroModPy sends a HEAD request to check the remote ETag and Last-Modified headers before downloading again. If the headers match, or if the pinned SHA-256 digest is already present in the cache, the cached file is reused without downloading.

Network downloads are constrained by execution bounds. The default byte limit is 2 GiB. Private network IP addresses are refused unless the host is explicitly permitted with the `--allow-host` command-line flag or the execution environment.

## Elevation model declaration

In earlier versions, a digital elevation model was declared through `dem_init_path` under `[geographic.catchment]`. This parameter has been removed.

The elevation model is now declared under `[[data.dem.sources]]` with `source = "file"` or `source = "url"`.

```
[[data.dem.sources]]
source = "file"
path = "inputs/dem.tif"
```

The pre-processing pipeline resolves the digital elevation model from this table and passes the resolved path to the catchment delineation steps.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/how-to/work-in-the-lab.html -->
# Work in the lab

`hmp.Lab` builds a model in memory, one step at a time, and lets you look at it, change it and solve it again. Use it when you write or debug a model from Python. Use `hmp.run` when the configuration is ready and you want a stored run.

A lab opens a `Project` and plays the same steps a run plays, from `validate` to `run_solver`. It writes no run folder and seals nothing. `lab.project` gives the project back, so a calibration or a spin-up still goes through it. The reference page of Lab lists every member.

## Go step by step

`hmp.Lab("project.toml")` builds nothing. `hmp.Lab(hmp.open("runs/my_run"))` opens the project of a run with the configuration the run kept, sealed or stopped after its facts, and builds nothing either. `lab.advance` then builds the model of that run again in memory, because a run stores results and not its model. `lab.set` starts from the configuration of the run, and `lab.run` writes a new run in the same project. `lab.advance()` plays the next step and `lab.advance("build_mesh")` plays every missing step up to that one. `lab.steps` is a table with one row per step, with its status (`built`, `stale` or `pending`), its last duration in seconds, the sections of the configuration it reads and the objects forced on it.

`lab.state` holds nine objects by name: `config`, `geographic`, `domain`, `flow`, `data`, `mesh`, `model`, `plan` and `solves`. Before its step plays, `geographic`, `domain`, `flow`, `mesh`, `model` and `plan` are `None`. After a change, a stale object stays in the state until its step plays again. Reading `lab.state` computes nothing. Each object prints a short summary at the prompt. `lab.state` names the nine objects on one line each. `lab.state.mesh` says how many cells it has, whether they form a regular grid and where its arrays are, with one row per cell on any mesh. `lab.state.model.properties` gives the value of each parameter. A sealed run does the same with `run.mesh` and `run.parameters`. The mesh of a lab and the mesh of a run answer the same calls: `n_cells`, `cell_centers()`, `cell_areas()` and `structured_shape`. `lab.solve()` plays up to `run_solver` and gives one solved run per run of the plan. `lab.read("head")` solves what is stale, then reads a variable of the solve as an array with one row per period and one column per cell, and writes nothing. The solver answers from its own files: `head` is the water table of every cell, `discharge` the flow that leaves the catchment, and `saturated_thickness` and `release_flux` hold one value per cell. `time` takes `"first"`, `"last"` or the index of a period. A run reads every stored variable, so keep the model with `lab.run` to read the others.

## Build the configuration section after section

`hmp.Lab({"geographic": {...}, "data": {...}}, base="my_project")` reads the dict as `hmp.Project(dict)` does, with the same refusals and the same old key names. When a run would lack content, such as `[simulation]`, the lab keeps the dict as a draft. `lab.set` adds the other sections when you need them, such as `lab.set(domain={...})` before `build_mesh` and `lab.set(flow={...}, simulation={...})` before `run_solver`. In a draft every `lab.set` reads the configuration again and plays the steps again from the start, so the data plan, the types of data and the solver always follow what is written. `lab.advance` refuses to play a step that reads a section the draft lacks, and names the step and the section. Today that is `[simulation]`, which `setup_process` reads to plan the runs. `lab.run` and `lab.write_config` refuse while the draft lacks what `hmp run` asks of a file, and list it, for example a real catchment without `[site]`. No run starts from a draft, so `lab.project.simulate()` refuses it too. Once the configuration is complete the lab works as a lab of a file, and a path that no step reads is refused.

## Change a value

`lab.set(K=5e-5)` changes the configuration of the lab. A key is a short name of `hmp config targets`, a dotted path of the TOML such as `flow.param.K.field.value`, or a whole section such as `data={...}`. The new configuration is checked at once, and when your changes bring the configuration back to the file, the lab forgets them, so a run seals none. `lab.set` returns the built steps that became stale, and `lab.steps` shows them. The next `advance` plays again from the first of them. `lab.config` is a frozen copy of the configuration with your changes.

## Force an object

Some objects cannot be said in the configuration, for example a mesh you built by hand. `lab.force("mesh", my_mesh)` puts it in the state. The lab keeps it each time its step plays, and the steps after it become stale. `lab.force` accepts `geographic`, `domain`, `flow`, `data`, `mesh` and `model`. `lab.release("mesh")` forgets the value, and the step builds the object again. While an object is forced, `lab.set` warns that this object does not follow the change.

## Look inside a function

`lab.capture` records the local variables and the returned value of the functions you name, each time one returns. A target is `"path/file.py:function"` or `"path/file.py:Class.method"`, and the file is matched by the end of its path. The block gives a dict from each target to the list of its calls. The hook slows the solve by about a factor of two, so name few targets.

## Keep the result

`lab.run("name")` seals the model of the lab as a run of the project, as `Project.simulate` does, and gives the run back. When `run_solver` is built and up to date, the run takes the solve of the lab and does not solve again, so its seal, its stored heads and its `profile.json` are those of `hmp.run` with the same changes. It uses the configuration of the lab, so it refuses to start while an object is forced. Release the object, or say the change with `lab.set`. A run made from a reopened run records its changes against the configuration of that run, whose `config.toml` is complete, so the new run replays. A project that keeps solver files solves again at `lab.run`, because the export keeps only the files of the run itself. The run cleans the solver files, so after it the steps from `prepare_solver` on are stale in the lab.

`lab.write_config("project_tuned.toml")` writes the configuration of the lab, with its changes, as a TOML file you can run with `hmp run`. `lab.close()` removes the scratch folder of the lab, and `with hmp.Lab(...) as lab:` does it for you.

## An example

The lines below come from a test that runs on every change.

```
lab = hmp.Lab(island)  # opens the project, builds nothing
lab.advance("build_mesh")  # plays validate to build_mesh in memory
cells = lab.state.mesh.n_cells  # the objects of the engine, by name
stale = lab.set(K=2e-5)  # a change returns the built steps it made stale
assert stale == ()  # nothing was built after the mesh yet
results = lab.solve()  # plays what is missing, up to run_solver
head = lab.read("head", time="last")  # a variable of the solve, one column per cell
lab.set(K=3e-5)
assert lab.steps.status[lab.steps.step == "run_solver"].item() == "stale"
lab.force("model", lab.state.model)  # keep this model, whatever the file says
assert lab.steps.forced[lab.steps.step == "prepare_solver"].item() == ("model",)
lab.release("model")  # the model is built from the configuration again
with lab.capture(WELL_CELL) as seen:  # watch a function the solve crosses
    lab.solve()
well = seen[WELL_CELL][0]["locals"]["well_id"]
written = lab.write_config(tmp_path / "lab.toml")  # the file of what the lab holds
```

## Limits

The lab plays in memory up to `run_solver`. The steps after it belong to a run, so `lab.advance` refuses them and names `lab.run`. `lab.solve(build_only=True)` builds each flow run without solving it, and a later `lab.solve(built)` solves these runs. That route plays no transport run. Two labs on one project work in separate scratch folders, so they do not disturb each other.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/how-to/write-calibration-phases.html -->
# Write calibration phases

This page shows how to split a calibration into phases and how to use a published protocol that writes them for you.

A calibration runs as one or more phases. A phase says which parameters it moves, in which flow regime, and against which objective blocks with which share for each. The search method follows from what is scored. A signed criterion (`distance_gap`) on one parameter in log space is a zero to find, searched by bisection (the stopping rule, the two roots and the budget arithmetic are in Downslope distance between two networks, section “How a search reaches the zero”). Anything else is a cost to minimize, by Nelder-Mead. That choice applies to a phase and, the same way, to a calibration with no phases at all (`optim.optimizer.choose_method`, read through `CalibrationConfig.method_for`). A `method` is written only to choose otherwise (`"cma_es"`, `"optuna"`, `"grid"` and so on). A protocol is a named recipe tied to a publication. It writes the phases of a published method, cites it, and lets the user set its options but not its sequence. Everything a protocol does, phases written by hand can say too, and `hmp calibrate FILE --expand` prints the phases a protocol writes, as TOML to start from.

One rule links the phases, in declaration order. A phase moves the parameters it lists. Every other parameter holds the last value an earlier settled phase found for it, or the value of the model file when no phase has calibrated it yet. A phase that lists a parameter an earlier phase calibrated moves it again, starting from that value when its search method accepts a start point.

Blocks are declared once under `[[calibration.objective_blocks]]`. A phase lists the ones it scores, or gives each a share. Shares are normalized to sum to one, so `{ hydrograph = 70, network = 30 }` reads as 70 % and 30 % of the cost. The share of a cost counts the same as an influence only when the costs are comparable. An efficiency (`nse_log`) is a pure number and a network distance is in meters, so `normalize_cost = true` is written on the network block. Each distance is then divided by the `validity_length` of the output (Eq. 4, `"auto"` is 2 h_obs), and a gap of one validity length costs 1, as much as an NSE of 0. `normalize_cost` stays refused on the efficiency, which is already a pure number.

A spin-up is left out by dates. `window.start` on the phase, or on `[calibration]`, is the first date scored, for every block alike, and a series keeps its stamps inside the window. A network output reads one state, dated at the stamp that closes its period. `time = "last"` is the default, and `"first"` or a date such as `"2002-10-15"` reads the period that holds it. The window has to hold that stamp, and `hmp check` says so before any solve when it does not. The former `warmup` and `warmup_periods` counted samples, so their span followed the time step. A file that writes them is refused with the new form, the start date of the window.

Dates can be kept apart from the search with `calibration.validation_window` on `[calibration]`, once for the session. `[metrics] window` minus those dates is then the default `window`. Each trial is scored on them from the series it has already simulated, as the `validation.cost` component, and the promoted run stores it as `checks.calibrated_by.validation_cost` with its period in `windows`. The cost never reads them. The score uses the blocks that compare a dated record, so a network block and a steady phase are left out of it. A window that overlaps a calibration window, leaves no data or falls outside `[metrics] window` is refused.

The declarations that the examples below share, since the published method writes its own objective blocks, are these.

```
[calibration.parameters.K]
bounds = [1e-7, 1e-3]

[calibration.parameters.Sy]
bounds = [5e-3, 0.35]

[calibration.outputs.streams]
support = "network"

[calibration.outputs.streams.map]
complete = "nancon_stream_network.gpkg"

[calibration.outputs.streams.model]
neighbours = "D8"

[calibration.outputs.gauge]
support = "point"
variable = "discharge"
observes = "NANCON"

[[calibration.objective_blocks]]
name = "network"
metric = "distance_gap"
uses_outputs = ["streams"]

[[calibration.objective_blocks]]
name = "network_share"         # the same gap, counted in validity lengths
metric = "distance_gap"
uses_outputs = ["streams"]
normalize_cost = true

[[calibration.objective_blocks]]
name = "hydrograph"
metric = "nse_log"
uses_outputs = ["gauge"]
```

K first, then Sy with K fixed. K alone in steady state against the mapped network, then Sy alone in transient against the gauge and the network, with 2000 left out as spin-up.

```
# not checked: fragment, continues the declarations of the first block
[[calibration.phases]]
name = "k_steady"
parameters = ["K"]
regime = "steady"              # one period over [simulation.time], or steady_window
objective_blocks = ["network"]
max_trials = 18

[[calibration.phases]]
name = "sy_transient"
parameters = ["Sy"]            # K holds what k_steady found
regime = "transient"
objective_blocks = { hydrograph = 0.8, network_share = 0.2 }   # two pure numbers
max_trials = 30

[calibration.phases.window]
start = "2001-01-01"           # the network state read, December 2002, lies inside
```

The soil capacity first. With a soil reservoir, `regime = "soil"` sets `ru` without a solver, to the capacity that closes the multi-year recharge plus runoff against the gauge (The daily soil reservoir, section “The capacity that closes the budget”). It lists the one parameter that moves `ru`, scores no block, and needs a phase after it, which calibrates K and Sy with `ru` fixed. The calibration then separates the volume, which the budget sets, from the dynamics, which the hydrograph sets.

```
# not checked: fragment, needs [flow.sinks_sources.recharge.soil] and [data.hydrometry]
[calibration.parameters.ru]
bounds = [20, 1000]            # mm

[[calibration.phases]]
name = "soil_capacity"
parameters = ["ru"]
regime = "soil"

[[calibration.phases]]
name = "k_sy_transient"
parameters = ["K", "Sy"]
regime = "transient"
objective_blocks = ["hydrograph"]
depends_on = "soil_capacity"
```

Both at once. One phase, both parameters, one regime. Two parameters and a cost to minimize give Nelder-Mead, and `method = "cma_es"` is written for a global search.

```
# not checked: fragment, continues the declarations of the first block
[[calibration.phases]]
name = "k_sy_transient"
parameters = ["K", "Sy"]
regime = "transient"
objective_blocks = ["hydrograph"]
max_trials = 120
```

In stages, then both together. A third phase after the two stages above moves K and Sy again, starting from what they found.

```
# not checked: fragment, continues the declarations of the first block
[[calibration.phases]]
name = "k_sy_refine"
parameters = ["K", "Sy"]       # starts at k_steady's K and sy_transient's Sy
regime = "transient"
objective_blocks = ["hydrograph"]
max_trials = 60
```

Narrower bounds in a later phase. A phase may write `bounds` for the parameters it moves, inside the bounds that `[calibration.parameters.<name>]` gives. The first phase searches wide and the refinement searches around what it found. A phase never widens a search, and bounds outside the section’s are refused when the file loads. `hmp calibrate --list-phases` prints them.

```
# not checked: fragment, continues the declarations of the first block
[[calibration.phases]]
name = "k_refine"
parameters = ["K"]
bounds = { K = [2e-6, 2e-5] }  # inside the bounds of [calibration.parameters.K]
```

The published method. The same first two stages, with the options that the paper leaves open and its citation recorded in the session.

```
# not checked: fragment, continues the declarations of the first block
[calibration.protocol]
name = "matching_hydrographic_network"
steady_max_trials = 18
transient_max_trials = 30
```

The transient stage scores itself through an objective block that reads a `support = "point"` output observing the gauging station. The output is added to `[calibration.outputs]` when the station is known from the file alone, which means one source named by `station_ids`, or `[site] gauge`. `--expand` then shows that output beside the two stages. A file that loads several stations, or one whose source only discovers its station once the data step runs, keeps the older form of the protocol, with `variable` and `objective` written on the phase and no output named.

From Python the keys are the same, as dictionaries. A call with phases writes the document it ran into the `sessions/` of the project as `<case>.toml`, so a Python run can be replayed from a file. The case takes the `[simulation] name` of the project, else the stem of its file, as on the command line.

```
import hydromodpy as hmp

project = hmp.Project("project.toml")
report = project.calibrate(
    parameters={"K": {"bounds": [1e-7, 1e-3]}, "Sy": {"bounds": [5e-3, 0.35]}},
    outputs={
        "streams": {
            "support": "network",
            "map": {"complete": "nancon_stream_network.gpkg"},
            "model": {"neighbours": "D8"},
        },
        "gauge": {"support": "point", "variable": "discharge", "observes": "NANCON"},
    },
    objective_blocks=[
        {"name": "network", "metric": "distance_gap", "uses_outputs": ["streams"]},
        {
            "name": "network_share",
            "metric": "distance_gap",
            "uses_outputs": ["streams"],
            "normalize_cost": True,
        },
        {"name": "hydrograph", "metric": "nse_log", "uses_outputs": ["gauge"]},
    ],
    phases=[
        {
            "name": "k_steady",
            "parameters": ["K"],
            "regime": "steady",
            "objective_blocks": ["network"],
            "max_trials": 18,
        },
        {
            "name": "sy_transient",
            "parameters": ["Sy"],
            "regime": "transient",
            "objective_blocks": {"hydrograph": 0.8, "network_share": 0.2},
            "max_trials": 30,
            "window": {"start": "2001-01-01"},
        },
    ],
)
```

A phase takes the search of `[calibration]` key by key. `method`, `max_trials`, `precision` and `method_options` written in the phase win, then the ones of the section, then the default, which is a method chosen from what the phase scores and `max_trials = "auto"`. A precision of the section reaches only a phase whose engine stops on one, and not a phase that writes that stopping option itself. The options of the section reach a phase that runs the method of the section, and `method_options = {}` in a phase states that it takes none. `hmp calibrate FILE --list-phases` says where each key comes from.

Each phase also says how wide its answer is, through `uncertainty` with the same keys as `[calibration.uncertainty]`, which stays the default for every phase. Left unwritten, the width follows what the phase scores. A phase scored only by network distances takes one mesh cell, in meters, since a stream cannot move by less, and any other phase takes 5 % of its best cost. `cost_margin` writes it with its unit, `"5%"` of the best cost or `"75 m"` of network distance. A bare number is refused, and a length is accepted only on a search scored by network distances. `hmp check` refuses a share on a phase scored only by network distances. The interval never moves the calibrated value. It says which values the search could not tell apart from it.

`hmp calibrate FILE --list-phases` shows, for each phase, the parameters it moves, the ones it re-opens and from which phase (when it moves a parameter an earlier phase calibrated, and whether its engine starts from that value), which method it runs and why, the width of its interval, and for each block what is compared with what, which is the simulated quantity and the observed source (a station of `[data.<family>]`, or a network file). After a phase, the report gives the share of the cost each block actually took, which differs from the declared share when the blocks have different units. `overrides` stays for any other configuration value a phase must change, as a dotted path into the project configuration.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/understand/can-i-check-what-was-run.html -->
# Can I check what was run?

Yes. A result of HydroModPy is not only a map. It comes with the record of what produced it, and that record can be read without the person who made the run. This page lists what is kept, and what you can ask for when you receive a result. The word for this record is provenance.

## What a run keeps

Every finished run has its own folder. In it you find:

- The configuration that ran. A frozen copy of the TOML file, not the file as it is today. The run is stored with a fingerprint of that configuration, so two runs can be told apart or matched.
- A provenance record, `provenance.json`. It names the version of HydroModPy, the commit of the code it came from, the version of Python, the machine, the packages installed, and the solver with its version and the SHA-256 checksum of its binary.
- The inputs it read, `inputs.json`: one entry per dataset, downloaded or yours, with the provider, the product and its version, the full request (extent, period, stations), the date of the download, the checksum and the licence.
- A manifest, `manifest.json`, written last. It names the catchment, lists the output files, the period, the geometry, the scores with the window they were computed on, and the checks of the run (water budget, convergence). A run folder without a manifest is an incomplete run by construction; its `outcome.json` says how it ended.
- A `README.md`, generated from the manifest: the same facts in words, the run label of the day, and the checksum of the manifest it summarizes.

A checksum is a short code computed from the content of a file. If one byte changes, the code changes. A checksum that matches is a strong sign that the file is the one that was used.

## What the project keeps

At the root of a project, the lockfile `hydromodpy.lock` pins what fed the runs: the version of the code, and every cached input with its source, licence, checksum and size, read from the sidecar that sits next to each file. The files you provide yourself, under `inputs/`, are listed too. You write it with `hmp data lock`, and a launch of many cases writes it once the data are fetched, not every run. Each run records the solver binary it used, with its checksum.

The lockfile answers a wider question than the manifest of one run: in what state was the whole data cache before the run?

## What you can ask for

| You want to know | You ask for | Command |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What exactly was run? | The summary of the run: solver, status, duration, size of the grid, parameters, scores and the start of the configuration fingerprint. The frozen configuration and the provenance record are files of the run folder, which you can open. | `hmp show <run>` |
| What differs between two runs? | The comparison of the two. | `hmp diff <run A> <run B>` |
| Whether the data cache is still the one that was used | A check of the cache against the lockfile. | `hmp data lock --check` |
| To replay a stored run with exactly the same data and settings | A run that pins each input at the digest of the seal, classed `bit` or `deviation` (Replay a run). | `hmp replay <run>` |
| To replay a project file on its pinned data | A run that refuses any fresh download and stops on a checksum that does not match the lockfile. | `hmp run --frozen <file>` |
| To rerun a stored run, changing one setting | A rerun from the stored configuration. A default that moved since gets a warning and a line in the lineage of the new run. | `hmp catalog rerun <run> --set path=value` |
| To hand a run to someone | A copy that stands alone, with the checksum of every file (Share a simulation with its data). | `hmp publish <run> --to <folder>` |
| To hand a run and its data to a colleague, who reruns it | The default copy, with every file the run read (Share a simulation with its data). | `hmp publish <run> --to sim.tar --container tar`, then `hmp catalog import sim.tar` |
| Whether a copy you received is intact | A check of every file of the copy against the checksums it carries. | `hmp publish --verify <folder>` |

The options of each command are in the command reference.

## What this does not prove

A record shows what was run. It does not show that the run was a good idea. Two identical records mean two identical computations, and a correct computation can still rest on a poor assumption or a poor dataset. For that, read What “validated” means here and Where the data come from.

A note on recorded data: the record contains the name of the machine and the user. `hmp publish` removes them from the copy it writes. A run folder copied by hand still carries them.

## Where to go next

- Where the data come from: the origin of each input.
- hmp run: `--frozen` runs from the cache, with no download.
- Glossary: the terms of this page.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/understand/conventions.html -->
# Conventions of a run

A run stores numbers. This page says how to read them: which date reads which period, which sign a flux has, what a station or a zone is called, and how layers and reaches are counted. The rules are the same for every solver and they do not change from one model to the next.

## A date reads the period that holds it

A run has one value per stress period, and the time stored with a value is the end of its period: the stamp. January 2000 of a monthly run is stamped 2000-02-01.

A date `t` reads the period `(s, e]` that holds it, where `s` is the start of the period and `e` its stamp. So a date equal to a stamp reads the period that stamp closes, and a date copied from the time axis of a NetCDF file or from a CSV finds its own value again. The first date of the record belongs to the first period.

| Monthly run from 2000-01-01, `time =` | Period read | Stored stamp |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"2000-01-01"` | January 2000 | 2000-02-01 |
| `"2000-01-15"` | January 2000 | 2000-02-01 |
| `"2000-02-01"` | January 2000 | 2000-02-01 |
| `"2000-02-02"` | February 2000 | 2000-03-01 |

A state, such as a head, is the value at the stamp. A flux, such as a drain flux, is the mean over the period. So a date inside a period reads the state at the end of that period. On a daily run, `time = "2002-10-15"` reads the period that ends at the start of 15 October, which is the day of 14 October.

A window from `start` to `end` keeps every period with some time between the two dates. Two stamps keep the periods between them, so `2001-01-01` to `2002-01-01` is the twelve months of 2001 on a monthly run. A window of one date reads the period that date reads. A window that only touches the record holds no period and is refused: it starts on the last stamp, or ends on the first date.

A window over a series keeps what falls in those periods. A simulated value is kept by its stamp, `(start, end]`. A measurement is kept by its date, `[start, end)`. So `2000-02-01` to `2000-03-01` is the one simulated value of February and the 29 daily measurements of February. A measurement taken before or after the simulated record is read with the whole series, without a window.

A list of dates reads one period per date. A list where two dates read the same period is refused, and the message names them: `2000-01-01` and `2000-02-01` both read January on a monthly run. To read every period between two dates, write a window.

The rule is the same in `Run.read`, `run.field`, `run.timeseries`, `[[export]]`, `[display]` and the `time` of a network output of a calibration. How a run stamps its periods is on Time alignment of outputs and observations.

## A budget flux is negative when water leaves the aquifer

Every per-cell flux of the `budget/` group of a run follows the sign of MODFLOW, for every solver: positive when water enters the aquifer, negative when it leaves. A drain flux is negative. A recharge is positive. A storage term is positive when the aquifer takes water from its storage. A well is negative when it pumps. A transient run of every solver writes its storage terms. Summed over the whole model domain, the signed fluxes add up to zero. This does not hold on one cell, because the flows between cells are not in `budget/`.

The fields rebuilt from these fluxes say what they hold in their name: `outflow_drain`, `release_flux` and the accumulation fluxes are positive outflows. The `budgets` table splits each term in `flux_in` and `flux_out`, both positive. In a budget table, `flux_in` is the water that enters the store named by `zone_id`: the aquifer for `DOMAIN`, the stream network for `sfr:<id>`, the lake for its station. The exchange between two stores is therefore read with the sign of the store its row names.

## A rate in a TOML file follows the same sign, or its name says the direction

A rate you write in a file has one of two forms, whatever the table.

A signed rate follows the rule of the budget: positive when water enters the store it acts on, negative when it leaves. These are the rate of a well, `flow.sinks_sources.wells.<name>.flux` and its forcing, the recharge, `flow.sinks_sources.recharge.values`, and the rate of a specified lake outlet, `flow.sinks_sources.lakes.<name>.outlets.rate`, where the store is the lake.

A rate whose name says its direction is a magnitude, zero or more, and a negative value is refused. These are the ETP values, and on a lake or a stream network `rainfall`, `evaporation`, `runoff`, `inflow`, `withdrawal` and `headwater_inflow`. So a withdrawal of 2 m3/s takes 2 m3/s out of the lake, and a well that takes as much says `-2`.

Water that leaves is written one of two ways. In the `budget/` group, and in a rate that is signed (a well, a recharge, a specified lake outlet), it is negative. In a rate whose name says the direction (`evaporation`, `withdrawal`, the ETP), it is a positive magnitude.

## One word for the whole catchment

`catchment` means the whole catchment wherever a table needs a word for it: the station of a catchment series such as `discharge`, the zone of a budget row, the zone of a uniform parameter, and the soil column of the basin mean. `domain` is the zone of a budget row over the whole model domain. The two differ when the mesh takes in a buffer around the catchment, so only the `catchment` row compares with a gauge at the outlet.

A station or a zone you name cannot be called `catchment`, in a file or in a TOML key. A gauge with this name would be scored against the simulated outlet, and a zone would read as a uniform parameter. Write the gauge code, such as `J0014010`, or name the zone after what it holds, such as `core` or `hillslope`. `domain` stays free: only a budget row reads it, and `catchment_zones` uses it as a zone label.

## A column says where a series comes from

The `source` column of the `timeseries` table says `simulated` or `observed`. A simulated discharge and a gauged one have the same variable, `discharge`. To read the gauge by name, `Run.read` and `[[export]]` take `discharge_obs`, which no table stores. A CSV export has the same `source` column.

## How things are counted

| What | First value | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Layer | 0, the top layer | Everywhere |
| Period and time step | 0 | `timestep` of a table, `time` of a read |
| Cell | 0 | `cell_id` of a table, rank on the face axis of a field |
| Reach | 1 | `reach` of `sfr_reaches`, `upstream` and `downstream` of a TOML reach |

A reach keeps one number between the TOML and the results. Its `reach_id`, `<network>:<reach>`, is its `station_id` in the `timeseries` table, and the table `sfr_reaches` gives its geometry and the reaches it drains into.

A NetCDF variable or a VTU cell array keeps its name at any number of layers. A VTU file has one component per layer. In a NetCDF file a field of a model of several layers has a `layer` dimension, and a field of a model of one layer holds that layer alone, with the scalar variable `layer` naming it, because QGIS leaves out of a mesh any field with a third dimension. QGIS lists a NetCDF export three times, as a raster, a mesh and a vector. Open the mesh: a raster of a field on the cells is one row high. On a model of several layers QGIS reads a file with one layer asked for, `hmp export` with `--layer` or `layer =` in `[[export]]`.

## Units

The `unit` column of a table, and the `units` attribute of a field, are written in udunits spelling: `m3 s-1`, `mm d-1`, `m`, `1` for a dimensionless value. A text that is not plainly a unit stays as its provider wrote it, such as `mg/L NO3` or `n/a`. The columns of the `soil_budget` table hold water depths in the unit its `unit` column says, `mm`.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/understand/how-sure.html -->
# How sure is the model?

Not completely, and no groundwater model is. This page says where the doubt comes from, what HydroModPy reports about it, and how to read a result with it in mind. The word for this doubt is uncertainty.

## Where the doubt comes from

- The inputs. The rain that reaches the water table, the relief, the position of the mapped streams and the flow measured at the gauge all carry errors. A model cannot be more precise than its inputs.
- The parameters. The hydraulic conductivity K and the specific yield Sy cannot be measured at the scale of a catchment. They are found by calibration, and calibration does not give a single answer.
- The structure. The model is a simplification: in example 04, one layer of constant thickness, one value of K for the whole aquifer, a monthly step and cells of 75 m (What HydroModPy does). Two models with different simplifications can both look right.
- The observations. The mapped network holds only the reaches someone chose to draw, and a gauge has its own error.

## Several answers can look equally good

Example 04 shows it. When K varies, the simulated discharge at the outlet does not tell the values apart, but the extent of the seepage does (Reading the results). This is equifinality: different sets of parameters reproduce the observations about equally well. A good fit to the discharge alone does not tell which set is right.

This is why HydroModPy can calibrate on several observations at once, such as the discharge and the stream network, and why it reports a range beside each calibrated value instead of a single number.

## What HydroModPy reports

A range beside the calibrated value. After the search, HydroModPy reports the range of values that the search tried and that scored almost as well as the best one. It reads this range off the trials already run. It is not a probability distribution: a probability needs an error model on each observation, and the scores used here do not provide one. Three methods exist: a free one that reads the trials already run, one that restarts the search from other starting points and can find a second optimum, and one that disturbs each parameter a little to see which ones trade off against each other. [calibration.uncertainty] lists them.

A narrow range has two possible causes. The parameter may be well constrained, or the search may never have tried far from the best value. The range alone does not tell which.

An ensemble band. When you run the same model many times with different parameters or inputs, the `ensemble_band` preset draws the median of the runs and a band between two percentiles of them. The wider the band, the less the runs agree. It shows the spread of the runs that you chose to make, so it is a lower bound of the doubt, not a full measure of it. The ensemble is only as varied as you made it.

Honest labels. Under every figure of Reading the results, a reliability label says whether the result was checked, calibrated or only indicative.

## What example 04 does not show

Each figure of example 04 comes from one run. None carries a range or a band. The example is a demonstration of how to read the outputs, and it does not claim the precision of a study.

## Reading a result with the doubt in mind

1. Ask what was calibrated. A result that the calibration sought is expected to look right.
1. Ask whether another set of parameters would give the same fit. If the report shows a range, look at its width.
1. Ask what the model leaves out (What HydroModPy does) and whether it matters for your question.
1. Prefer a comparison to an absolute value. The difference between two scenarios, run with the same inputs and assumptions, is more robust than either run alone.
1. Read the verification and the validation of the model (What “validated” means here).

## Where to go next

- What “validated” means here: what has been checked, and how.
- [calibration.uncertainty]: the ranges, method by method.
- Glossary: the terms of this page.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/understand/network-metrics.html -->
# Scoring a simulated stream network

A model makes a network of streams. A map draws another one. To say how well they agree, you need a number, and there are several ways to get one. This page tells what each way answers, and separates two uses that look alike: a diagnostic, which you read, and a criterion, which a calibration drives to a target.

It has no equation and no name of a metric. The equations of the downslope method are in Downslope distance between two networks. The names of the metrics, and how to write them to a file, are in hmp diff and [calibration.outputs].

## The two networks

- The simulated network is not computed by a river model. The model finds the cells where the water table reaches the ground, and the network extends these seepage cells downstream, following the slope of the ground (What HydroModPy does).
- The mapped network is the network drawn on a map. In example 04, it is the permanent reaches of the BD TOPO.

A score never gives the truth about the model. It gives the distance between two drawings, and each drawing has its own errors. The mapped network holds the reaches someone chose to draw. The simulated one depends on the cell size, on the threshold that decides what counts as seepage and, in a run that changes with time, on the month you look at.

## Four ways to compare two networks

| Way | What it compares | What it answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Overlap of lines | The two networks as lines | What share of the length of each network lies near the other? |
| Overlap of cells | The cells of the simulated network and the cells the map crosses | How many cells do the two share, miss or add? |
| Straight-line distance | The same two sets of cells | How far apart do the two patterns sit, as the crow flies? |
| Downslope distance | The two networks, along the paths the water takes | How far must the water walk to get from one network to the other, in each direction? |

### Overlap of lines

Both networks are treated as lines, with a small tolerance around each. A stretch of one network is matched when it lies inside the tolerance of the other, and missing or extra when it does not. The result is a set of lengths and shares, and the largest gap between the two drawings.

Use it to compare two maps, such as the observed network and the one derived from the relief. It does not read the model cells and it does not know where the water goes: a stretch near the map counts as matched even if the water leaves it in another valley.

### Overlap of cells

This way works on the cells of the model. A cell is simulated when the model puts water there, and mapped when the map crosses it. Then the cells are counted:

- the cells in both sets (the overlap);
- the mapped cells the model did not reach (missing);
- the simulated cells away from the map (extra).

From these counts come two shares: the coverage, the share of mapped cells that the model found, and the precision, the share of simulated cells that are on the map. A low coverage says the simulated network is under-developed. A low precision says it spreads where the map has nothing. Two combined scores fold the two shares into one number.

One detail changes the numbers. This way marks every cell the map touches, so a line becomes a ribbon of cells. The downslope method draws the map one cell wide, like the simulated network. The cell counts of the two ways are therefore not comparable.

### Straight-line distance

Same cells, but now the question is how far. For each simulated cell, the code measures the straight distance to the nearest mapped line. For each mapped cell, it measures the distance to the nearest simulated cell. That gives two numbers, one per direction, each summarized by its mean, its median, its high values and its maximum.

A distance gives more than a count. Two simulated cells that miss the map, one by a cell and one by a kilometer, count the same in the overlap and weigh very differently here. But the distance is straight, so it ignores the relief. It crosses a ridge as if it were not there.

### Downslope distance

This is the method of [Abhervé et al., 2023]. The distance is the length of the path the water follows downslope, not the straight line.

- From each simulated cell, how far does the water go before it meets the mapped network? The mean is the excess side: if the model makes too much stream, simulated water travels far to reach a map that has no stream near it.
- From each mapped cell, how far does the water go before it meets the simulated network? The mean is the deficit side: if the model makes too little stream, mapped streams have no simulated stream to flow into.

The two directions are kept apart on purpose, because they tell opposite stories. The calibration uses the gap between them, in absolute value, as its cost. It also keeps their average as a diagnostic, and the three classes of cells that the confusion map draws: valid, excess and missing. The maps are explained on Comparison with the mapped network.

The average walk has a validity length. When it is longer than that length, the two networks are further apart than the map can be trusted to place them, and the score says little about the hydrogeology. By default the length is two cells, widened by the positional accuracy you declare for the map. A violation is a warning unless you ask for an error with `on_invalid`.

## Diagnostic or criterion

The same number can be read, or it can be minimized. The two uses have different needs.

A diagnostic describes. You read it, put it in a report, compare two runs with it. It has no need to be symmetric or monotonic. The four ways above all work as diagnostics, and the overlap and straight-line ways are only diagnostics.

A criterion is a cost that a search drives to a target, over many trials. It must behave well along that search. For the downslope method, the cost is the gap between the excess side and the deficit side, and its target is zero. Zero does not mean that the two networks coincide. It means that the simulated network has as much excess as deficit. A model can reach it with a large excess and a large deficit that cancel, which is why the confusion map and the average walk stay on the table next to it.

Why not use a straight-line distance as the criterion?

- A straight-line distance crosses divides. A seepage cell on the far side of a ridge counts as close to the map, when its water leaves into the other valley. The downslope distance follows the water, so it cannot cheat that way.
- A mean straight-line distance has no sign. It cannot say whether the model has too much stream or too little, and a search needs that sign to know which way to move the parameter.
- A count of cells moves in steps, and its best value depends on how the map is drawn on the grid.

Why not minimize the average walk, then? It is large at both ends of a parameter sweep, so it does have a minimum in the middle. But nothing puts that minimum at the point where excess and deficit balance. They are two different estimators. Use the average walk to compare two structures that are both balanced, and the gap to find the parameter inside one structure.

## What moves a score

Before you compare two scores, check that they were computed the same way.

- The seepage threshold. A cell counts as seepage only above a share of the mean basin recharge over its own area (seepage threshold). Another threshold changes the simulated network, and so every score.
- The way the map is drawn on the grid. The rule for the mapped network (`calibration.outputs.<name>.map.drawn_by`) moves the number of mapped cells and where they sit. A one-cell gap can come from this rule and not from the model.
- The cell size. Distances are in meters, but they are measured from cell to cell. A coarse grid cannot place a stream closer than about a cell.
- The state that is read. A steady run gives one network. A run that changes with time gives one network per time step. A calibration can score one state, or two bounds: the complete network and the permanent one. A cell is counted as flowing above a visible flow.
- The map. The permanent network of a map does not hold the temporary streams. An “excess” can be a real stream the map ignores.
- The cells that are scored. Only the cells inside the catchment, active, and off open water enter a score. The share of the minimal map outside the maximal one (`frac_minimal_outside_maximal` in the trial journal) is read on these cells too.

A figure redrawn from a sealed run takes the same inputs as the trial, as How the model makes streams says.

## Where to go next

- Reading the results: the maps that show these scores for example 04.
- How the model makes streams: how the model makes a network.
- Downslope distance between two networks: the equations, the assumptions and the limits of the downslope method.
- [calibration.outputs]: the network criterion of a calibration.
- hmp diff: `hmp diff`, the overlap and distance scores of several runs.

# Reading the results

This page is a reading guide to the main outputs of example 04 (the Nançon catchment, see What HydroModPy does). For each map or curve: what it shows, how to read it, the pitfalls, and what makes it reliable or only indicative. Every figure and every number on this page comes from one run, described in Where these figures come from.

## Three rules before reading

1. One map, one month. Snapshot maps show a single month. In example 04, it is October 2002, the driest month of the series according to the comments in the configuration file: so the map shows the case where the network is at its smallest. A map of a wet month would show much more.
1. A cell is 75 m wide. A stream fills one cell in width, and we count cells, not meters of stream. The maps are read at the hillslope scale (see resolution).
1. Calibrating is not validating. The simulated network and the discharge are what the calibration tried to reproduce (Calibration in two stages), so their agreement is expected (What “validated” means here).

## In one table

Three reliability labels are used, and each figure below carries one:

- An internal check of the computation, independent of the calibration.
- The agreement was sought by the calibration.
- No field measurement was compared with this result in the example.

| Figure | Question | Label |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water table depth | How deep is the water table? | |
| Seepage cells | Where does water come out of the ground? | |
| Comparison with the mapped network | Does the model find the mapped streams? | |
| Flow persistence | Which reaches dry up, and when? | |
| Simulated against observed discharge | Are the volume and the season of the discharge right? | |
| The water budget | How much water comes in and goes out? | for the closure, for the values |

## Water table depth

Fig. 2 Look at: where the water table is close to the ground (dark) and where it is deep (pale). Does not show: a measured level, or any depth beyond the 30 m of the model.

Request `variable = "watertable_depth"`, October 2002. Color bar: “Depth of the water table below land surface (m)”.

What the map shows. The distance between the ground and the top of the water table, in meters, for each cell. It is derived from the hydraulic head: ground elevation minus water table elevation, set to zero when the water table reaches the ground. This is the depth to water table.

How to read it. Dark blue: the water table is close to the ground, which is where water can come out. Pale yellow: the water table is deep. The water table is close to the ground in the valley bottoms and deep under the interfluves (the higher ground between two valleys), which the map shows clearly.

Pitfalls.

- The scale stops at the model thickness. The modeled aquifer is 30 m thick (an assumption, see What HydroModPy does). A pale yellow color means “at the bottom of the model”, not “at exactly 30 m”. In this run, about 5.2% of the cells of the catchment (598 of 11,488) have, in October 2002, the water table within 0.5 m of the bottom (computed from the stored data of the run).
- The pattern follows the relief by construction. K is uniform and the drains are at the surface: a water table close to the ground in the valleys is the expected result of the setup, not a discovery.
- This is a monthly mean state, not the level of a given day.

Reliability. Indicative. Example 04 does not compare this map with piezometer levels. The overall shape is consistent with the physics of the setup; the absolute depths are not validated.

## Seepage cells

Fig. 3 Look at: the blue cells, where the water table reaches the ground and water comes out. Does not show: streams, or how much water comes out of a cell.

Request `variable = "seepage_mask"`, October 2002. Legend: “seepage (112 cells)”, “no seepage (11,376 cells)”.

What the map shows. The cells where the water table reaches or exceeds the ground surface, one by one, with no extension downstream. This is the raw state of the model: in this run, 112 cells of the 11,488 cells of the catchment in October 2002.

How to read it. Each blue cell is a point where water appears, a spring. These are not streams: isolated cells or short lines of cells are normal. The pale cells outside the catchment outline are in the model margin and are not counted.

Pitfalls.

- This is not the network. The simulated network extends the seepage cells downstream (Comparison with the mapped network). The two maps do not use the same definition of a cell that “seeps”, so their cell counts cannot be compared.
- The extent depends on K. Example 04 observes this: when K varies, the simulated discharge does not tell the values apart, but the seepage area does. This is why the calibration of K relies on the network.
- A cell is a yes or no state. It says nothing about the flow that comes out.

Reliability. Indicative. The map is consistent with the computation, but no observation of a spring or a seep is compared with it in the example.

## Comparison with the mapped network

Fig. 4 Look at: how much yellow and red remain around the dark blue. Does not show: which of the two networks is right, or the months other than October.

Request `variable = "network_agreement"`, October 2002. Dark blue “valid” (297 cells), yellow “excess” (62), red “missing” (174).

What the map shows. Each cell belongs to a single class:

- valid (dark blue): the simulated network and the mapped network both pass through this cell;
- excess (yellow): only the model puts a stream there;
- missing (red): only the map puts a stream there;
- gray: no stream.

The mapped network is made of the permanent reaches of the BD TOPO, placed on the model grid. The simulated network is the downstream extension of the seepage cells, following the slope of the terrain (What HydroModPy does).

How to read it. A perfect agreement would be all dark blue: we look for little yellow and little red at the same time. In this run, the model misses 174 of the 471 mapped cells (37%), mostly at the upstream ends and on the side branches (red), and adds 62 cells (yellow) in a few short stretches beside the main axis. A plain count of cells does not say whether a small gap comes from a good fit or from two errors that cancel each other: the map shows it.

Fig. 5 Look at: the cells far from the mapped network, in the darker classes. Does not show: whether the mapped network itself is complete.

Request `variable = "downslope_distance"` with `scale = "log"`, October 2002. Distance traveled downslope by each simulated cell before it reaches the mapped network. The image shows four classes: 0 to 75 m (299 cells), 75 to 500 m (54), 500 to 1000 m (10), more than 1000 m (0).

The second map no longer counts the cells that coincide: it measures how far each one is off. A simulated cell that coincides with the mapped network is at 0 m. The four classes are those of the reference paper (Abhervé et al., 2023). Its counts cannot be compared one to one with those of the previous map: the two maps do not count exactly the same cells. How the scores are built is on Scoring a simulated stream network.

Pitfalls.

- The mapped network holds only the permanent reaches. An “excess” can be a real temporary stream that the map ignores, or an error of the model: the map does not settle it.
- One month only, October 2002.
- The threshold matters. A cell is counted as seepage above the `calibration.outputs.<name>.model.seepage_threshold` (How the model makes streams). Another threshold moves the three classes.
- The mapped network is placed on the 75 m grid with a transfer rule: a one-cell gap can come from the transfer and not from the model. This run uses the `heads` rule (`calibration.outputs.<name>.map.drawn_by`), the default when it was made, where the default now draws the map as the data gives it. It places each stream head of the map on a nearby cell, within 100 m, and draws the rest of the reach down the slope of the model, so that field ditches below a head do not count as model errors (How the model makes streams).

Reliability. Calibrated. K was adjusted so that this network looks like the map. The method itself is published and peer reviewed (Abhervé et al., 2023).

## Flow persistence

Fig. 6 Look at: the dark cells that flow almost all the time and the light ones that flow only in the wettest months. Does not show: the discharge of a reach, or any year-to-year change.

Request `variable = "simulated_active_network"` with `reduce = "frequency"`, January 2000 to December 2002. Color bar: “Timesteps flowing (%)”. Title: 772 cells ever flowing in the 36 months.

What the map shows. For each cell, the share of the 36 months during which it flows (the persistence). Dark blue: almost always. Light blue: only in the wettest months. Gray: never.

Fig. 7 Look at: the orange stream heads, which dry up first, and the blue trunk that keeps flowing. Does not show: which reaches really dry up in the field.

Request `variable = "simulated_active_network"` with `reduce = "frequency"`, year 2002. Blue “perennial” (336 cells), orange “intermittent” (128), gray “dry” (11,024).

The second map classes each cell over a single calendar year (2002): perennial if it flows all 12 months, intermittent if it flows some months, dry if it never flows. The stream heads are orange: they dry up first.

How to read it. A cell “flows” if it is downstream of a seepage cell and carries at least the `calibration.outputs.<name>.model.extent.visible_flow` of water coming from the aquifer (How the model makes streams). This is not the same meaning as on the seepage map, which counts only the exit points.

Pitfalls.

- The time step is monthly. A reach that dries up for two weeks does not appear. “Intermittent” means: dry at least one month in the year.
- The visible flow is a convention. Another threshold changes the layout (How the model makes streams).
- The three years include the first year, 2000, which serves as the spin-up of the model. And three years say nothing about the year-to-year variability.
- The year 2002 is the driest year of the series according to the comment in the example. So the orange reaches are orange for a dry year.
- The two maps do not cover the same duration (36 months against 12): a cell can be dark on one and orange or gray on the other without any contradiction.

Reliability. Indicative. The only network compared with a map is the permanent network of October. The example uses no field observation of dry reaches: the distinction between perennial and intermittent is a model output, not verified.

## Simulated against observed discharge

Fig. 8 Look at: whether the blue line follows the black dashes in season and in volume, in the gray window. Does not show: daily discharge, or a period the calibration has not used.

Request `preset = "hydrograph"` with `scale = "log"`. Blue line: total simulated discharge. Black dashes: discharge observed at the NANCON station. Gray area: scoring window, 24 of the 36 months. Logarithmic vertical axis, in m³/s.

What the curve shows. The monthly discharge at the outlet, simulated and measured at the NANCON station (the daily measurement is averaged over each month). The simulated discharge is the total: what leaves the aquifer through the drains, plus the runoff given as input data, since this model has no stream network. The figure itself states: “total discharge only: this run stores no groundwater / surface split”. This curve is a hydrograph.

How to read it. The axis is logarithmic: low flows weigh as much as floods, and a gap of 0.1 to 0.2 m³/s is as visible as a gap of 1 to 2. This is intended: the calibration of Sy uses a Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency computed on the logarithms, which gives weight to the recessions (Calibration in two stages). The gray area is the scoring window (2001 and 2002); 2000, the spin-up year, is not scored.

The scores of this run. The run metrics table covers the 36 months, spin-up included: Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) 0.68, and volume bias (PBIAS) -20.5%. A negative PBIAS means that the model underestimates: here the simulated discharge is lower than the measured one, so the model is too dry. Recomputed on the 2001 and 2002 window only, from the stored series, the same measures give an NSE of about 0.94 and a bias of about -8%. The first year therefore weighs a lot: the model clearly underestimates the discharge of 2000.

To put these numbers in context, Moriasi et al. (2007) propose, for catchment models at the monthly time step, to judge an agreement “satisfactory” from an NSE of 0.50 and a volume bias of ±25%, and “good” from 0.65 and ±15%. This scale comes from other catchment models: it gives a reference, not a threshold specific to HydroModPy.

Pitfalls.

- Runoff is an input. It is given to the model as data: only the groundwater part is computed. A good agreement of the total does not prove that the groundwater part is right.
- Sy was calibrated on this window. A high NSE on 2001 and 2002 shows that the calibration worked.
- A good discharge agreement does not tell K values apart. Several K values give a similar discharge (see Seepage cells). This is equifinality, and How sure is the model? comes back to it.
- The monthly time step smooths the flood peaks and says nothing about the discharge of a given day.

Reliability. Calibrated. The season and the volume are well reproduced over the calibrated period. The example holds no test on a period or a catchment that the calibration did not use.

## The water budget

Fig. 9 for the closure, for the values. Look at: the winter months, when recharge exceeds drainage, and the summer months, when drainage continues alone. Does not show: the change in storage, or the water outside the delineated catchment.

Request `preset = "water_budget"`. Blue: recharge, which enters the aquifer. Red: drainage, which leaves it. In m³/s, over the delineated catchment. Title: “positive = into the aquifer”.

What the curve shows. The two fluxes that cross the aquifer, month by month: recharge (positive, it enters) and drainage through the drains (negative, it leaves). The change in storage is not plotted: it is the difference between the two curves. Together they form the water budget.

How to read it.

- In winter, the aquifer fills up. In January 2001, recharge reaches 3.1 m³/s for a drainage of 1.7 m³/s: the difference goes into storage.
- In summer, it slowly empties and feeds the streams. From July to September 2002, recharge is almost zero (0.01 to 0.02 m³/s) and drainage continues at 0.24 to 0.29 m³/s. This is the baseflow: the water stored in winter that sustains the streams in dry periods.
- The first month is in steady state, so recharge and drainage are roughly equal there.

Pitfalls.

- m³/s and mm. The image above gives each line in m³/s. The `water_budget` preset gives each line as a water depth in mm per day, which is easier to compare with rainfall, as set out in the figure requests. As a depth, the figure divides each line by the area of its own zone: the whole cells of the catchment for the `catchment` line, and the active domain for the line of the domain. The axis names the zone. Here the recharge of the catchment line, 0.71 m³/s over 64.8 km², and the recharge of the domain line, 1.31 m³/s over 120.4 km², both give 0.94 mm per day, as expected since the recharge is uniform.
- The catchment and not the domain. The model extends beyond the catchment (a margin of 10% more area); the figure says “frame: the delineated catchment”.
- The bar panel of the `water_budget` preset has another use: it adds up the flows stored at each time step: it is a sum of flows, not a volume.

Reliability. Two things to tell apart. The closure of the budget is a numerical check: the run reports a budget error of 0.00%, meaning that the solver conserves water. It does not say that the model is right. The values are what was put in as input (the recharge) and what K and Sy allow to store and release: they stay indicative as long as the recharge has not been compared with another estimate.

## Other figures you will meet

A report made with HydroModPy can contain figures that example 04 does not use. The reading rules below hold for any run. Each figure has an entry in the figure requests.

| Figure | How to read it | Take care |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water-table elevation (`variable = "watertable_elevation"`) | Elevation of the water table at one time step, in the same datum as the ground. Water flows from high to low, across the lines of equal height. | It is the head of the model, not a measurement, unless the report overlays measured levels. |
| Piezometric head, simulated against observed (`preset = "hydrograph"` with `variable = "head"`) | The simulated level at one well, against the level measured there, time step after time step. | A model can follow the season and miss the level by meters: look at both. Check that the well was not used to calibrate. |
| Flow-duration curve (`variable = "discharge"`, `type = "distribution"`, `cumulative = true`) | The flow on the vertical axis, and on the horizontal axis the share of time during which that flow is exceeded. The left end is the floods, the right end the low flows. | It forgets the order of events: two very different years can give the same curve. |
| Simulated against observed scatter (`variable = "discharge"`, `type = "xy"`, `observed = true`) and residuals (`preset = "residuals"`) | Each dot is one time step. On the 1:1 line the model is exact. The residuals are the simulated value minus the observed one. | A residual that has a pattern, such as always positive in winter, shows a missing process. A random residual is the best case. |
| Mass-balance closure error (`variable = "mass_balance.percent_error"`, `type = "series"`) | The gap between what the solver put in and took out, in percent, time step by step. It should stay small and steady. | It checks the arithmetic of the solver only. A small error means the solver converged, not that the model is right (label Numerical check). |
| Ensemble envelope (`preset = "ensemble_band"`) | The median of a set of runs and a band between two percentiles. The wider the band, the less the runs agree. | The band shows the spread of the runs you made. It is not a full measure of the uncertainty (How sure is the model?). |

## Where these figures come from

The eight figures are real outputs of the run `nancon_intermittence_mf6_calibrated_transient_storage`. It was produced on 2026-10-09 by a two-stage calibration of example 04 with HydroModPy 2.0.0a4. It is the run promoted from trial 8 of the second calibration stage: K = 7.96e-5 m/s, then Sy = 0.045. The mapped network is placed on the grid by the `heads` rule, the default of that version, as described under Comparison with the mapped network.

The images are drawn from the stored run, the way `hmp show --figure` draws them, for instance `hmp show nancon_intermittence_mf6_calibrated_transient_storage --figure seepage_mask`. The titles carry no run name, and the legends are in English. The repository keeps, for every image, the run, the command and the option that made it, in `tools/docs/figures/figures.toml`.

Each figure exists in a light and a dark version, and the page shows the one that matches the theme. The dark version recolors the background, the texts and the light grays, such as the dry cells of the intermittence map and the ground of the seepage map.

To draw a figure of an existing run again, at another date, see the figure requests and hmp show.
