# How the model makes streams

HydroModPy does not draw rivers. It computes a water table. Where the water table reaches the ground, water leaves the aquifer. Those exits are the sources of the streams, and the stream network is what they generate downhill.

This page follows that chain: the exits, the network they generate, why the network breathes with the seasons, and how it is compared with a map. It uses no equation. The equations are in Downslope distance between two networks.

## Where the water table reaches the ground

With the drainage condition, the model places a drain in every cell that has no fixed head, at the elevation of the ground. A drain lets water out when the water table rises to the ground surface, and in that direction only. Water that has left does not come back, and a river does not feed the aquifer in this setup.

Fig. 10 Look at: the cells where the head of the water table is above the ground line: only they release water. Does not show: how much water a drain releases, or a real catchment.

How much water a drain passes for a given rise of the water table depends on the hydraulic conductivity K of the cell: the more permeable the ground, the more freely it drains. The drain is not a free exit. Unless you declare a conductance, the model derives it from K and from the thickness of the clogging layer of the drain bed (the thin, less permeable film that lines a stream bed). The drain follows K, and this is why the extent of the network carries information on K.

In example 04, drains are the only way water leaves the aquifer: the list of boundary conditions of the model names the drain and nothing else.

## A seepage cell is a point, not a stream

A cell where the aquifer gives water back to the ground is a seepage cell. It is a point where water appears, a spring, and not a stretch of river. Isolated cells and short lines of cells are normal.

Fig. 11 Look at: the isolated blue cells, each a point where water leaves the aquifer. Does not show: any stream, which is drawn in the next step.

The request `variable = "seepage_mask"` of example 04, October 2002, the driest month of the series according to the comments of the example file (Reading the results).

The map above shows the raw state of the water table. For the network, the model asks a slightly different question: how much water leaves the cell. A cell counts as a source when it gives back more than a small share of the mean recharge over its area (the seepage threshold, 0.01 % of its own recharge by default). Another threshold changes the network maps. The test is made on the flux because the water budget fixes the flux, while “the head touches the ground” is a geometric condition that changes a lot when the drain conductance moves. The setting is `seepage_threshold`.

## Seepage cells draw the network

The water that leaves the aquifer in a seepage cell flows downhill over the ground. The simulated network is every cell this water goes through, from each source as far as the slope leads it. The slope is the one of the digital elevation model, read on the model cells. Pits (cells lower than all their neighbors, where water would be trapped) are filled first, so that every cell has a way down.

Fig. 12 Look at: the order of the steps: sources, routing downstream, then a threshold that gives the active network. Does not show: a river volume. The network is a view drawn after the computation, and the water budget fields stay untouched.

Fig. 13 Look at: the blue trunk and the orange upstream ends. Does not show: which reaches dry up in the field.

The request `variable = "simulated_active_network"` with `reduce = "frequency"` on example 04, year 2002, from the calibrated run. Blue cells flow every month of the year, orange cells some months, gray cells never.

Three things follow from this construction.

- The network has no width, depth or velocity. In the drain setup, the model does not compute the river. A cell “flows” means that the aquifer feeds it, directly or from upstream. There is no water level, no flood and no travel time in the channel. The routed streams described below are the exception.
- Its shape depends on the relief. A coarser cell size or a different digital elevation model moves the paths. A stream occupies one cell, so a map is read at the scale of the hillside, not of the field (see resolution).
- A flow threshold keeps only cells that carry water. On the flow maps, a downstream cell flows only if the water routed to it reaches a minimum discharge (the visible flow, `calibration.outputs.<name>.model.extent.visible_flow`, 1 L/s by default). It is a convention, and it does not mean the same as the seepage threshold, which counts only the exit points. No value is agreed on. Thresholds from 1 to 3 L/s are used in the field, and Zanetti et al. (2024) use 10 L/s for a simulated discharge. Another threshold changes the layout.

## Why the network grows in winter and shrinks in summer

The recharge feeds the water table. In winter the recharge is large and the water table rises. More cells reach the ground and give back water above the threshold, and the water of each of them reaches farther downhill. In summer the recharge is small, the water table drops, and the sources retreat toward the valley bottoms. The upstream ends of the streams dry up first, and only the reaches fed by the lowest water table keep flowing.

The model repeats this at every stress period, a month in example 04. For each period it finds the seepage cells, draws the network, and counts the cells that flow. Over a year, a cell is then:

- perennial, if it flows at every time step of the year;
- intermittent, if it flows at some time steps and not all;
- dry, if it never flows.

Example 04 shows it. The comment of its configuration file says that the seepage cells and the active network expand and contract with the wet winters and the dry summers. The maps of the example draw October 2002 because it is the driest month of the record.

Two limits come with a monthly step. A reach that dries up for two weeks does not appear, and “intermittent” means dry for at least one time step.

## What sets the size of the network

Two quantities compete: how fast the ground carries water away (K) and how much water arrives (the recharge). If the ground is permeable compared with the recharge, the water table stays deep, and the network retracts into the valley bottoms. If it is not, the water table reaches the ground on the hillsides, and the network reaches the upper slopes. The extent of the network is a function of the ratio of K to the recharge. This is what the calibration on the stream network exploits (Downslope distance between two networks). In example 04, the discharge at the outlet does not tell values of K apart, but the extent of the seepage does.

## What else can take water out

The drain is the way the model lets the aquifer produce streams. Other conditions exist, and they answer other questions. They should not be confused with it.

| You want | The model uses | What you give | What the model computes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The model to decide where water emerges | A drain at the ground, the `drainage` boundary of `flow.bc` | Nothing, or a drain conductance (`flow.bc.<name>.value`) | Where the water table reaches the ground, and how much water leaves |
| To impose the water level of a river on known cells | A fixed-head stream boundary (a `[flow.bc.stream]` table) | The head, on the cells tagged as river | The exchange with the aquifer, in either direction |
| The water that leaves to travel down a river | A routed stream network ([flow.sinks_sources.sfr]) | The reaches and their properties | The routing of the water along the reaches |
| A lake whose level moves | A lake package ([flow.sinks_sources.lakes]) | A footprint and a stage-volume-area table | The stage and the exchange with the aquifer |

The stream boundary is not available with MODFLOW-NWT. It prescribes a level: it supposes you know where the river is and how high its water stands. A drain supposes neither. Choose the drain when the network is the question.

Fig. 14 Look at: the direction of the arrows. With a stream boundary, you impose the water level of the river and the model computes the exchange. Does not show: the drain, which decides by itself where water comes out.

Whatever the condition, the network is read from the same quantity: the water the aquifer releases to the surface in each cell, summed over every condition that releases water.

## Comparing with a mapped network

A mapped network is the set of streams drawn on a map, such as the permanent reaches of the BD TOPO. It is a reference. The model never receives it.

- It is not burned into the relief.
- It does not place drains.
- It does not set K.

The model is built from the relief, the geology, the recharge and the thickness. The map is read afterwards, to score and to draw (Reading the results). You declare it as a data source ([data.hydrography]), and the code treats it as a diagnostic, not as a model input.

To compare the two networks, the lines of the map are first placed on the model cells (`drawn_by`). By default HydroModPy draws the map as the data gives it, on every cell a line crosses, the rule of the paper. The `heads` rule keeps only the places where the map says a stream starts, and lets the slope of the model draw the path below them. Field ditches and rectified reaches follow paths that a model on a digital elevation model cannot reproduce, and drawn cell by cell they count as errors of the model, which the `heads` rule avoids.

Then the comparison goes both ways, along the slope.

- From each cell of the simulated network, follow the slope down until you meet the mapped network. A long walk means the model makes a stream where the map has none: an excess.
- From each cell of the mapped network, follow the slope down until you meet the simulated network. A long walk means the model misses a stream of the map: a deficit.

When K increases, the simulated network retracts and the deficit grows. When K decreases, the network spreads and the excess grows. The calibration looks for the value of K where the two mean walks are equal. Scoring a simulated stream network says how to read these scores, and Downslope distance between two networks defines the distances.

A figure drawn from a finished run reads what the calibration trial read: the cell centers of the solver, the cells of open water, the outline of the catchment and the mean recharge the run kept. Lake cells leave both networks, because a line drawn across a lake is no stream and a lake cell is no hillslope seepage. So the map of a run shows the partition behind the score it reports. A run that kept no mean recharge cannot show a seepage threshold above zero, and a run that kept no cells of open water cannot be drawn. Both are refused with a sentence that says to replay the run with `hmp replay`, or to set `seepage_threshold = 0` for the first.

Calibrating on the map is not validating against it (What “validated” means here).

## Limits of the simulated network

In the drain setup the channel has no hydraulics, so the network gives no water depth and no velocity. The budget counts the water that leaves the aquifer as the release of the drains, and the network shows where this water leaves and where it goes. A simulated network counts as evidence once it is compared with a map that the calibration has not seen. The network is a set of cells, and this set changes at each time step.

## Where to go next

- Reading the results: the maps of example 04, one by one.
- Scoring a simulated stream network: how a simulated network is scored.
- [calibration.outputs]: the network criterion of a calibration.
- Downslope distance between two networks: the distances and the criterion, with equations.
- How water leaves the aquifer: how water leaves the aquifer.

# What HydroModPy does

One map and five sentences first. The rest of the page says what the model computes, from what, with which assumptions, and when not to use it. It needs no prerequisite, and every technical term links to the glossary.

Fig. 1 Look at: the blue trunk that flows all year and the orange ends that dry up first. Does not show: which reaches dry up in the field, or any other year.

Request `variable = "simulated_active_network"` with `reduce = "frequency"`, year 2002, demonstration model of example 04.

1. HydroModPy computes, for a whole catchment and for each month, the level of the groundwater under the ground, from the relief, the properties of the rock and the rain that reaches the water table.
1. Where that level reaches the ground, water comes out: these points are the springs of the model.
1. The streams are what these springs feed downhill. On the map, a stream is blue when it flows all year, orange when it flows part of the year, and gray when it never flows.
1. This map is a demonstration, not a study of the catchment: it was not compared with observations of dry reaches, so it is labeled indicative. Other results carry the labels calibrated or numerical check, and the label says how far to trust them (reliability label).
1. Every result depends on assumptions and on data, so read its caption, its label and the limits before you decide anything with it.

## What it automates

One TOML file drives these steps, the same way on every catchment:

1. Catchment extraction from a digital elevation model.
1. Forcing and observations: recharge, climate series, groundwater heads, gauged discharge, mapped stream networks and intermittency.
1. Mesh and vertical discretization suited to shallow basement aquifers, with parameters given per zone, per pixel of a raster or per cell, in steady state or in transient.
1. Calibration that combines heads, discharge and the extent of the stream network to constrain the hydraulic properties.
1. Outputs that can be reopened, stored with their provenance and the licence of the data they come from, then drawn as figures or exported to standard formats.

## In one diagram

HydroModPy solves the flow of water in the saturated part of the ground of a catchment, the part that lies below the water table. For each cell of the map and each time step, it computes the height of the water table (the hydraulic head), given how much water arrives from the soil, how fast the ground carries and stores it, and where it can leave. Everything else (water table depth, seepage, flow, stream network) is derived from this.

In example 04, the stream network is not an input. The model produces springs, and the network is derived from these springs. The mapped streams and the flow measured at the outlet are used to compare and to calibrate (see Calibration in two stages).

## What it computes

| Result | What it means in the model | Where to read it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The water table | The hydraulic head of each cell, hence the elevation of the water table and its depth below the ground (never negative). | Water table depth |
| Seepage | The cells where the water table reaches the ground surface. Water leaves the aquifer there through a drain placed at the surface. | Seepage cells |
| Baseflow | The water that leaves the aquifer through the drains, summed over the whole catchment: the groundwater part of the flow at the outlet. | Simulated against observed discharge, The water budget |
| Intermittence | For each month, the cells that flow. Over a year: always (perennial), sometimes (intermittent), never (dry). | Flow persistence |
| The budget | What enters the aquifer (the recharge), what leaves it (the drainage) and the change in the stock of water. | The water budget |

A note on the “simulated network”. A cell where the aquifer gives water back to the surface is a point where a stream appears, not a stretch of river. The model extends these cells downstream, following the slope of the ground, down to the outlet. This extension is the simulated network, the one that is compared with the map of streams. In this setup, which is the default, there is no hydraulic computation of the river. The How the model makes streams page shows the options that route the water along declared reaches.

## What it is computed from

| Data | Role | In example 04 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Relief | It gives the ground surface, hence the elevation at which water leaves. It delimits the catchment from the outlet and tells where the water flows downstream. | A digital elevation model, 75 m cells; 64.6 km² catchment traced from the outlet. |
| Geology | It sets how easily water moves (the hydraulic conductivity K) and the volume of water released when the water table drops (the specific yield Sy). One value for the whole aquifer, one per zone of a geological map, or one per pixel of a raster ([flow.param]). | A single value of K and a single value of Sy for the whole catchment: the geological map is not used. Both are calibrated (Calibration in two stages). |
| Recharge | The water that reaches the water table. It is provided (a series from a file, or SIM2 data from Météo-France), or computed by a soil reservoir from rainfall and potential evapotranspiration (theory). | A single monthly recharge series for the whole catchment, and a runoff series (data sources). |
| Thickness | The depth of the aquifer below the ground surface. It is an assumption, not a measurement. | 30 m everywhere. |
| Observations | The mapped network and the flow measured at the outlet are not part of the physical computation. They are used to compare the results and to calibrate K and Sy. | The permanent stretches of the BD TOPO and the NANCON station. |

Where each dataset comes from is on Where the data come from.

In the drain setup of example 04, the solver is MODFLOW 6, the reference code of the United States Geological Survey (USGS). HydroModPy prepares the data, runs MODFLOW 6 and reads its results back. Other solvers exist, see Other solvers below.

## The assumptions to keep in mind

Each row says what the model assumes and what that changes when reading the maps. The rows marked “example 04” describe that configuration file, not the software: another model can lift them. The rows marked “drain setup” hold for the drain condition used in example 04 and not for the other conditions of How the model makes streams.

| Assumption | Consequence for reading |
| --- | --- |
| Unconfined aquifer, a single layer of constant thickness below the ground (example 04: 30 m). | No deep aquifer and no layers of different kinds. The depth of the water table cannot exceed the thickness of the model. |
| Uniform K and Sy (example 04). | The pattern of the water table mostly follows the relief. Geological contrasts are not represented. |
| Water leaves through drains placed at the ground surface, in one direction only (drain setup). | Water that leaves does not return to the aquifer. A river does not feed the aquifer in this setup. |
| The efficiency of a drain depends on K and on the thickness of the clogging layer of the drain bed (How the model makes streams). | The larger K is, the more the aquifer is drained. This is why the seepage network carries information on K. |
| Identical recharge over the whole catchment, monthly average (example 04). | No variation of rainfall from one hillside to another, or from one day to another within the month. |
| One stress period per month, and the first month in steady state. | The first month sets the starting state. The documentation of the setting that cuts a month into several steps, `simulation.time.substeps_per_period`, states that a single step per month changes the monthly flow by 4 to 28 % compared with a refined computation, depending on the case. |
| No hydraulic model of the rivers (drain setup). | No water level, flood or propagation. A stream that “flows” means: the aquifer feeds it. |
| The simulated network follows the slope of the ground downstream of the seepage cells. | Its shape depends on the digital elevation model and on the cell size. |
| If the recharge comes from the soil reservoir (theory): the soil ignores the height of the water table, and snow counts as rain. | A high water table does not reduce the soil reserve. The documentation of the soil reservoir judges it unsuitable for a snow-covered catchment. Available with MODFLOW 6 only. |

The intended range of validity of the project, as the scientific documentation states it: shallow aquifers at catchment scale, unconfined or weakly confined, where the relief, the stream network and the geology organize the flow. Large deep sedimentary basins and coupled surface and atmosphere models fall outside this range. The limits are listed in the theory of the flow problem, and the page What “validated” means here says how far the model has been tested.

## Other solvers

Example 04 uses MODFLOW 6. HydroModPy runs two other flow solvers behind the same configuration file: MODFLOW-NWT, an older code of the same family, and a Boussinesq solver that is part of HydroModPy. They do not support the same boundaries or the same meshes. Lakes, reservoirs and routed streams, for example, need MODFLOW 6. The list of solvers says what each one supports. Every statement about the solver on this page is about example 04.

## Calibration in two stages

K cannot be measured at catchment scale. The model of example 04 infers it, a step called calibration, in two stages, with the method published by Abhervé et al. (2023, Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 27, 3221-3239). The example file also cites their 2025 article for the second stage:

1. K is adjusted, in steady state, until the simulated seepage network matches the mapped network.
1. Sy is adjusted, in monthly transient state, against the flow measured at the outlet, with the first year used as spin-up.

Direct consequence: in a calibrated run, the map of the network and the flow curve show what was adjusted. Their agreement is expected. It does not prove on its own that the model is right. The page Reading the results comes back to this point map by map. The settings of this method are those of [calibration.protocol].

## What it does not compute

- River hydraulics in the drain setup: water level, floods, propagation, storage in the riverbed. The routed stream option of MODFLOW 6 adds a routing of the water along declared reaches (How the model makes streams).
- Surface runoff, unless it is provided as data (example 04) or, with the soil reservoir, for the sealed part of the surface. The groundwater model does not produce floods.
- The unsaturated zone in detail. The soil reservoir is a simple budget (usable reserve, evapotranspiration, delay before reaching the water table), not an infiltration model.
- Abstractions, unless they are declared as wells in the configuration.
- Water quality. Solute transport and particle tracking exist separately and are not covered here. Neither are lakes and reservoirs, which exist as an option of MODFLOW 6.
- The future by default. The model replays the forcings it is given. For a climate projection, projection data must be provided. Comparison with measurements then no longer makes sense.

## The limits of this example

- A single catchment and three years: the result says nothing about the variability from one year to the next.
- The figures and the numbers of Reading the results come from one calibrated run, described at the end of that page. A new run gives different values.
- No comparison with piezometer levels or with field flow observations: example 04 does not use them.
- A 75 m cell: a map is read at the scale of the hillside, not of the field.

## When not to use this

HydroModPy is built for shallow groundwater at the scale of a catchment. Do not rely on it for these cases, or only with an expert.

- Deep or confined aquifers, and large sedimentary basins. The model describes a shallow aquifer whose top rises and falls with the recharge. See the limits in the theory.
- Aquifers where water moves mostly through conduits, such as karst. The model treats the ground as a continuous porous medium.
- Floods and river hydraulics. In the default setup there is no water level, no flood and no travel time in the channel (How the model makes streams).
- Decisions at the scale of a field or a plot. A cell is 75 m wide in example 04, and a map is read at the scale of the hillside.
- Water quality, unless a transport computation has been set up for it. The maps of this part of the site are about water, not about what it carries.
- Climate projections taken as forecasts. The model replays the forcing it is given. A projection is only as good as the climate data and the evaluation behind it.
- A single result taken as certain. Read a result as an indication unless it was validated (What “validated” means here, How sure is the model?).

## One catchment as a common thread

The pages rely on example 04 of HydroModPy: the Nançon catchment (Ille-et-Vilaine, 64.6 km²), simulated from 2000 to 2002 with a monthly step. The example shows how the seepage network grows in winter and shrinks in summer, and how the hydraulic conductivity and the specific yield of the aquifer are calibrated against the mapped network and against the flow measured at the outlet.

This is a demonstration example. Its results illustrate how to read the outputs. They are not a study of the catchment.

Next: Reading the results.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/understand/what-validated-means.html -->
# What “validated” means here

The word validated is used loosely. In this documentation it has a narrow meaning. This page separates four kinds of evidence, because they do not answer the same question.

## Four kinds of evidence

| Evidence | The question it answers | What it does not answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Numerical verification | Does the code solve the equations it claims to solve? | Whether the equations describe your catchment. |
| Calibration | Can the parameters be tuned so that the model reproduces the observations? | Whether the model would predict anything it was not tuned on. |
| Validation | Does the calibrated model reproduce measurements it has not seen, on another period or on another catchment? | Whether it holds under conditions unlike all those tested. |
| Peer review | Have independent experts read the method and found it sound? | Whether a given run is right. |

### Numerical verification

HydroModPy checks its solvers against references that do not come from HydroModPy: a closed-form solution, a published MODFLOW 6 example, a manufactured solution, or a parameter that a calibration must find again. Each check is a test, run in continuous integration, and Validation lists every one with the reference it uses and the threshold it must stay under. On the maps of Reading the results, the label refers to this kind of evidence, for instance the closure of the water budget.

### Calibration

A calibration adjusts parameters until the results look like observations. When a calibrated result agrees with those observations, the agreement is what the calibration looked for. It is not independent evidence. The label says so.

### Validation

A validation compares the model with measurements that the calibration did not use, such as a period held out, or a neighboring catchment. This is the test that counts for a prediction. Example 04 contains none: the same years are used to calibrate and to look at the results, and the figures say so. A study that relies on HydroModPy for a decision should include one.

The papers and the catchments where HydroModPy has been used are listed in Applications and papers.

### Peer review

The two-stage method of calibration used in example 04 is published and peer reviewed (Abhervé et al., 2023, Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 27, 3221-3239). The technical note that describes the toolbox is published and peer reviewed too (Gauvain et al., 2026, Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 30, 5571-5592), but it describes version 1.0. The review did not cover the code of version 2 that this site documents. A published method does not make a particular run right, and a run is no more reliable for being made with a reviewed method.

## The label of a run

A sealed run also carries a run label, one of four words computed when the run is read: exploratory, calibrated, evaluated or failed. It follows rule 3 of `hydromodpy.results.validity_rules`. A run promoted by a calibration session is calibrated only when a window was scored. That window is a calibration period the seal records, the headline window of the run with at least one sample, or the single state of a steady run whose cost the session read. A transient run promoted without any of them is exploratory, with the reason “no scored window”. A calibrated run scored on days the calibration never saw is evaluated. A run whose solver did not converge is failed.

Each label comes with its reasons, in English or in French. A parameter that ended on a bound of its range adds the reason “a parameter reached its bound”, whatever the label. This does not change the label, but it says that the search wanted to go further than the range allowed, so the value found is a limit and not a best estimate. The method text of a run (`hydromodpy.results.method.method_text`) writes the label, its rule, its reasons and the state of each check, passed, failed or unknown.

The label, with its rule and the date, is printed in the footer of every figure of a sealed run, for instance “Nancon · 2010-2015 · HydroModPy 2.0 · calibrated, rule 3, 2026-11-07”. A figure drawn from a directory without a seal reads “unlabelled”.

## What this means for a decision

- A result labeled Numerical check is safe to read as a statement about the solver.
- A result labeled Calibrated shows that the calibration worked.
- A result labeled Indicative is a model output that no measurement has confirmed.
- None of the three labels is a validation. If a decision depends on a result, ask for a validation on data that the calibration did not see, and read How sure is the model?.

## Where to go next

- Validation: every test of the code against a reference.
- How sure is the model?: how far a result can be wrong.
- Can I check what was run?: how to check what produced a result.

# Where the data come from

A result is only as good as its inputs. This page names the data that HydroModPy can read, who produces them, how fine they are, and what to do about their licences. It is written for a reader who must judge a result, not for one who must download data: the keys that declare the data are in [data].

## What the model reads

The model reads its data from files that you give it, or from public providers that it can download from. Example 04 uses files of the project. The last column says what it used.

| Data | Producer | Form and fineness | Example 04 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Relief (digital elevation model) | The national mapping agency (IGN): BD ALTI at 25 m, or RGE ALTI at 1 m or 5 m | Regular grid | A raster file with 75 m cells |
| Geological map | The geological survey (BRGM): a map at 1:1,000,000, or the harmonized map at 1:50,000 | Polygons, with the scale of the map as limit | Not used: one value of K for the catchment |
| Mapped streams | Sandre and the French Biodiversity Office (BD Topage); the Copernicus land service (EU-Hydro); OpenStreetMap. A file of your own works too, such as the BD TOPO of IGN | Lines | The permanent reaches of the BD TOPO, from a file of the project |
| Discharge at a gauge | The public interface Hub’Eau (French Biodiversity Office and BRGM), for the national hydrometry | Daily series at a station | The NANCON station, averaged by month |
| Observed flow state of small streams | Hub’Eau, from the national low-flow observatory | Visits at stations | Not used |
| Groundwater levels | Hub’Eau, from the national portal for groundwater data (ADES) | Series at wells | Not used |
| Rain and evapotranspiration | Météo-France, the SIM2 reanalysis | 8 km grid | The recharge and the runoff are series given as files of the project |
| Climate projections | Météo-France, distributed through the DRIAS portal (Explore2) | 8 km grid | Not used |
| Sea level | The naval hydrographic service (SHOM), tide gauges | Series at a gauge | Not used |

This list is read from the data sources that the code knows. The generated page Data sources gives the complete list of the sources, the producer of each and the section of the file that takes it.

## A DEM conditioned elsewhere

A DEM you give may already be filled or breached by another tool. You say so with `state = "conditioned"` on its `[[data.dem.sources]]` entry, the default being `state = "raw"`. HydroModPy then skips its own conditioning and still computes the D8 directions and the accumulation. It refuses an aggregation, a crossing notch or a declared conditioning method beside a conditioned DEM, because those would undo what the other tool did. If the DEM still keeps cells with no lower neighbour, the run warns with their count: D8 gives those cells no direction and the catchment may stop there.

## Fineness matters

Each input has its own scale, and the model cannot be finer than the inputs that control a result.

- The rain comes on an 8 km grid. The catchment of example 04 is 64.6 km², so a few grid points cover it. In example 04, one monthly recharge series serves the whole catchment: no difference between two hillsides.
- The relief sets where water leaves the ground, and the cell of the model is 75 m. A map is read at the scale of the hillside (resolution).
- A geological map at 1:50,000 draws zones that are hundreds of meters wide. It does not tell the conductivity of a particular field.
- A mapped stream network draws what someone chose to draw, with a positional error. The score of a network takes it into account only if that error is declared (Scoring a simulated stream network).

## Licences

Public data do not all carry the same licence. The licence of each source, when the code knows it, is listed on the generated page Data sources. Where the code does not know it, the page says so. It does not guess.

A file keeps its licence in its companion file, the sidecar. A download writes the licence of its source there, and a run reads it back from there when it records the file.

Three rules follow from the way the code records licences.

- A file you provide has the licence you declare. The model cannot know the licence of your file. You state it in a small companion file next to the data.
- A result inherits from its inputs. A run states the combined licence of what it read, and writes it into the attributes of its field files and the footers of its tables. If one input has no known licence, the run states undetermined. A run cannot promise more than its least known input allows.
- Undetermined is not forbidden. It means that nobody recorded the terms. Read the terms of the producer before you reuse or redistribute a result. `hmp publish --public` warns when the project declares no licence or an input has none, writes the copy anyway, and states undetermined for what has no licence.

This page is not legal advice. Cite the producer of the data that a result relies on.

## Can I check which data were used?

Yes. Each run lists its input files with their checksums, and the project can pin the whole data cache with `hmp data lock`. See Can I check what was run?.

## Where to go next

- Data sources: every source, its producer and its licence.
- [data]: declare or download the data of a project.
- What “validated” means here: why a good input is not a validated result.

| --- | --- |

# `[calibration]`

Top-level `[calibration]` section.

- `calibration`[table] · optional · 116 user keys, 5 dev or expert
- Start a file: `hmp config template --modules calibration` (download it), then `hmp check file.toml`. Minimal file
[calibration]

`# method = ‹string›` : Optimization method. experimental
**Path**: `calibration.method`
**More**: Unset, it follows from what the calibration scores: 'bisection' when it moves one parameter in log space and every one of its blocks is signed (distance_gap), since the answer is then a zero to find; 'scipy_nelder_mead' otherwise, a cost to minimise. Write it to depart from that choice, and whenever method_options are given. A phase of [[calibration.phases]] names its own. Built-ins: 'grid' (regular sweep, sized by method_options.points_per_dim), 'lhs' (stratified Latin hypercube, sized by method_options.n_samples), 'lhs_zoom' (Latin hypercubes in turn, each in the zone the trials so far leave open, sized by method_options.levels, one parameter), 'random_search', 'bisection' (root of a signed criterion on one parameter, the stream-network stage), 'optuna' (TPE), 'cma_es', 'scipy_de', 'scipy_nelder_mead' and 'gp_mapping'. An unknown name is refused when the file is read, with the list installed here. Optuna is installed by default; install the calibration extra for cma_es and Optuna's cmaes sampler.
**Accepted**: string

`# evaluator = ‹string›` : What turns one parameter sample into a cost. experimental
**Path**: `calibration.evaluator`
**More**: Unset runs the HydroModPy pipeline, which is what every calibrated number in this repository was produced with. A string and not an enumeration: the values that resolve depend on what is installed beside HydroModPy, which is how a surrogate or a foreign model is named without a patch. This build also ships 'analytic_bowl', which runs no model and scores a closed-form surface whose minimum is the midpoint of each parameter's interval: it rehearses a whole search -- space, optimizer, stopping rule, report -- in milliseconds, against an answer known in advance.
**Accepted**: string

`# max_trials = "auto"` : Maximum number of evaluations of the search. > 0 experimental
**Path**: `calibration.max_trials`
**More**: It is the only bound on how long a search runs: no method option counts evaluations of its own. 'auto' lets an engine that counts its evaluations before the first solve size its own budget. Four do. The grid, the Latin hypercube and the zoomed Latin hypercube count their design, one evaluation per point (per point of every level for the zoom), and refuse a smaller number before the first solve, since a sweep cut short is not its design. The bisection counts with d the declared interval in decades, t = log10(1 + rel_tol), S the sweep points (counted as 2 for sweep_points 0), s = d / (S - 1) and E = bracket_expand, a root inside the bounds costs S + ceil(log2(s / t)) and one found after e expansions S + 2e + ceil(log2(1 / t)); 'auto' budgets the largest, 23 on [1e-7, 1e-3] m/s with seven points and one per cent (15 inside the bounds). A number below the nominal count is refused before the first solve, one below the worst case is announced, and a budget that still runs out gets exactly the halvings left, once. Any other engine gets 100 from 'auto' and no extension: a search that spends its budget before its own stopping rule is reported as not converged, and a re-run with a larger max_trials replays the trials already solved from the cache.
**Values**:
- `"auto"`
**Accepted**: integer or "auto"
**Valid range**: > 0 (refused outside)
**Was**: `calibration.max_iter`

`# precision = ‹number›` : How precisely the search has to pin a parameter before it stops, as a relative precision on the parameter itself: 0.01 asks for one per cent, 0.1 for ten. - > 0 experimental
**Path**: `calibration.precision`
**More**: On a parameter searched in log space that is a ratio, which is how a conductivity is known in the first place, and it holds wherever the value sits; on any other search space there is no scale on the value to be relative to before the search has one, so it reads as a fraction of the declared interval. Each engine's own stopping option is written from it, so the same number survives a change of engine, and the engine's own option stays available for reproducing a published call verbatim. Unset, the engine's default applies. An engine that stops on its budget rather than on a precision refuses this rather than ignore it.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: > 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: -
**Was**: `calibration.tolerance`

`# batch_size = 1` : Number of suggestions drawn per ask, at least `parallel`. - >= 1 experimental
**Path**: `calibration.batch_size`
**Accepted**: integer
**Valid range**: >= 1 (refused outside)
**Unit**: -

`# parallel = 1` : Trials solved side by side, each in its own folder, for every phase that sets none of its own. - >= 1 experimental
**Path**: `calibration.parallel`
**More**: A grid or a random search evaluates its points together; a root search cuts its bracket into parallel + 1 parts; a simplex evaluates the candidates of one step together and keeps the sequential answer, so a width above 4 buys it nothing, and CMA-ES and differential evolution stop at their population. A width above 1 gives each worker process its own copy of the model (about 0.5 GiB, 3 s to start); 1 solves the trials one after the other in this process.
**Accepted**: integer
**Valid range**: >= 1 (refused outside)
**Unit**: -

`# reject_water_budget_above = 1.0` : Percent water-balance discrepancy of the whole model past which a trial is rejected instead of scored. % >= 0 experimental
**Path**: `calibration.reject_water_budget_above`
**More**: The figure is the one the solver prints for the volume budget of the entire model, not the budget of a single package such as the lake package, which divides by small flows and reads higher. A rejected trial is marked failed, so it is neither ranked nor promoted: part of the water it routed came from nowhere and its cost is not comparable to a run that closed. Default 1.0 (one per cent). Raise it for a transient model whose lake or routed network legitimately sits higher. A TOML file has no null: to switch the gate off write a value no run reaches, such as 1000, or pass None from Python. The worst time step of the run decides, not the last.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: >= 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: %

`# seed = ‹integer›` : Seed of the random draws of the search (starting points, samples). - experimental
**Path**: `calibration.seed`
**More**: The same seed with the same file gives the same trials.
**Accepted**: integer
**Unit**: -

`# save_runs = "best_n"` : Which trials become runs once the search ends. experimental
**Path**: `calibration.save_runs`
**More**: Every trial leaves one line in sessions/<case>/trials.jsonl whatever the mode. 'best_n' promotes the best trial of the last phase to runs/<case>/, the calibrated run, and keeps the save_best_n - 1 next ones under sessions/<case>/trials/<n>/. 'all' keeps every completed trial there. 'none' promotes nothing.
**Values**:
- `"none"`
- `"best_n"`
- `"all"`
**Accepted**: "none" | "best_n" | "all"

`# save_best_n = 1` : Number of trials the 'best_n' mode of save_runs keeps as runs: 1 is the calibrated run alone, under runs/<case>/. - >= 0 experimental
**Path**: `calibration.save_best_n`
**Accepted**: integer
**Valid range**: >= 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: -

`# promote_phases = false` : Also promote the best trial of each phase before the last one, under sessions/<case>/phases/<phase>/best/. experimental
**Path**: `calibration.promote_phases`
**More**: The calibrated run of the case is the best trial of the last phase whatever this says.
**Accepted**: true | false

`# objective = "nse"` : Metric scoring the single simulated series, when no objective block is declared. experimental
**Path**: `calibration.objective`
**More**: Same vocabulary as a block's 'metric'; typed here so a bad value is reported against the key that was written.
**Values**:
- `"rmse"` : Root-mean-square error, in the observed unit; penalizes large misfits most.
- `"nse"` : Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency against the observed mean; the standard choice for a level or discharge series.
- `"kge"` : Kling-Gupta efficiency, 2009 form (bias as the ratio of sums, variability as the ratio of standard deviations); separates correlation, variability and bias when NSE alone is ambiguous.
- `"mae"` : Mean absolute error, in the observed unit; less sensitive to outliers than RMSE.
- `"nse_log"` : NSE on log-transformed series; weights low flows as heavily as peaks, good for recessions.
- `"nse_delta"` : NSE on the increments of the series rather than its level; a level is an integral and can hide flux errors that compensate, which only its increments show.
- `"nse_seasonal"` : NSE against the seasonal cycle rather than the overall mean; asks whether the model beats climatology.
- `"reservoir"` : Half nse_seasonal plus half nse_delta, built for an impounded level: a plain NSE there is beaten by the seasonal cycle, and the increments are what carry the flux errors.
- `"distance_gap"` : Balances the simulated stream network against the mapped one; zero marks the crossing.
- `"distance_mean"` : Mean spatial offset between simulated and mapped streams; a diagnostic, not a substitute for distance_gap.
- `"bfi_error"` : Distance between the simulated and observed baseflow indices (Wallingford, daily discharge only); asks whether the stream is fed by its aquifer in the right share. Blind to volume and timing, so it goes beside a fit, never alone.
**Accepted**: "rmse" | "nse" | "kge" | "mae" | "nse_log" | "nse_delta" | "nse_seasonal" | "reservoir" | "distance_gap" | "distance_mean" | "bfi_error"

`# variable = "head"` : Name of the simulated variable, or of a [calibration.outputs] entry, that objective scores when no objective block is declared. experimental
**Path**: `calibration.variable`
**See**: calibration.outputs
**Accepted**: string

`# method_options = {}` : Options of the method, named as that method names them: points_per_dim for 'grid', sampler for 'optuna', sweep_points for 'bisection'. experimental
**Path**: `calibration.method_options`
**More**: They belong to one method, so a calibration that gives them writes method beside them. A key the method does not take is refused when the file loads.
**Accepted**: table { key = any value }
**Was**: `calibration.optimizer_kwargs`

`# persist_iteration_detail = "summary"` : How much of each trial's cost the session keeps: 'none' skips component metrics; 'summary' keeps block totals; 'full' also stores per-block raw and normalized costs. experimental
**Path**: `calibration.persist_iteration_detail`
**Values**:
- `"none"`
- `"summary"`
- `"full"`
**Accepted**: "none" | "summary" | "full"

`# persist_trial_series = true` : Write the simulated and observed series of every point/series output a completed trial scored (discharge at a gauge, head at a well...), as a small Parquet table per trial under the session folder, about 2 kB per trial on the island case. experimental
**Path**: `calibration.persist_trial_series`
**More**: Network and spatial outputs carry no series and are never written here.
**Accepted**: true | false

`# use_cache = true` : Enable params_hash content-addressable cache. dev experimental
**Path**: `calibration.use_cache`
**Accepted**: true | false

`# materialize_candidates = false` : Write a standalone overlay TOML for each candidate under sessions/<case>/candidates/, so a trial can be replayed by hand. dev experimental
**Path**: `calibration.materialize_candidates`
**Accepted**: true | false

# `[data]`

Top-level `[data]` configuration for the data variables.

- `data`[table] · optional · 337 user keys, 136 dev or expert
- Start a file: `hmp config template --modules data` (download it), then `hmp check file.toml`. Minimal file

Connections found in the code (1)
- The code says `flow.sinks_sources.recharge.soil`: [flow.sinks_sources.recharge.soil] computes the recharge from the precipitation and the ETP, and data.types also loads one from [data.recharge]: the model would receive one and ignore the other. Remove "recharge" from data.types to keep the soil reservoir (and write recharge__delete = true under [data] if a base file declares it), or remove [flow.sinks_sources.recharge.soil] to use the loaded rech

[data]

`# types = []` : Ordered list of data variables explicitly requested in [data].
**Path**: `data.types`
**More**: The launcher may append inferred types deduced from other sections (for example domain.zone_ids, a [flow.bc.stream] table). Allowed values: 'crossings', 'curve_number', 'dem', 'etp', 'geology', 'humidity', 'hydrography', 'hydrometry', 'impervious', 'infiltration_ratio', 'intermittency', 'lake_abacus', 'lake_bathymetry', 'lake_geometry', 'lake_inflow', 'lake_levels', 'lake_outflow', 'lake_withdrawal', 'layer_base', 'oceanic', 'piezometry', 'precipitation', 'property_map', 'radiation', 'recharge', 'runoff', 'soil_capacity', 'soil_moisture', 'substratum', 'temperature', 'water_quality', 'wind'.
**Accepted**: list of string

`# inference_mode = "warn"` : Policy applied when the planner infers types not explicitly listed in data.types.
**Path**: `data.inference_mode`
**More**: 'warn': keep inferred types and continue even if data.<type> is missing. 'strict': raise when an inferred type has no explicit data.<type> section (except geology, which can use its default typed config).
**See**: data.types
**Values**:
- `"warn"`
- `"strict"`
**Accepted**: "warn" | "strict"

# `[flow]`

Flow-process configuration.

- `flow`[table] · optional · 373 user keys, 105 dev or expert
- Start a file: `hmp config template --modules flow` (download it), then `hmp check file.toml`. Minimal file
[flow]

`# flow_regime = "transient"` : Whether the flow is solved as one equilibrium state or through time over the stress periods of [simulation.time].
**Path**: `flow.flow_regime`
**See**: simulation.time
**Values**:
- `"steady"` : Solves one equilibrium state, with no storage term: one stress period over the whole [simulation.time] window, whatever its step_value says, with the forcings averaged over the window.
- `"transient"` : Solves the heads through time; it starts from the state [flow.ic] gives.
**Accepted**: "steady" | "transient"
**Example**: `"steady"`, `"transient"`

`# first_period_steady = true` : For transient flow, mark the first solver stress period as steady-state.
**Path**: `flow.first_period_steady`
**More**: Ignored for steady flow, where all solver periods are steady.
**Accepted**: true | false
**Example**: `true`, `false`

`# param_list = []` : Ordered list of the flow parameter ids the run builds, for example ['K', 'Ss', 'Sy'].
**Path**: `flow.param_list`
**More**: Each id is described by its [flow.param.<id>] table.
**Accepted**: list of string
**Example**: `["K", "Sy", "Ss"]`

# TOML parameters

Every section of the configuration file, generated from the models. Each page reads like the file you write: one block per table, the keys you must write first, optional keys commented with their default, developer and expert keys behind a switch, one tab per shape when a table has several. Click a line for its card.

Two commands go from a block to a verdict:

```
hmp config template --modules flow > flow.toml   # the keys of one section
hmp check my_run.toml                     # validate a file
```

[[data.hydrography.sources]]

`source = "file"` : Data provider. required example value
**Path**: `data.hydrography.sources.source`
**More**: Any source id this installation resolves and that serves river linework is accepted, so a third-party source registered on the 'hydromodpy.data.source' entry-point group is named here by its id.
**Accepted**: string
**Example**: `"file"`

**Path**: `data.hydrography.sources.url`
**Accepted**: string

**Accepted**: string

**More**: Unset means undetermined.

**Workspace file**: `workspace:<name>` reads `data/hydrography/<name>` of the workspace, and `workspace:.` the folder itself

# Python API

`import hydromodpy as hmp`. The functions below are the entry points of the package; the objects they return hold the results. The Command line column names the `hmp` command that is the twin of each function.

## A minimal session

```
import hydromodpy as hmp

run = hmp.run("path/to/config.toml").open()   # simulate, then open the Run
head = run.read("head")           # an xarray.DataArray
run.figure("water_budget")   # draw a shipped preset

proj = hmp.open("path/to/project")     # reopen the project later, read only
run = proj["baseline"]                 # one of its runs, by name
```

How these objects relate, and what `Run.read` returns for each kind of variable, is on Objects and how they relate. What can be raised, with the `HMPY.Exxx` codes, is on Exceptions and error codes.

## Stability

This page documents `hydromodpy 2.0.1`. The public surface is the 52 names of `hydromodpy.__all__` (17 functions, 7 classes, 27 exceptions and 1 other names), the classes they return, and the exceptions of this reference. A name outside this reference is internal, except the modules for extensions on the contracts page. So is the `hydromodpy.project.api` module.

This is a final release: a name listed here changes only under the rules of the versions page. Versions follow semantic versioning with PEP 440 pre-release tags. What each kind of version may change is on the versions page.

## Functions

| Function | What it does | Returns | Command line |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `hmp.calibrate()` | Run the calibration a configuration declares, or say what it would run. | `CalibrationReport`, `CalibrationPlan` | `hmp calibrate` |
| `hmp.check()` | Check a configuration, a draft or a file, and return every diagnostic it holds. | `Diagnostic` | `hmp check`, `hmp run` |
| `hmp.compare()` | Compare sealed runs, the first one as the reference. | `Comparison` | `hmp diff` |
| `hmp.doctor()` | Say what this machine runs: Python, HydroModPy, the packages and the solvers. | `DoctorReport` | `hmp doctor` |
| `hmp.example()` | List the examples this build ships, show some, or install one, several or all. | `ExampleEntry`, `ExampleEntry`, `InstallReport`, `InstallReport` | `hmp example` |
| `hmp.export()` | Export data of a run to files, or deliver what its `[[export]]` blocks name. | `PublishedLine` | `hmp export` |
| `hmp.open()` | Open what a path stands for: a project, a run, a session or a workspace. | `Project`, `Run`, `Session`, `Workspace` | `hmp show`, `hmp export` |
| `hmp.publish()` | Copy a sealed run, the summary or every sealed run of a project out of the tree. | `PublishedProject` | `hmp publish` |
| `hmp.replay()` | Play a sealed run, or a published copy, again, and class the values it computes. | `RunOutcome` | `hmp replay` |
| `hmp.run()` | Run a simulation or an overview. | `RunOutcome`, `PlanDraft`, `OverviewResult` | `hmp run` |
| `hmp.show()` | Read one thing of a run, a session, a set of runs or a project. | `dict or DataFrame or Series or DataArray or Figure or Path` | `hmp show` |
| `hmp.spinup()` | Run a cyclic spin-up, and a production run from its state when asked. | `SpinupResult` | `hmp spinup` |
| `hmp.status()` | Say where runs and sessions stand, read from the disk and never from the index. | `RunOutcome`, `RunOutcome`, `StatusReport` | `hmp ls` |
| `hmp.stop()` | Ask a running run or calibration session to stop, and return its flag. | `pathlib.Path` | `hmp stop` |
| `hmp.trash()` | Move a run or a session to `trash/`, or bring a trashed one back. | `list of pathlib.Path` | `hmp catalog` |

<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/reference/calibration-methods.html -->
# Calibration methods and metrics

Every search method a calibration file can name, and every metric an objective block can score with. Both lists are read from the code at each build: the optimizer registry, the options model and the declared traits of each engine, the metric kernels and their formulas. Why the objective is built this way is in The inverse problem of a calibration.

## Methods

A file names a method with `calibration.method`, or per phase with `calibration.phases.method`. Left unset, the search gets the first method whose conditions it meets: `hmp calibrate FILE --list-phases` prints the choice and the reason, for each phase or for the one search of a file without phases. A name that is not registered is refused before anything is prepared, at the start of every launch and by `hmp check`, with the list of the names that are.

| Method | What it does | Parameters | Stops on | Parallel |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| bisection | A root search on one parameter: a coarse log sweep, then the bracket is halved. | One, in log space only | precision | yes |
| cma_es | Covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy, from the `cma` package. | Any number | budget | yes |
| gp_mapping | A Gaussian-process surrogate of the cost, refined where the expected improvement is highest. | Any number | budget | yes |
| grid | Every point of a regular grid, in the space each parameter is sampled in. | Any number | design | yes |
| lhs | One Latin hypercube design, drawn before any solve and evaluated whole. | Any number | design | yes |
| lhs_zoom | Latin hypercubes in turn, each one in the zone the trials so far leave open. | One | design | yes |
| optuna | An Optuna study driven trial by trial, with the TPE sampler by default. | Any number | budget | yes |
| random_search | Independent draws from the sampling of each parameter. | Any number | budget | yes |
| scipy_de | Differential evolution, `scipy.optimize.differential_evolution`. | Any number | budget | yes |
| scipy_nelder_mead | A local simplex, `scipy.optimize.minimize(method='Nelder-Mead')`. | Any number | precision | yes |

### `bisection`

A root search on one parameter: a coarse log sweep, then the bracket is halved.

It reads a signed residual, so every block it scores must use `distance_gap`, and the parameter must be searched in log space. It stops on the width of the bracket, never on the size of the residual. It is the method a search that names none gets when those conditions hold. Use it for the stream-network stage: one conductivity against a mapped network.

Options, written under `calibration.method_options` with `method` beside them, or in the `method_options` of a phase:

| Option | Type | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `rel_tol` | float | `0.01` | Relative width of the bracket at which the search stops, on the calibrated parameter. The paper’s one per cent. The criterion is never the size of the residual: it steps over zero and would never get small enough. |
| `signed_component` | str | `"J_signed"` | Name of the component carrying the signed residual whose sign the search brackets. Left at ‘J_signed’, a network output scored on two bounds is searched on J_signed_minimal and J_signed_maximal, one root each, and the value returned is their weighted geometric mean. Any other name is one root. |
| `sweep_points` | int | `7` | Points of the coarse log sweep run before the bisection. It checks the monotonicity the paper assumes instead of supposing it, sees every crossing, and produces the crossing curves for free. Zero gives the pure bisection of the paper. |
| `bracket_expand` | int | `4` | How many times the interval may be widened by one decade when no sign change is found. Beyond that the search raises rather than returning the better of the two ends. |

- Parameters: One, in log space only
- Criterion: A signed one only: every block it scores reads a signed residual, `distance_gap`.
- Stops: On a precision on the parameter: `calibration.precision` writes `rel_tol`, a relative precision on the parameter, passed through as is.
- Budget: `max_trials = "auto"` counts the evaluations its rule needs before the first solve. A smaller number is refused or warned before anything is prepared, at every launch and by `hmp check`.
- Parallel trials: Yes, with `calibration.parallel`.
- Starts from an earlier phase: No.
- Restarts: Refused by the `multistart` uncertainty: it returns the same answer every time.
- Without a method: Chosen first, when the search meets every condition above.

### `cma_es`

Covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy, from the `cma` package.

It needs the `calibration` extra. It can start from the value an earlier phase passed on. Use it on several parameters with a broad box and a cost with plateaus.

Options, written under `calibration.method_options` with `method` beside them, or in the `method_options` of a phase:

| Option | Type | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sigma0` | float | `0.25` | Initial step size, in the unit cube when normalize is true, else in the space the search walks. |
| `popsize` | int | `6` | Points evaluated per generation. |
| `normalize` | bool | `true` | Rescale the box to the unit cube before the strategy runs. |
| `restarts` | int | `0` | Fresh strategies started from a perturbed point when one stops before the budget is spent. Zero keeps one strategy. |

- Parameters: Any number
- Stops: On its budget, or on a rule of its own options. Spending the budget is not convergence: the search says it spent its budget, and a phase freezes its best saying it froze the best of a budget-only search. `calibration.precision` is refused.
- Budget: `max_trials = "auto"` gives 100 evaluations.
- Parallel trials: Yes, with `calibration.parallel`.
- Starts from an earlier phase: Yes: a parameter an earlier phase passed on starts at that value.
- Restarts: Accepted by the `multistart` uncertainty.

### `gp_mapping`

A Gaussian-process surrogate of the cost, refined where the expected improvement is highest.

Every candidate it returns was run through the real model. It needs scikit-learn, which the base install carries. Use it when each run is expensive and the parameters are few.

Options, written under `calibration.method_options` with `method` beside them, or in the `method_options` of a phase:

| Option | Type | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `n_init` | int | `10` | Random points of the initial design, drawn from the sampling of each parameter. |
| `ei_tol` | float | `1e-06` | Expected improvement under which an iteration counts as converged. |
| `ei_patience` | int | `3` | Iterations in a row under ei_tol before the search stops. |
| `xi` | float | `0.0` | Exploration margin of the expected improvement. |
| `n_restarts` | int | `5` | Starts of the optimiser that maximizes the acquisition. |
| `n_refine` | int or None | not set | Refinement rounds after the initial design. When set, the design is sized so that n_init + n_refine * batch_size evaluations fit in the search budget max_trials. |
| `batch_size` | int | `1` | Candidates proposed per refinement round. |
| `kappa` | float | `0.0` | When not zero, the acquisition is the lower confidence bound mu - kappa * sigma instead of the expected improvement. |
| `alpha` | float | `1e-06` | Noise floor of the Gaussian-process regressor. |
| `jitter` | float | `0.0` | Added to alpha: the nugget of the regressor is alpha + jitter. |

- Parameters: Any number
- Stops: On its budget, or on a rule of its own options. Spending the budget is not convergence: the search says it spent its budget, and a phase freezes its best saying it froze the best of a budget-only search. `calibration.precision` is refused.
- Budget: `max_trials = "auto"` gives 100 evaluations.
- Parallel trials: Yes, with `calibration.parallel`.
- Starts from an earlier phase: No.
- Restarts: Accepted by the `multistart` uncertainty.

### `grid`

Every point of a regular grid, in the space each parameter is sampled in.

A log parameter gets a log axis. The grid is the same whatever the seed, so the search is a deterministic map of the cost. Use it on one or two parameters, for a first look at the cost or a reference to judge another method against.

Options, written under `calibration.method_options` with `method` beside them, or in the `method_options` of a phase:

| Option | Type | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `points_per_dim` | int or list of int or None | not set | Points sampled per dimension. Scalar applies to every axis; a list must match the parameter-space dimension. `None` defaults to 5. |

- Parameters: Any number
- Stops: When every point of its design is solved: a budget below the design is refused. `calibration.precision` is refused.
- Budget: `max_trials = "auto"` counts the evaluations its rule needs before the first solve. A smaller number is refused or warned before anything is prepared, at every launch and by `hmp check`.
- Parallel trials: Yes, with `calibration.parallel`.
- Starts from an earlier phase: No.
- Restarts: Refused by the `multistart` uncertainty: it returns the same answer every time.

### `lhs`

One Latin hypercube design, drawn before any solve and evaluated whole.

Each stratum of each parameter is hit once. Use it for an even scan with a fixed budget on more parameters than a grid affords.

Options, written under `calibration.method_options` with `method` beside them, or in the `method_options` of a phase:

| Option | Type | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `optimization` | ‘random-cd’ | ‘lloyd’ or None | not set | Post-processing passed to scipy.stats.qmc.LatinHypercube: None keeps the raw stratified draw and ‘random-cd’ spread the points further apart while still hitting every stratum exactly once; ‘lloyd’ can spread points further apart too, but is a best-effort relaxation that is not guaranteed to keep the one-point-per-stratum property. |
| `n_samples` | int | required | Points drawn in the design. Required. |

- Parameters: Any number
- Stops: When every point of its design is solved: a budget below the design is refused. `calibration.precision` is refused.
- Budget: `max_trials = "auto"` counts the evaluations its rule needs before the first solve. A smaller number is refused or warned before anything is prepared, at every launch and by `hmp check`.
- Parallel trials: Yes, with `calibration.parallel`.
- Starts from an earlier phase: No.
- Restarts: Accepted by the `multistart` uncertainty.

### `lhs_zoom`

Latin hypercubes in turn, each one in the zone the trials so far leave open.

Level 1 covers the bounds of the phase. Each next level covers the range of the trials whose cost stays within the phase margin of the best one, widened to the solved trial on each side and by at least one stratum of the level before. It moves one parameter, whose cost curve it reads. Use it to find a flat bottom and its width with a fixed budget.

Options, written under `calibration.method_options` with `method` beside them, or in the `method_options` of a phase:

| Option | Type | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `optimization` | ‘random-cd’ | ‘lloyd’ or None | not set | Post-processing passed to scipy.stats.qmc.LatinHypercube: None keeps the raw stratified draw and ‘random-cd’ spread the points further apart while still hitting every stratum exactly once; ‘lloyd’ can spread points further apart too, but is a best-effort relaxation that is not guaranteed to keep the one-point-per-stratum property. |
| `levels` | list of int | `[24, 16]` | Points of each level, in order. Each level is a Latin hypercube. At least two levels of at least two points. The budget is their sum. A multiple of `parallel` keeps the workers busy. |

- Parameters: One
- Stops: When every point of its design is solved: a budget below the design is refused. `calibration.precision` is refused.
- Budget: `max_trials = "auto"` counts the evaluations its rule needs before the first solve. A smaller number is refused or warned before anything is prepared, at every launch and by `hmp check`.
- Parallel trials: Yes, with `calibration.parallel`.
- Starts from an earlier phase: No.
- Restarts: Accepted by the `multistart` uncertainty.

### `optuna`

An Optuna study driven trial by trial, with the TPE sampler by default.

Use it for a first adaptive search on a few parameters. Set `calibration.seed` so a re-run proposes the same trials.

Options, written under `calibration.method_options` with `method` beside them, or in the `method_options` of a phase:

| Option | Type | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sampler` | ‘tpe’ | ‘random’ | ‘cmaes’ | ‘nsga’ | `"tpe"` | Optuna sampler. ‘tpe’, ‘random’ and ‘nsga’ come with the base install; ‘cmaes’ needs the calibration extra. |
| `direction` | ‘minimize’ | `"minimize"` | Direction of the study. The calibration cost is always minimised. |

- Parameters: Any number
- Stops: On its budget, or on a rule of its own options. Spending the budget is not convergence: the search says it spent its budget, and a phase freezes its best saying it froze the best of a budget-only search. `calibration.precision` is refused.
- Budget: `max_trials = "auto"` gives 100 evaluations.
- Parallel trials: Yes, with `calibration.parallel`.
- Starts from an earlier phase: No.
- Restarts: Accepted by the `multistart` uncertainty.

### `random_search`

Independent draws from the sampling of each parameter.

It never decides it has converged, so it runs to its budget. Use it as a cheap baseline to judge another method against.

It takes no option.

- Parameters: Any number
- Stops: On its budget, or on a rule of its own options. Spending the budget is not convergence: the search says it spent its budget, and a phase freezes its best saying it froze the best of a budget-only search. `calibration.precision` is refused.
- Budget: `max_trials = "auto"` gives 100 evaluations.
- Parallel trials: Yes, with `calibration.parallel`.
- Starts from an earlier phase: No.
- Restarts: Accepted by the `multistart` uncertainty.

### `scipy_de`

Differential evolution, `scipy.optimize.differential_evolution`.

A population search over the whole box. It scores a generation at once, so `parallel` helps up to the size of the population. It follows another path from the one it follows at a width of one. Use it for a robust global search.

Options, written under `calibration.method_options` with `method` beside them, or in the `method_options` of a phase:

| Option | Type | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `popsize` | int | `15` | Population size, as a multiple of the number of parameters, SciPy’s popsize. |
| `tol` | float | `0.01` | Relative spread of the population costs at which SciPy stops, its tol. |

- Parameters: Any number
- Stops: On its budget, or on a rule of its own options. Spending the budget is not convergence: the search says it spent its budget, and a phase freezes its best saying it froze the best of a budget-only search. `calibration.precision` is refused.
- Budget: `max_trials = "auto"` gives 100 evaluations.
- Parallel trials: Yes, with `calibration.parallel`.
- Starts from an earlier phase: No.
- Restarts: Accepted by the `multistart` uncertainty.

### `scipy_nelder_mead`

A local simplex, `scipy.optimize.minimize(method='Nelder-Mead')`.

It starts from the center of the sampling, or from the value an earlier phase passed on. It is the method a search that names none gets when its cost has no sign to bracket. Use it when the range is already narrow, or to refine the result of a coarse search.

Options, written under `calibration.method_options` with `method` beside them, or in the `method_options` of a phase:

| Option | Type | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `xatol` | float or None | not set | Width of the simplex at which it stops, in the space the search walks (log10 units for a log parameter). Written from calibration.precision; set one or the other. |
| `fatol` | float or None | not set | Spread of the costs over the simplex at which it stops, SciPy’s fatol. None leaves SciPy’s default. |

- Parameters: Any number
- Stops: On a precision on the parameter: `calibration.precision` writes `xatol`, a width in the space the search walks, converted from the relative precision.
- Budget: `max_trials = "auto"` gives 100 evaluations.
- Parallel trials: Yes, with `calibration.parallel`.
- Starts from an earlier phase: Yes: a parameter an earlier phase passed on starts at that value.
- Restarts: Accepted by the `multistart` uncertainty.
- Without a method: Chosen when the methods before it do not fit.

## Metrics

An objective block names one metric with `calibration.objective_blocks.metric`. The search always minimizes a cost: the Cost minimized column gives how the score of each metric enters it. In the formulas of a metric that reads a series, \(s_t\) is the simulated value and \(o_t\) the observed one at the same date, over the \(n\) dated pairs the scoring window keeps. A metric that reads a network defines its own terms under its formula.

| Metric | Family | Cost minimised | Unit of the cost | Reads | Signed | `normalize_cost` divides by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `bfi_error` | error | score | none | series output | no | refused |
| `distance_gap` | network distance | score | m | network output | yes | validity length of the output |
| `distance_mean` | network distance | score | m | network output | no | validity length of the output |
| `kge` | efficiency | 1 - score | none | series output | no | refused |
| `mae` | error | score | unit of the observation | series output | no | standard deviation of the observations |
| `nse` | efficiency | 1 - score | none | series output | no | refused |
| `nse_delta` | efficiency | 1 - score | none | series output | no | refused |
| `nse_log` | efficiency | 1 - score | none | series output | no | refused |
| `nse_seasonal` | efficiency | 1 - score | none | series output | no | refused |
| `reservoir` | efficiency | 1 - score | none | series output | no | refused |
| `rmse` | error | score | unit of the observation | series output | no | standard deviation of the observations |

**`bfi_error`**: Whether the simulated stream is fed by its aquifer in the share the gauge shows, whatever its volume and its timing. \[\left\lvert \dfrac{\sum_t b^s_t}{\sum_t s_t} - \dfrac{\sum_t b^o_t}{\sum_t o_t} \right\rvert\] where \(b^x_t = \text{Wallingford baseflow of } x \text{ on day } t\). Lower is better; the search minimises it as it is. The Wallingford filter (Gustard et al. 1992) takes the minimum of each block of five days and joins the minima below 1/0.9 of their neighbours. Both series are filtered on the same days, cut at the gaps of the record, and summed only where both baselines exist. Daily series only: a coarser step scores NaN. The index is the one of the whole window, not ESPERE’s lowest yearly index.
**`distance_gap`**: Eq. 1 of the stream-network method: zero where the simulated network reaches as far as the mapped one. \[\lvert D_{so} - D_{os} \rvert\] where \(J = D_{so} - D_{os}\). Lower is better; the search minimises it as it is. D_so is the mean downslope distance from the simulated network to the mapped one, D_os the reverse. J is the signed residual a root search brackets. With two bounds, the cost sums the weighted gap of each bound.
**`distance_mean`**: Eq. 2 of the stream-network method: the mean mismatch of the two networks. \[\tfrac{1}{2}\,(D_{so} + D_{os})\] Lower is better; the search minimises it as it is. A diagnostic, and a cost only to choose between structures already balanced by distance_gap. With two bounds, the cost sums the weighted mean of each bound.
**`kge`**: Correlation, variability and bias in one number. \[1 - \sqrt{(r - 1)^2 + (\alpha - 1)^2 + (\beta - 1)^2}\] where \(r = \mathrm{corr}(s, o),\quad \alpha = \sigma_s / \sigma_o,\quad \beta = \textstyle\sum_t s_t \big/ \sum_t o_t\). Higher is better; the search minimises one minus the score. The 2009 form of Gupta et al.: alpha is the ratio of the standard deviations and beta the ratio of the sums. The 2012 form, which takes alpha as a ratio of coefficients of variation, is not used and scores the same series differently.
**`mae`**: The typical miss, less driven by a few large ones. \[\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_t \lvert s_t - o_t \rvert\] Lower is better; the search minimises it as it is.
**`nse`**: The fit against a model that always predicts the observed mean. \[1 - \dfrac{\sum_t (s_t - o_t)^2}{\sum_t (o_t - \bar{o})^2}\] Higher is better; the search minimises one minus the score.
**`nse_delta`**: The fit of the change from one sample to the next, blind to the absolute level. \[\mathrm{NSE}(\Delta s,\ \Delta o)\] where \(\Delta x_t = x_{t+1} - x_t\). Higher is better; the search minimises one minus the score. Pair it with a metric on the level. An increment never spans a gap in the dates of the series.
**`nse_log`**: The NSE of the logarithms: recessions and low flows weigh as much as the peaks. \[\mathrm{NSE}\big(\ln(s + \varepsilon),\ \ln(o + \varepsilon)\big)\] where \(\varepsilon = \max\big(10^{-9},\ 0.01\,\mathrm{median}\{o_t > 0\}\big)\). Higher is better; the search minimises one minus the score. Negative values are clipped to zero first, and the trial counts them.
**`nse_seasonal`**: The fit beyond the seasonal cycle of the observations. Below zero, the model does worse than that cycle alone. \[1 - \dfrac{\sum_t (s_t - o_t)^2}{\sum_t (o_t - c_t)^2}\] where \(c_t = a_0 + \textstyle\sum_{k=1}^{2} \big(a_k \cos\tfrac{2\pi k t}{P} + b_k \sin\tfrac{2\pi k t}{P}\big),\ \text{fitted to } o \text{ by least squares},\ P = 365.25\,\text{days} / \Delta t\). Higher is better; the search minimises one minus the score. P is one year counted in samples of the series, whose step Delta t is read from its dates, and t is the date of each sample in the same steps, so a gap in the record keeps the cycle in phase. Two years are needed: a shorter series scores NaN. A series with no dates is taken as daily.
**`reservoir`**: Built for an impounded level: the seasonal half keeps the level honest, the increment half makes the water balance count. \[\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{NSE}_{\mathrm{seasonal}}(s, o) + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{NSE}(\Delta_{n} s,\ \Delta_{n} o)\] where \(\Delta_{n} x_t = x_{t+n} - x_t,\ n = \max(1,\ \mathrm{round}(10\,\text{days} / \Delta t))\). Higher is better; the search minimises one minus the score. The seasonal half reads the dates as nse_seasonal does. The increments span ten days, or one sample on a coarser series, and never a gap in the dates.
**`rmse`**: Large misses weigh more than many small ones. \[\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_t (s_t - o_t)^2}\] Lower is better; the search minimises it as it is.

# Register of changes

The register is the file `hydromodpy/schema/changes.toml`. One row says one change that a reader of an older run or an older file has to know about. The code reads the same rows that this page lists. The label of a run reads the bugs. The loader and `hmp doctor --fix-config` read the key moves of the configuration. The `Numbers` section of the changelog is generated from the bugs, the defaults and the recipes that change a number. Nobody writes this page: a row added to the register shows up here at the next build.

A key that only a pre-release of 2.0 wrote has no row. It is refused since 2.0.0 with a message that names every such key of the file, as Versions and stability says.
