# The inverse problem of a calibration

A calibration turns a question about the site, such as “which conductivity makes the model reproduce the gauge and the mapped streams?”, into the search for the minimum, or the root, of one number computed from the model. This page writes that number down: the space the search walks, the cost each objective block adds, the metrics, the root a network criterion has instead of a minimum, the likelihood of the one sampler, and what the width printed beside a value means. Every option of every method is in the reference Calibration methods and metrics.

## What the search walks

The file declares the parameters \(\theta = (\theta_1, \dots, \theta_p)\), each with a box \([a_i, b_i]\) under `calibration.parameters.<name>.bounds`. The search does not walk \(\theta_i\) itself. It walks \(y_i = g(\theta_i)\), with the search space `calibration.parameters.<name>.search_space`:

\[g(\theta) = \theta \ \ \text{(identity)}, \qquad g(\theta) = \log_{10}\theta \ \ \text{(log)}, \qquad g(\theta) = \ln\frac{\theta}{1 - \theta} \ \ \text{(logit)}.\]

A conductivity spans several decades, so it is walked in \(\log_{10}\): a step of the search is then a factor on \(K\), not an increment. A logit needs \(0 < a_i < b_i < 1\). A target whose physical range reaches below zero, such as an angle of the K tensor, is walked as written, with a uniform sampling, whatever search space the field declares for K. Bounds such as \([-30, 30]\) degrees need no `search_space`. The calibrated problem is

\[\theta^\ast = \arg\min_{\theta \in [a, b]} J(\theta),\]

where \(J\) is the cost defined below. Every evaluation of \(J\) is one run of the model, with the values of \(\theta\) written in place of the configuration they name. A parameter not listed keeps the value of the file. A method that samples instead of stepping draws from the sampling `calibration.parameters.<name>.sampling`: uniform on \([a_i, b_i]\), uniform on \([\log_{10} a_i, \log_{10} b_i]\), or normal.

## From outputs to one cost

An output pairs a simulated quantity with what it is compared to: a station of a loaded record, or a mapped stream network. An objective block \(b\) scores one or more outputs with one metric, which gives a raw cost \(c_b(\theta)\), always to be minimized. The blocks add up as

\[J(\theta) = \sum_b \tilde w_b \; T_b\!\left(\frac{c_b(\theta)}{s_b}\right), \qquad \tilde w_b = \frac{w_b}{\sum_k w_k}.\]
- \(w_b\) is `calibration.objective_blocks.weight`. The weights are divided by their sum, so only their ratios matter. A phase that writes a share table in `calibration.phases.objective_blocks` replaces them for that phase.
- \(s_b\) is 1 unless `calibration.objective_blocks.normalize_cost` is true. Then, for an error (\(\mathrm{RMSE}\), \(\mathrm{MAE}\)), \(s_b\) is the standard deviation of the observations, or their mean absolute value when that is zero. For a network distance, each distance is divided by the validity length \(L\) of its output, two mesh cells under `"auto"`, so a gap of one validity length costs 1. An efficiency score is already a pure number, and the key is refused on it.
- \(T_b\) is `calibration.objective_blocks.cost_transform`: the identity, \(\log_{10}(c + 10^{-6})\), or \(-1/(c + 10^{-6})\). It reshapes a cost before the weighting. It is not the log of the series, which is what the metric `nse_log` takes.

Without normalization, a cost in meters and a cost without unit add up, and the unit sets the balance instead of the weight. A file with no block scores one series with `calibration.objective` and `calibration.variable`: one block of weight one.

A cell output reads one cell of the grid. Without `calibration.outputs.<name>.layer`, it reads the top active cell of its column, like any point given without a layer (The top active layer). A column with no active cell reads layer 0, and a row or a column outside the grid is refused with the name of the output. A layer written in the file is used as it is.

Only the dated pairs inside the scoring window enter \(c_b\). `calibration.window` names the first and last dates that count, so the spin-up of the model stays out of the cost at any time step. `calibration.validation_window` keeps other dates apart. Each trial is scored on them with the same blocks, on the series it has already simulated, and \(c_b\) never reads them.

## The metrics

Each metric declares its family, the unit of its cost, whether it reads a series or a network output, and whether its cost is the absolute value of a signed residual. In the formulas, \(s_t\) is the simulated value and \(o_t\) the observed one at the same date, over the \(n\) dated pairs the scoring window keeps.

| Metric | Family | Cost minimised | Unit of the cost | Reads | Signed | `normalize_cost` divides by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `bfi_error` | error | score | none | series output | no | refused |
| `distance_gap` | network distance | score | m | network output | yes | validity length of the output |
| `distance_mean` | network distance | score | m | network output | no | validity length of the output |
| `kge` | efficiency | 1 - score | none | series output | no | refused |
| `mae` | error | score | unit of the observation | series output | no | standard deviation of the observations |
| `nse` | efficiency | 1 - score | none | series output | no | refused |
| `nse_delta` | efficiency | 1 - score | none | series output | no | refused |
| `nse_log` | efficiency | 1 - score | none | series output | no | refused |
| `nse_seasonal` | efficiency | 1 - score | none | series output | no | refused |
| `reservoir` | efficiency | 1 - score | none | series output | no | refused |
| `rmse` | error | score | unit of the observation | series output | no | standard deviation of the observations |

**`bfi_error`**: Whether the simulated stream is fed by its aquifer in the share the gauge shows, whatever its volume and its timing. \[\left\lvert \dfrac{\sum_t b^s_t}{\sum_t s_t} - \dfrac{\sum_t b^o_t}{\sum_t o_t} \right\rvert\] where \(b^x_t = \text{Wallingford baseflow of } x \text{ on day } t\). Lower is better; the search minimises it as it is. The Wallingford filter (Gustard et al. 1992) takes the minimum of each block of five days and joins the minima below 1/0.9 of their neighbours. Both series are filtered on the same days, cut at the gaps of the record, and summed only where both baselines exist. Daily series only: a coarser step scores NaN. The index is the one of the whole window, not ESPERE’s lowest yearly index.
**`distance_gap`**: Eq. 1 of the stream-network method: zero where the simulated network reaches as far as the mapped one. \[\lvert D_{so} - D_{os} \rvert\] where \(J = D_{so} - D_{os}\). Lower is better; the search minimises it as it is. D_so is the mean downslope distance from the simulated network to the mapped one, D_os the reverse. J is the signed residual a root search brackets. With two bounds, the cost sums the weighted gap of each bound.
**`distance_mean`**: Eq. 2 of the stream-network method: the mean mismatch of the two networks. \[\tfrac{1}{2}\,(D_{so} + D_{os})\] Lower is better; the search minimises it as it is. A diagnostic, and a cost only to choose between structures already balanced by distance_gap. With two bounds, the cost sums the weighted mean of each bound.
**`kge`**: Correlation, variability and bias in one number. \[1 - \sqrt{(r - 1)^2 + (\alpha - 1)^2 + (\beta - 1)^2}\] where \(r = \mathrm{corr}(s, o),\quad \alpha = \sigma_s / \sigma_o,\quad \beta = \textstyle\sum_t s_t \big/ \sum_t o_t\). Higher is better; the search minimises one minus the score. The 2009 form of Gupta et al.: alpha is the ratio of the standard deviations and beta the ratio of the sums. The 2012 form, which takes alpha as a ratio of coefficients of variation, is not used and scores the same series differently.
**`mae`**: The typical miss, less driven by a few large ones. \[\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_t \lvert s_t - o_t \rvert\] Lower is better; the search minimises it as it is.
**`nse`**: The fit against a model that always predicts the observed mean. \[1 - \dfrac{\sum_t (s_t - o_t)^2}{\sum_t (o_t - \bar{o})^2}\] Higher is better; the search minimises one minus the score.
**`nse_delta`**: The fit of the change from one sample to the next, blind to the absolute level. \[\mathrm{NSE}(\Delta s,\ \Delta o)\] where \(\Delta x_t = x_{t+1} - x_t\). Higher is better; the search minimises one minus the score. Pair it with a metric on the level. An increment never spans a gap in the dates of the series.
**`nse_log`**: The NSE of the logarithms: recessions and low flows weigh as much as the peaks. \[\mathrm{NSE}\big(\ln(s + \varepsilon),\ \ln(o + \varepsilon)\big)\] where \(\varepsilon = \max\big(10^{-9},\ 0.01\,\mathrm{median}\{o_t > 0\}\big)\). Higher is better; the search minimises one minus the score. Negative values are clipped to zero first, and the trial counts them.
**`nse_seasonal`**: The fit beyond the seasonal cycle of the observations. Below zero, the model does worse than that cycle alone. \[1 - \dfrac{\sum_t (s_t - o_t)^2}{\sum_t (o_t - c_t)^2}\] where \(c_t = a_0 + \textstyle\sum_{k=1}^{2} \big(a_k \cos\tfrac{2\pi k t}{P} + b_k \sin\tfrac{2\pi k t}{P}\big),\ \text{fitted to } o \text{ by least squares},\ P = 365.25\,\text{days} / \Delta t\). Higher is better; the search minimises one minus the score. P is one year counted in samples of the series, whose step Delta t is read from its dates, and t is the date of each sample in the same steps, so a gap in the record keeps the cycle in phase. Two years are needed: a shorter series scores NaN. A series with no dates is taken as daily.
**`reservoir`**: Built for an impounded level: the seasonal half keeps the level honest, the increment half makes the water balance count. \[\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{NSE}_{\mathrm{seasonal}}(s, o) + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{NSE}(\Delta_{n} s,\ \Delta_{n} o)\] where \(\Delta_{n} x_t = x_{t+n} - x_t,\ n = \max(1,\ \mathrm{round}(10\,\text{days} / \Delta t))\). Higher is better; the search minimises one minus the score. The seasonal half reads the dates as nse_seasonal does. The increments span ten days, or one sample on a coarser series, and never a gap in the dates.
**`rmse`**: Large misses weigh more than many small ones. \[\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_t (s_t - o_t)^2}\] Lower is better; the search minimises it as it is.

## A root, not a minimum

The two network metrics compare the simulated network with a mapped one through two mean downslope distances: \(D_{so}\) from the simulated network to the map, and \(D_{os}\) back (Downslope distance between two networks). Too low a conductivity leaves too much simulated stream and \(D_{so}\) large. Too high a conductivity leaves too little, and \(D_{os}\) large. The balance is where the signed residual

\[J_s(\theta) = D_{so}(\theta) - D_{os}(\theta)\]

changes sign. `distance_gap` scores \(\lvert J_s \rvert\), but its zero is a crossing, not the minimum of a smooth cost: the simulated network changes cell by cell, so \(J_s\) steps over zero instead of reaching it. The method `bisection` uses that. It sweeps the box in log space, keeps the two neighbors where the sign changes, and halves that bracket until its relative width falls under the precision `calibration.precision`. It never stops on the size of \(\lvert J_s \rvert\), which may never get small. The value it returns is the completed trial of lowest cost inside the final bracket.

With a minimal and a maximal map, each bound has its own root, \(K^\ast_{\min}\) and \(K^\ast_{\max}\). The value returned is their weighted geometric mean,

\[\log_{10} K^\ast = w_{\min} \log_{10} K^\ast_{\min} + w_{\max} \log_{10} K^\ast_{\max}, \qquad w_{\min} + w_{\max} = 1,\]

with the weights \(w_{\min}\) and \(w_{\max}\) of the permanent and the complete map, written in `calibration.outputs.<name>.map.calibrate_on`.

What the root identifies is the ratio of the conductivity to the recharge, not \(K\) alone, as long as the drains take their conductance from \(K\). The argument is in Downslope distance between two networks.

## The methods

A method proposes the next values of \(\theta\) from the costs it has seen. It changes how the minimum is found, never what is minimized. A search that names none gets `bisection` when it moves one parameter in log space on signed criteria only, and `scipy_nelder_mead` otherwise.

| Method | What it does | Parameters | Stops on | Parallel |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| bisection | A root search on one parameter: a coarse log sweep, then the bracket is halved. | One, in log space only | precision | yes |
| cma_es | Covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy, from the `cma` package. | Any number | budget | yes |
| gp_mapping | A Gaussian-process surrogate of the cost, refined where the expected improvement is highest. | Any number | budget | yes |
| grid | Every point of a regular grid, in the space each parameter is sampled in. | Any number | design | yes |
| lhs | One Latin hypercube design, drawn before any solve and evaluated whole. | Any number | design | yes |
| lhs_zoom | Latin hypercubes in turn, each one in the zone the trials so far leave open. | One | design | yes |
| optuna | An Optuna study driven trial by trial, with the TPE sampler by default. | Any number | budget | yes |
| random_search | Independent draws from the sampling of each parameter. | Any number | budget | yes |
| scipy_de | Differential evolution, `scipy.optimize.differential_evolution`. | Any number | budget | yes |
| scipy_nelder_mead | A local simplex, `scipy.optimize.minimize(method='Nelder-Mead')`. | Any number | precision | yes |

## The score of `da_mh_gp`

`da_mh_gp` is a sequential search: a Metropolis-Hastings chain that spends its runs around the low-cost region. It is not in the list of methods above, because its chain is neither stored nor diagnosed, but it runs when a file names it. It reads the cost of each trial as an \(\mathrm{RMSE}\) and builds the log-score

\[\ln \pi(y) = -\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\mathrm{RMSE}(\theta)}{\sigma_n}\right)^2 + \ln p(y) + \text{const},\]

where \(\sigma_n\) is its option `sigma_noise` and \(y = g(\theta)\) is the point in the space the search walks. The prior \(p\) is flat on the box, unless the options `prior_mean`\(\mu\) and `prior_std`\(\sigma_p\) are set:

\[\ln p(y) = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_i \left(\frac{y_i - \mu_i}{\sigma_{p,i}}\right)^2 .\]

A proposal \(y' = y + \varepsilon\), with \(\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_q^2)\) and \(\sigma_q\) the option `proposal_sigma`, is dropped when it leaves the box. Otherwise a Gaussian process [Rasmussen and Williams, 2006], fitted to the log-scores already computed, screens it. A proposal that passes the screen is then run through the model, which corrects the acceptance so the chain targets \(\pi\) and not the surrogate (Christen and Fox [2005], delayed acceptance). The candidate the calibration returns is the state of highest log-score.

Read this score for what it is. A Gaussian likelihood of \(n\) independent residuals of standard deviation \(\sigma\) is \(-\tfrac{n}{2}(\mathrm{RMSE}/\sigma)^2\). The one above has no \(n\): it scores the whole record as one residual of size \(\mathrm{RMSE}\). The spread of the chain therefore follows \(\sigma_n\), a number of the file, and not the length of the record, so it measures no uncertainty on the parameters. On any metric other than `rmse`, the number squared is not a residual at all. Use the chain to find the best state, and read the width of a value from `calibration.uncertainty.method` below.

## The width beside a value

Every calibrated value is printed with an interval, and the interval never moves the value. Three methods, set by `calibration.uncertainty.method`, produce it. None of them is a posterior.

- `cost_profile`, the default, reads the trials already run. With \(J^\ast\) the best cost and \(\tau\) the margin `calibration.uncertainty.cost_margin`, a trial is kept when \(J \leq J^\ast(1 + \tau)\) for a share such as `"5%"`, or \(J \leq J^\ast + \tau\) for a length such as `"75 m"`. The interval of \(\theta_i\) is the range of \(\theta_i\) over the kept trials. The default is \(\tau = 0.05\), a share. A phase scored on network distances only takes one mesh cell, a length, because a fraction of a cost solved at zero is zero.
- `multistart` runs the whole search again from other starting points and reports the spread of the optima. A parameter whose optima span more than a factor ten is flagged as not identified.
- `linearized` gives the first-order parameter covariance. It differentiates the simulated values at the answer with a forward step of `calibration.uncertainty.perturbation` times the value, one run per parameter, and scales the covariance by \(s^2 = \mathbf{r}^\top \mathbf{r} / (n - p)\), with \(\mathbf{r}\) the residuals and \(n - p \ge 1\). It prints \(\sigma_i\) and the correlation that names the parameter each one trades off against.

A narrow `cost_profile` interval means either that the cost rises fast around the value, or that the search never tried far from it. A high correlation means two parameters were not told apart: they are one number and a ratio. How sure is the model? says how to read each case.

## Limits

- A low cost does not identify a parameter on its own. Several parameter sets can reach the same cost, and a calibration on one criterion returns one of them.
- The weights of a multi-target cost are a modeling decision. Changing them changes which model is called the best.
- In a staged calibration, each phase is conditional on the values the earlier phases froze. Its width does not carry their uncertainty.
- The observed data enter the cost only. A mapped network or a gauged record is never an input of the model it scores.

# Downslope distance between two networks

A mapped stream network and a simulated one rarely coincide. This page defines how far apart they are, measured along the paths the water takes, and the criterion built on that distance, the method of Abhervé et al. [2023]. It answers one question. Given a model that makes a network of streams and a map that draws another, how long is the walk downslope from one to the other, in each direction, and at which value of the calibrated ratio do the two walks balance?

How a model makes streams in plain words is on How the model makes streams. The keys of a calibration on a network are in [calibration.outputs].

Note

Scope. The page covers the distances, the criterion, what it identifies, and how the mapped network is drawn on the mesh. The simulated network itself, from the release flux to the flowing cells, is on Where the water table reaches the surface. The search that moves a parameter until the criterion reaches zero is described only where it shapes the criterion.

## The graph the distances follow

A distance follows a flow path, and a flow path exists only where the depressions are resolved. The code floods the model top on the mesh with the priority flood of Routing on the mesh: the descent D, (41), seeded on the border of the active domain, and reads the receivers \(r(n)\) of (43) on the flooded copy. The edge length \(\ell(n)\) is the distance from the center of \(n\) to the center of \(r(n)\).

The flood is seeded on the whole border, where water leaves the model, not on the outlet alone: sealing one outlet would fill a valley of the buffer up to a col of the divide. The criterion does not read the descent \(D\) the build stores (The graph of the stream criterion). The map is never burned into the surface: an observation never enters the routing surface or the model top.

## 1. The downslope distance to a set

For a target set \(T\), the distance from a cell to \(T\) is the length of its descent down to the first cell of \(T\):

(54)\[\begin{split}d_T(n) = \begin{cases} 0 & n \in T, \\ \ell(n) + d_T\bigl(r(n)\bigr) & n \notin T,\ r(n) \text{ exists}, \\ +\infty & n \notin T,\ r(n) \text{ does not exist.} \end{cases}\end{split}\]

With one receiver per cell, exactly one descending path leaves a cell, so there is no shortest path to search for. The distance is not a Euclidean nearest distance: a source fifty meters from a stream but across a divide is far away downslope. And it is not symmetric: \(d_{\mathcal{O}}\) on the simulated cells and \(d_{\mathcal{S}}\) on the mapped cells differ, which is what lets one cost weigh an excess of simulated stream against a missing one. An empty target gives \(+\infty\) everywhere and does not raise: an empty simulated network is the legitimate end of a search interval.

Fig. 65 Two networks on an 8 by 8 grid of 10 m cells, with the receivers of the flooded top. Left: from each simulated cell down to the map, the two hillside cells walk 42 m. Right: from each mapped cell down to the simulated network, the three upper cells walk 10, 20 and 30 m. The two means differ, and so do the cells that carry them. Every number is a call of `downslope_distance_to_mask`.

In the code: `downslope_distance_to_mask`.

## 2. The outlet, the catchment and the saturation length

The outlet \(o\) closes the catchment, usually at the gauging station. With \(A_d(n) = a_n + \sum_{m : r(m) = n} A_d(m)\) the area drained through \(n\), the outlet is the most drained cell within two neighbor rings of the cell nearest to the pour point the catchment was delineated from (two cells is the `SnapPourPoints` distance of the paper, read on the mesh). Without a pour point, the most drained cell of the delineated polygon closes the catchment, and without the polygon the largest basin of the mesh does, with a warning.

The catchment scored, and the longest descent in it, are read on the same graph:

(55)\[\Omega_o = \{\, n : d_{\{o\}}(n) < \infty \,\}, \qquad L_{cap} = \max_{n \in \Omega_o} d_{\{o\}}(n) .\]

The delineated polygon builds the domain and places the outlet; it is not the support. Their symmetric difference over the area of the polygon, the outline the mesh followed when it followed one, is published as `catchment_mismatch`. The same gap to the basin of D the build kept, the cells the budget zone sums, is published as `basin_mismatch`. A wrong outlet closes the basin of D on the same wrong branch, so only the first one shows it. Above `max_catchment_mismatch`, 5 per cent by default, the search is refused before its first solve. On the Nançon the gap is 0.2 per cent on the default grid of 27 004 cells, 4.2, 3.0, 2.1 and 4.2 per cent on grids of 45, 60, 80 and 120 cells a side, and 0.2 per cent on a Voronoi mesh of 100 m that follows the smoothed outline. It passes 5 per cent on the grid of 30 cells a side (9.4), on a Voronoi mesh of 400 m (6.6) and on a Voronoi mesh of 200 m (11.2), where the outlet closes on another branch. \(L_{cap}\) is static: it is the value an unreachable cell takes in the means (5. The two mean distances).

In the code: `resolve_outlet`.

## 3. The two networks on the cells

The simulated network \(\mathcal{S}\) is the downstream closure of the sources \(\Sigma\), the cells whose release flux exceeds a share of their own recharge, (50). The release flux is the union of (49), the same union for the criterion and for the stored field. A steady phase reads one state of the run.

The mapped network \(\mathcal{O}\) is a set of lines, drawn on the cells by one of three rules chosen by `drawn_by`. It is first cut to the delineated catchment (`clip_to_catchment`), with the shape `data.hydrography` clips what it loads to, so a file and that section draw the same map, and so does a figure redrawn from the run.

Heads keeps only where the map says a stream starts, and lets the receiver graph draw the rest: the path a ditch gave a mapped line is something a model on a DEM cannot reproduce, and drawn cell by cell it would count as error.

1. The lines are merged between junctions and free ends. A free end on the outline the map was cut along was made by the cut: the stream goes on beyond it, so it is no head. It is counted as `n_cut_ends`.
1. A free end is a head when the largest drained area within the radius \(r_s\) of it does not exceed the same quantity at the other end of its reach. The drained area decides, never the direction the line was drawn in.
1. A head lands on the nearest active cell within \(r_s\) that drains at least \(A_{d,\min}\), or is lost.
1. From each landing cell, the trace follows the receivers until the descent ends or meets a traced cell.
1. The foot of each dam of a lake with a declared spillway is a forced head: the stream under a reservoir has no free end. Only the MODFLOW 6 build stores the dam feet.

The traced map is connected to the outlet by construction.

Fig. 67 The heads rule on a toy valley of 25 m cells, from one call of `trace_from_heads`. The two upstream free ends drain less than the confluence and are kept; the downstream end drains more and is not a head. The drawn map follows the descent of the model, not the line.

Crossing, the default, draws the map as the data gives it. It keeps a cell when a mapped line crosses the segment joining the centers of two cells that share an edge: on a structured grid, the cell medians, which is what the WhiteboxTools tool `VectorLinesToRaster` of the paper tests. The map is one cell wide, like the simulated network. A reach that crosses no segment marks the cell holding its midpoint instead, and the count is published per trial as `n_observed_features_fallback`. This is the rule for a map that is not a tree: canals, braids, polders, karst.

Touch keeps every cell a line touches, corners included. Each diagonal step of the map then gains the two cells that share the corner, so a model that reproduces the map exactly is pulled towards a smaller K. It is kept to replay a session recorded before 2026-09.

In the code: `trace_from_heads`.

## 4. The supports and the targets

The means are taken over the catchment, without the water bodies \(\mathcal{E}\):

(56)\[\Omega_o^\ast = \Omega_o \setminus \mathcal{E}, \qquad \mathcal{S}^\ast = \mathcal{S} \cap \Omega_o^\ast, \qquad \mathcal{O}^\ast = \mathcal{O} \cap \Omega_o^\ast .\]
- \(\mathcal{S}\) is closed downslope, \(\mathcal{O}\) is taken as drawn: closing the map would build observation out of the DEM.
- The target of \(D_{so}\) is \(T_{so} = \mathcal{O} \cup \mathcal{E} \cup \{o\}\). The outlet is added because mapped lines may stop short of it.
- The target of \(D_{os}\) is \(T_{os} = \mathcal{S}\).
- Water bodies stay in the graph and leave both supports: a lake cell in a support would add one zero per cell and move the root with the size of the lake.

The supports split the cells into three classes, published per trial: `n_valid` (\(\mathcal{S}^\ast \cap \mathcal{O}\), simulated where the map has a stream), `n_excess` (\(\mathcal{S}^\ast \setminus \mathcal{O}\), simulated where it has none) and `n_missing` (\(\mathcal{O}^\ast \setminus \mathcal{S}\), mapped where the model makes none).

The graph is not cut to \(\Omega_o\), the supports are: on a buffered domain many cells drain out of the basin and never meet the map.

## 5. The two mean distances

Write \(\hat d_T(n)\) for the distance in which an unreachable cell takes the value \(L_{cap}\). An unreachable cell is never dropped and never counted as infinite: \(+\infty\) would make the mean infinite, and dropping it would move the support with the parameter. With \(\mu(n)\) the weight of a cell,

(57)\[D_{so} = \frac{\sum_{n \in \mathcal{S}^\ast} \mu(n)\, \hat d_{T_{so}}(n)}{\sum_{n \in \mathcal{S}^\ast} \mu(n)}, \qquad D_{os} = \frac{\sum_{n \in \mathcal{O}^\ast} \mu(n)\, \hat d_{T_{os}}(n)}{\sum_{n \in \mathcal{O}^\ast} \mu(n)} .\]

With \(\mu = 1\), each cell has one vote, as in the paper; with \(\mu = a_n\) the mean is weighted by area, which matters on a mesh refined along the streams. Both pairs are reported at every trial, and `weighting` selects the one the criterion reads.

\(D_{so}\) large means a simulated network spilling far from the mapped one, an excess. \(D_{os}\) large means a simulated network that never grew to the mapped one, a deficit. At a balanced point most distances are zero, so the means are carried by a few cells: they are tail statistics.

The unreachable shares \(f_{so}\) and \(f_{os}\) are reported on both sides, and neither refuses a trial. \(f_{so}\) is zero by construction: the target of \(D_{so}\) holds the outlet, and every cell of the catchment reaches the outlet. The target of \(f_{os}\) is the simulated network the calibration moves: at a high conductivity it retracts into the talwegs, and mapped cells legitimately have nothing left to descend into. `frac_outlet_terminated` is the share of the simulated support whose descent meets the target only at the sealed outlet. It says how much of \(D_{so}\) rests on that one cell, and a network in excess legitimately gives a large share, so it bounds nothing.

In the code: `mean_downslope_distance`.

## 6. The criterion

The criterion is equations 1 to 4 of Abhervé et al. [2023]:

(58)\[\begin{split}\begin{aligned} J_{signed} &= D_{so} - D_{os}, & J &= \lvert J_{signed} \rvert, \\ D_{optim} &= \tfrac{1}{2}\,(D_{so} + D_{os}), & r_{optim} &= D_{optim} / h_{obs} . \end{aligned}\end{split}\]

When the simulated network is empty, \(D_{so}\) has no support, and the residual is set to \(J_{signed} = -L_{cap}\): the negative value a root search needs at the end of its interval where nothing seeps.

The cost is \(J\), and its zero is a crossing. The two curves \(D_{so}\) and \(D_{os}\), drawn against the calibrated parameter, cross, and the crossing is the answer. \(D_{optim}\) is large at both ends of a sweep, so it has an interior minimum, and minimizing it is a tempting substitute. It is a different estimator: nothing places its minimum at the crossing.

Fig. 69 \(D_{so}\) and \(D_{os}\) against \(K/\bar N\) on a toy catchment of 60 by 60 cells of 20 m. No solver runs: a cell is a source when the recharge it drains exceeds what a 30 m saturated thickness carries down its slope, \(\bar N A_d > K B s\,w\), and the map holds the cells draining more than 0.03 km². Every distance is a call of the code. The curves are steps, because the masks are discrete. The minimum of \(D_{optim}\) (dotted) is not at the crossing.

The two estimators are needed and are not interchangeable. Inside one model structure, \(J\) finds the parameter, and \(D_{optim}\) cannot separate two points that both balance. Between structures already balanced at \(J = 0\), only \(D_{optim}\) separates them. The code names them apart in `metric`: `distance_gap` is the cost \(J\) and carries the signed residual; `distance_mean` is \(D_{optim}\), a diagnostic. With two maps, each bound is this same pair evaluated once, and the cost is the sum of the weighted gaps. A run with a permanent map beside the full one, in one state, scores the state against the permanent map; the full map is scored at the same state as a validation and never enters the cost.

In the code: `seepage_distance_cost`.

## 7. When a result is valid

The length scale. \(h_{obs}\) is the median distance between the centers of cells that share an edge, over the mapped cells of \(\Omega_o\): the cell size on a regular grid, the size of the fine cells on a mesh refined along the streams. It is static, since the map does not move with \(K\).

The bound. The paper reads \(r_{optim} \leq 2\): two cells, one of which budgets for the error of the map. The code writes it as a length:

(59)\[D_{optim} \leq V, \qquad V = 2\,\max(h_{obs},\ \sigma_o) .\]

With no declared accuracy, \(V = 2 h_{obs}\), the bound of the paper. A declared accuracy \(\sigma_o\) above \(h_{obs}\) widens \(V\) and leaves \(r_{optim}\) comparable with the paper. A declared `validity_length` replaces the computation. The bound is read on the trial the search returns, and qualifies the value without replacing it: a violation logs a warning, or is refused after the session is saved when `on_invalid` is `"error"`. Each trial publishes `r_optim` and `r_optim_valid`.

The map against the surface. Wherever the mapped lines do not sit in the talwegs of the model top, the distances measure a disagreement between two datasets rather than hydrogeology. The code publishes the share of the downstream closure of the map that the map itself holds, inside the catchment:

(60)\[\alpha_o = \frac{\lvert \mathcal{O} \cap \Omega_o \rvert}{\lvert \mathrm{closure}(\mathcal{O}) \cap \Omega_o \rvert},\]

as `alpha_obs_closure_catchment`. A value below `alpha_warning_threshold` logs a warning, once per process.

## What the criterion identifies

Take a steady water-table aquifer with drains at the surface whose conductance is derived from \(K\), (44). Per unit area, the balance of a cell is

(61)\[\nabla \cdot \bigl( K\, B\, \nabla h \bigr) + N = \frac{K}{b_d}\,\bigl(h - z^d\bigr)_+ ,\]

with \(B\) the saturated thickness ((24)) and \(z^d\) the drain elevation, the cell top by default. Dividing by \(K\) gives

\[\nabla \cdot \bigl( B\, \nabla h \bigr) + \frac{N}{K} = \frac{1}{b_d}\,\bigl(h - z^d\bigr)_+ ,\]

which depends on \(N/K\) and on the geometry alone. When \(K\) is scaled by one factor everywhere and \(N\) keeps its shape, the head field, and so the seepage mask, the release flux and the criterion, depend only on \(K/\bar N\). What the criterion calibrates is that ratio, not \(K\). A \(K\) read from it inherits the recharge series entirely: report \(K/\bar N\) and name the recharge beside it.

When the search moves the homogeneous conductivity alone, the report publishes the ratio with what it rests on: `k_over_r` (\(K/\bar N\)), `k_optim_m_s`, `R_mean_m_s` (\(\bar N\)), `d_sat_m` (the saturated thickness averaged over the catchment, \(\bar B\)), and `t_over_r_m` (\(T/\bar N = K \bar B / \bar N\), a length). For any other search they are not published.

This is why a search that moves \(K\) is refused when a conductance does not follow \(K\) (see the limits).

## How a search reaches the zero

The masks are discrete, so \(J_{signed}\) steps over zero instead of reaching it. On a real catchment \(|J|\) never drops below three meters while the root is bracketed to a factor 1.0015. The zero is a plateau whose width sets how precisely the parameter is known. A bisection therefore stops on the width of its bracket, on a logarithmic transform, never on the size of the residual. A search that stops on \(|J| < \epsilon\) may never stop at all.

Monotonicity is not proven, since the direction of variation was established on three points. A coarse sweep runs first, checks it instead of assuming it and sees every crossing. Its solves are the same ones that draw the diagnostic curves. A bracket with no sign change is reported, never closed: returning the better end would be a minimized mean distance in disguise, which is the drift this criterion exists to correct. The search raises and prints both residuals. The options are on Calibration methods and metrics.

### Two roots

A network output scored on two bounds (\(n_{bounds} = 2\), a transient extent table and a minimal map) publishes one residual per bound, `J_signed_minimal` and `J_signed_maximal`, and no `J_signed`. The search sweeps once, keeps one bracket per bound on the same trials, and halves each until its width reaches the tolerance. The value it returns is the weighted geometric mean of the two roots

\[\log K = w_\mathrm{min} \log K^*_\mathrm{min} + w_\mathrm{max} \log K^*_\mathrm{max},\]

with the weights the output publishes. This value is solved once more, so every number published beside it comes from a real solve. The two roots and their spread \(\Delta = \log_{10}(K^*_\mathrm{max} / K^*_\mathrm{min})\) are published in `roots_record`. A bound weighted zero is not searched, because its root would move nothing and a missing sign change on it would refuse a search that does not depend on it.

### Points asked together

An engine that asks for \(n\) points at once gets \(n\). The sweep is fixed in advance, so it is handed out \(n\) points at a time. A bracket is cut by \(n\) points into \(n + 1\) equal parts in the log variable, all solved together, and the part whose ends change sign is kept. A round that needs fewer points to reach the tolerance places only those. With two roots the \(n\) points of a round are shared between the two brackets, one each first, then one at a time to the bracket that would stay widest, and a bracket both bounds share is cut once. One point per ask is the binary search, trial for trial.

When one round leaves several parts that change sign, the residual is not monotone there. The part kept is the one binary bisection keeps. Its halvings are followed through the points evaluated, as far as each midpoint is one of them, which is all the way when \(n + 1\) is a power of two. Past the last midpoint evaluated, the lowest crossing left is kept, the rule the sweep applies to crossings of one width.

### The budget before the first solve

The budget is known before the first solve, from `root_search_budget`. Let \(d\) be the declared interval in decades, \(t = \log_{10}(1 + \mathrm{rel\_tol})\), \(S\) the sweep points (two when `sweep_points` is zero), \(s = d / (S - 1)\) the sweep step, \(h(w) = \lceil \log_2 (w / t) \rceil\) the halvings of a bracket \(w\) decades wide and \(E\) the `bracket_expand`. Then

- one root inside the declared bounds costs \(N_\mathrm{nominal} = S + h(s)\),
- one root found after \(e\) expansions costs \(S + 2e + h(1)\), since each expansion solves two new ends and leaves a bracket one decade wide,
- two roots inside the bounds cost \(S + 2 h(s) + 1\), the last one being the solve at the combined value,
- two roots of which one needed \(e\) expansions cost \(S + 2e + h(1) + \max(h(s), h(1)) + 1\),
- \(N_\mathrm{worst}\) is the largest of these, reached at \(e = E\) whenever the sweep step is at most a decade.

On the Nançon, \([10^{-7}, 10^{-3}]\) m/s, seven sweep points and one per cent, one root costs 15 evaluations inside the bounds and 17, 19, 21 and 23 after one to four expansions. Two roots cost 24 inside the bounds and 26 to 32 after expansions. `max_trials = "auto"` budgets the worst case, and a declared budget below the nominal case is refused before the first solve. When a budget still runs out, the search publishes the halvings its brackets still need (`evaluations_remaining`), and the engine grants exactly those, once.

With \(n\) points per ask, \(h(w)\) becomes the number of evaluations that close the bracket \(n\) cuts at a time, and the two brackets of a two-root search are closed together. With \(n = 1\) the counts above hold. There are more evaluations and far fewer rounds. On the Nançon with four points, one root costs 20 evaluations in 6 rounds instead of 15 in 15, and two roots cost 26 in 8 instead of 24 in 24.

### The interval around the root

The interval reported beside the root is read on the cost curve. The trials give one cost per point of the search variable, the first solved cost when a point was asked twice, and none on a point that did not solve. From the root the cost is followed on each side to its first crossing of the margin, by a straight line between two points, so no solve is added. A point with no cost stops the walk, since a line drawn to it would claim a crossing no solve showed.

## Assumptions

- Water leaves a cell by one receiver (single flow direction).
- The model top, flooded on the mesh graph, is the surface water follows.
- Distances are lengths along links between cell centers, not straight lines.
- The mapped network is independent of the DEM. It is never burned into the surface.
- The release flux is the whole of what leaves the aquifer for the surface.
- For the reading of \(K/\bar N\): the state is steady, the drain conductance follows \(K\), and \(K\) is scaled by one factor while \(N\) keeps its shape.
- The threshold \(\tau_\mathrm{s}\) and the mean recharge \(\bar N\) are frozen over a search.

## Limits

What the code refuses:

- a search whose scored catchment differs from the delineated outline by more than its bound, before the first solve: an outlet on another branch, or a mesh too coarse for the catchment;
- a mapped network that lands on no active cell, or on no cell of the catchment. The message names the CRS as the first suspect;
- a heads rule that draws no stream: no free end on an active cell, every free end draining more than the other end of its reach, or every head lost;
- a release record in the budget that no declared package reads, which would report its water as dry land;
- a search that moves a conductivity while a drain has a fixed conductance, or while SFR or LAK is active: those conductances do not follow \(K\), so (61) does not hold. A search driving another parameter gets a warning instead;
- a bisection on more than one parameter, or on a parameter without a logarithmic transform.

What the code does not represent:

- Monotonicity. The criterion does not prove that \(J_{signed}\) varies one way with the parameter. It checks it on a sweep.
- \(r_{optim}\) is not a quality indicator. It measures agreement with the map, and it moves with the grid: refining a mesh lowers \(h_{obs}\) and raises \(r_{optim}\) at constant agreement. Two verdicts are comparable when their validity lengths are.
- Tail statistics. Reading \(r_{optim} \leq 2\) as “the typical gap is under two cells” is wrong when the median distance is zero.
- The surface is not repaired. `dem_correc_type` conditions the DEM before the catchment is delineated (`fill`, the tool of the paper, or `breach`[Lindsay, 2016], or `capped_breach`). A DEM declared `state = "conditioned"` on its source is treated as `provided`: HydroModPy skips the conditioning and still computes the D8 directions and the accumulation. The criterion always floods the model top on the mesh; a breached raster reaches it only through the domain and the outlet.
- The recharge of the steady stage. The protocol averages it over the window the run loads, three years in example 04, where the paper reads a normal of sixty years, 1960 to 2019. It is a declared departure, and \(K\) is only readable with the \(\bar N\) and the window printed beside it. Write a long `steady_window` when the forcing covers one. A window across 31 July 2015 reads a break of the SIM2 product: the summer drainage over example 04 no longer falls under 0.3 mm/day after it (The daily soil reservoir).
- The visible flow. In one state the simulated network is the closure of the sources, whatever it carries. A visible flow exists in a transient run only, in the two-bound mode and in the persistence figures, which apply `calibration.outputs.<name>.model.extent.visible_flow` (How the model makes streams), so such a figure and a one-state score do not read the same network.
- The two-bound mode is outside the protocol. The protocol scores its network output at its steady stage, and an extent table is refused on a steady search. Its transient stage scores the hydrograph alone. A two-bound search is written by hand.
- Intermittent reaches. A complete map mixes the reaches that flow all year with those that flow part of it. A one-state output scores it against one state, so an intermittent reach counts as if it flowed in that state. Only `calibration.outputs.<name>.map.permanent` and the two-bound mode separate the two, and only when the source says which reach is permanent. The code does not know when an intermittent reach flows.
- The resolution of the DEM. The model top and the descent \(D\) come from the DEM, so the simulated network cannot sit closer to a talweg than the DEM places it. A mesh finer than the DEM does not place it better. Under the heads rule the map is drawn on the same descent and shares that error. Under `crossing` or `touch` it is drawn where the lines are, so a talweg the DEM shifts leaves a distance that no parameter closes.
- Tracing error and snapping. The cost reads the mapped lines as exact. `calibration.outputs.<name>.map.position_accuracy` enters the validity length only. Under the heads rule a head lands up to `calibration.outputs.<name>.map.heads.radius` from its point, on a cell that drains at least `calibration.outputs.<name>.map.heads.min_drained_area`. A head that lands in the next talweg, or is lost, changes the drawn map, and no part of that uncertainty is carried into the score.
- Domain of validity. The method was built for unconfined aquifers in a temperate humid climate, with gentle gradients and a strong groundwater-stream connection. Outside that, the criterion still computes, and it means less.

## Measured

A twin with six heads. A comb basin of 5600 cells of 20 m makes a network one cell wide at \(K/\bar N = 600\), and that network, written as a map of six lines, is the truth. The protocol finds \(K\) again to 0.45 per cent on MODFLOW-NWT, MODFLOW 6 and a Voronoi mesh, with \(J = 0\), inside a band of 3 per cent that the width of the zero plateau and the stop of the search set. A map drawn at another \(K\) gives that \(K\). A wrong map moves the answer, and the last two rows below are what a balanced \(J\) does not show:

| The map | \(K\) off by | \(D_{optim}\) | \(r_{optim}\) valid |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The truth | 0.45 % | 0 m | yes |
| One head missing | 6.5 % | 2.2 m | yes |
| All valley heads three cells low | 8.6 % | 0.3 m | yes |
| All valley heads five cells south, three valleys shorter and two longer | 2.4 % | 6.0 m | yes |
| 200 m off, five of six heads lost | a factor of 9.6 | 0 m | yes |

The bound of two cells passes every row, so it does not check a map. Read \(D_{optim}\) against zero on a twin, and `n_heads_lost` on any run: a lost head logs a warning, because the reach under it leaves the map and \(K\) reads higher. A map that wanders a cell off its talwegs below its heads gives the same \(K\) to the last bit under the heads rule, and \(K\) 11.6 per cent low under the crossing rule.

On the Nançon. The default grid of 27 004 cells, protocol 1.3, recharge over 2000 to 2002, with the 29 heads the cut map holds, none lost (31 under D4), is below. One root over four decades of \(K\) in each case.

| Case | \(K\) (m/s) | `Sy` | NSE | \(J\) (m) | \(D_{optim}\) (m) | Mapped cells | \(K\) where \(\lvert J \rvert\) is under one cell |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Heads, D8 | 1.01e-4 | 0.0253 | 0.9580 | -1.46 | 105.0 | 471 | 7.82e-5 to 1.09e-4 |
| Crossing, D8 | 1.06e-4 | 0.0253 | 0.9576 | 2.63 | 112.2 | 496 | 7.65e-5 to 1.26e-4 |
| Heads, D4 | 8.82e-5 | 0.0253 | 0.9588 | 2.89 | 98.0 | 659 | 8.11e-5 to 1.13e-4 |

The two rules agree on \(K\). The 5.5 per cent between them is about the size of the tie under heads, where trials from 1.01e-4 to 1.06e-4 m/s read the same \(J\). Heads misses 99 cells and adds 167 where crossing misses 195 and adds 232, and its root is no sharper: \(\lvert J \rvert\) stays under a tenth of a cell over about 6 per cent of \(K\) under both rules.

D4 moves \(K\) by 12.4 per cent, far more than the tie. Its root sits just above a step of the curve, where \(J\) falls by 62 m over 0.2 per cent of \(K\), and \(D_{optim}\) is not comparable, because the walk differs. It draws 40 per cent more cells, and its catchment leaves the outline by 1.1 per cent against 0.2. On a twin whose valleys run along the grid diagonal it leaves the outline by 17 per cent, which the bound refuses, and with the bound lifted it lands 4.5 per cent off against 2.4 per cent for D8. On valleys along the grid axes the two are equal.

The hydrograph does not decide. NSE moves by 1.2e-3 over these three values of \(K\), and `Sy` stays within the 5 per cent the search stops on.

The visible flow. In the two-bound mode, \(K\) depends on the flow a reach must carry to count as a stream. On the Nançon with the BD Topage maps, the mean of the two roots is 1.73e-5, 1.29e-5 and 7.80e-6 m/s at 0.5, 1 and 2 L/s, a factor of 2.2. Most of it comes from the root on the complete map, 4.97e-6, 2.95e-6 and 1.32e-6 m/s, because \(\lvert J \rvert\) stays under one cell over half a decade of \(K\) or more there. The root on the permanent map moves less, 6.01e-5, 5.61e-5 and 4.61e-5 m/s, but its \(D_{optim}\) is over 260 m, past the bound of 150 m. The two roots lie 1.1 to 1.5 decades apart, so their mean meets neither map. Quote each root with its visible flow.

K and Sy on two maps. A twin whose two maps come from a run at a known \(K\) and `Sy` finds \(K\) to a few per cent. It does not find `Sy`. Over a factor of 16 in `Sy`, \(\lvert J \rvert\) stays under one cell on both maps at the true \(K\), and two of three search methods return a `Sy` near 80 per cent high. Where the two maps are nearly the same, \(K\) lands 32 per cent high and `Sy` 70 per cent low at a cost of zero. On the Nançon only the permanent root follows `Sy`, with a slope of 0.61 in log-log. The two roots meet at \(K\) = 9.1e-6 m/s and `Sy` = 0.0040, which is below the usual range. There NSE falls from 0.96 to 0.77 and the NSE on log discharge from 0.98 to 0.43. So the route is allowed, and it is not recommended. A minimiser on one parameter is refused, because the same trials give 1e-7 m/s, the search bound, where the root search gives 1.29e-5.

The step of D4. The 12.4 per cent of D4 comes from one cell. It lies on a hillslope at 170 m, and it dries between \(K\) = 8.697e-5 and 8.715e-5 m/s. With it go 37 cells of stream under D4 and 27 under D8, all absent from the map. Under D4 this takes \(J_{signed}\) from +65 to +3.0 m, within 3 m of zero, and the root falls just above it. D8 loses the same cell at the same \(K\), and \(J_{signed}\) stays positive, from 83 to 34 m. A solver closure a hundred times tighter gives the same \(J\), so the step belongs to the model and not to the solver. Under D4, \(K\) is set by that one cell, and its narrow band is apparent precision.

Comparing structures. Two structures compare only at an equal balance, so a plain bisection closes the root of \(J\) at each one and gives its \(D_{optim}\). On the Nançon, thicknesses of 10 to 90 m give \(D_{optim}\) of 142, 168, 107, 112 and 123 m, each in 24 solves at a width of 8, except 10 m, whose root lies above the search bound of \(K\) and costs 27. Between 17.3 and 90 m, \(K \cdot \bar B\) stays within 13 per cent, as the ratio \(T/\bar N\) predicts. One step of \(J\) moves \(D_{optim}\) by 30 m at 17.3 m, so a smaller gap between two structures says nothing. Scoring \(D_{optim}\) without the balance finds 105 m at \(J\) = +24 m, with a network 21 per cent longer than the map.

Triangles. The twin has no triangle column. With XT3D and Newton, MODFLOW 6 keeps cycling by 2 to 5 cm on one border triangle, whatever the under-relaxation. Without Newton it closes, and the side triangles then seep beside the talweg. The network is wider than one cell, so no map of lines can equal it. The Voronoi column, whose cells follow the talwegs, passes.

## Parameters of this page

[[calibration.objective_blocks]]

`metric = ‹"rmse" | "nse" | "kge" | "mae" | "nse_log" | "nse_delta" | "nse_seasonal" | "reservoir" | "distance_gap" | "distance_mean" | "bfi_error"›` : Metric that scores this block against its observations. required experimental
**Path**: `calibration.objective_blocks.metric`
**Values**:
- `"rmse"` : Root-mean-square error, in the observed unit; penalizes large misfits most.
- `"nse"` : Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency against the observed mean; the standard choice for a level or discharge series.
- `"kge"` : Kling-Gupta efficiency, 2009 form (bias as the ratio of sums, variability as the ratio of standard deviations); separates correlation, variability and bias when NSE alone is ambiguous.
- `"mae"` : Mean absolute error, in the observed unit; less sensitive to outliers than RMSE.
- `"nse_log"` : NSE on log-transformed series; weights low flows as heavily as peaks, good for recessions.
- `"nse_delta"` : NSE on the increments of the series rather than its level; a level is an integral and can hide flux errors that compensate, which only its increments show.
- `"nse_seasonal"` : NSE against the seasonal cycle rather than the overall mean; asks whether the model beats climatology.
- `"reservoir"` : Half nse_seasonal plus half nse_delta, built for an impounded level: a plain NSE there is beaten by the seasonal cycle, and the increments are what carry the flux errors.
- `"distance_gap"` : Balances the simulated stream network against the mapped one; zero marks the crossing.
- `"distance_mean"` : Mean spatial offset between simulated and mapped streams; a diagnostic, not a substitute for distance_gap.
- `"bfi_error"` : Distance between the simulated and observed baseflow indices (Wallingford, daily discharge only); asks whether the stream is fed by its aquifer in the right share. Blind to volume and timing, so it goes beside a fit, never alone.
**Accepted**: "rmse" | "nse" | "kge" | "mae" | "nse_log" | "nse_delta" | "nse_seasonal" | "reservoir" | "distance_gap" | "distance_mean" | "bfi_error"

[calibration.outputs.<name>]

`variable = "head"` : Simulated variable to extract (e.g. 'head', 'outlet_discharge'). required experimental example value
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.variable`
**Accepted**: string
**Example**: `"head"`

[calibration.outputs.<name>.map]

`# complete = ‹"data.hydrography" or path›` : The complete map, every mapped reach: a vector file, read only from here, or 'data.hydrography', the network the hydrography data family loaded (a local file or an osm / bdtopage / euhydro download), clipped to the delineated catchment. varies by site experimental
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.map.complete`
**Values**:
- `"data.hydrography"`
**Accepted**: "data.hydrography" or path
**Varies by site**: yes: in a project of many sites, bind it to a column with `sites.bind` or set it in a per-site overlay; a literal value is refused
**Was**: `calibration.outputs.stream_geometry_path`, `calibration.outputs.observed_network`

`# permanent = ‹"data.hydrography" or path›` : The permanent map, the reaches that flow all year, which the complete map contains: a vector file, read as it is and never filtered by attribute, or 'data.hydrography', the permanent reaches the hydrography data family wrote beside its network. experimental
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.map.permanent`
**More**: A source that does not say which reaches flow all year gives none. The complete map scored is the union of the two, and the share of this map outside the complete one is published.
**Values**:
- `"data.hydrography"`
**Accepted**: "data.hydrography" or path
**Was**: `calibration.outputs.minimal_stream_geometry_path`, `calibration.outputs.minimal_observed_network`

`# drawn_by = "crossing"` : How the map is drawn on the mesh cells. experimental
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.map.drawn_by`
**More**: 'crossing', the default, draws the map as the data gives it: it keeps the cell holding each point where a line crosses the segment joining two edge-sharing cell centres. On a structured grid it reproduces WhiteboxTools VectorLinesToRaster, the paper's tool, and draws the map one cell wide like the simulated network, so a model that matches the map scores J = 0. 'touch' keeps every cell the line touches, corners included, and replays a session made before 2026-09; it thickens every diagonal step of the map and departs from the paper. 'heads' keeps only the free ends of the map whose largest drained area within 'heads.radius' does not exceed that of the other end of their reach, lands each on a nearby cell and draws the rest down the criterion's own descent: the field ditches and rectified reaches below a head stop counting as model error, and the drawn map reaches the outlet. 'heads' does not suit a map that is not a tree: canals, braids, polders, karst.
**Values**:
- `"heads"`
- `"crossing"`
- `"touch"`
**Accepted**: "heads" | "crossing" | "touch"
**Was**: `calibration.outputs.observed_rasterization`

`# clip_to_catchment = true` : Cut the map to the delineated catchment before drawing it, with the shape the hydrography data family clips what it loads to, so a file and 'data.hydrography' draw the same map from the same data. experimental
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.map.clip_to_catchment`
**More**: Under 'heads' an end the cut made is no stream head. false reads a file whole and takes every free end as a candidate head.
**Accepted**: true | false
**Was**: `calibration.outputs.clip_map_to_catchment`

`# position_accuracy = ‹number or "<n> m"›` : Positional accuracy of the map. m experimental
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.map.position_accuracy`
**More**: It enters the automatic validity length only, so it is refused beside a 'verdict.validity_length' written as a length: the cell size h there is max(h_obs, this), because a map is not placed better when the mesh is refined. r_optim stays D_optim / h_obs, the paper's Eq. 3. Unset is the literal reading of the paper.
**Accepted**: number or "<n> m" (a bare number is read in the canonical unit)
**Unit**: m
**Was**: `calibration.outputs.observed_position_accuracy`

[calibration.outputs.<name>.model]

`# seepage_threshold = 0.0001` : A cell releasing less than this fraction of the mean basin recharge, taken over its own area, is not a seepage face. - >= 0 experimental
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.model.seepage_threshold`
**More**: Zero reproduces the purely geometric criterion of the paper. Frozen over the whole search: a threshold moving with the trial would cost the criterion its monotonicity.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: >= 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: -
**Was**: `calibration.outputs.tau_specific_ratio`

`# weighting = "cell"` : Average one cell one vote (the paper) or weighted by cell area. experimental
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.model.weighting`
**More**: Both values are always reported; use 'area' on a mesh refined along the streams, where cell density is highest exactly where distances are smallest.
**Values**:
- `"cell"` : Every cell counts once in the average, as in the paper.
- `"area"` : Every cell counts in proportion to its area.
**Accepted**: "cell" | "area"
**Was**: `calibration.outputs.weighting`

`# neighbours = "D8"` : The graph the descent walks. experimental
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.model.neighbours`
**More**: 'D8' descends over shared nodes, the eight neighbours of a quad mesh, and is the paper: its distances are traced by WhiteboxTools on a D8 pointer, and the delineation that produced the catchment uses one too. 'D4' descends over shared edges only and departs from the paper. It is not a second-decimal choice: on a synthetic valley whose talweg runs along the grid diagonal, the most accumulated cell collects 100 per cent of the domain over shared nodes and 6.6 per cent over shared edges. On a mesh whose faces are not all quadrilaterals no cell has a diagonal and the descent walks shared edges either way; on a Voronoi mesh the two graphs are the same one.
**Values**:
- `"D8"`
- `"D4"`
**Accepted**: "D8" | "D4"
**Was**: `calibration.outputs.diagonal_neighbors`

[calibration.outputs.<name>.map.heads]

`# radius = 100.0` : The largest distance, a length (a bare number is in metres), between a mapped stream head and the centre of the cell it lands on. m experimental
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.map.heads.radius`
**More**: A head with no landing cell that close is lost, draws nothing and is counted in n_heads_lost.
**Accepted**: number or "<n> m" (a bare number is read in the canonical unit)
**Unit**: m
**Was**: `calibration.outputs.heads_snap_radius`

`# min_drained_area = 0.02` : The drained area a cell needs before a head may land on it, so a head next to its valley lands in the valley and not on the ridge cell beside it. km2 >= 0 experimental
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.map.heads.min_drained_area`
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: >= 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: km2
**Was**: `calibration.outputs.heads_min_drained_area_km2`

[calibration.outputs.<name>.verdict]

`# validity_length = "auto"` : Validity bound of Eq. 4, a length: the calibration is valid when D_optim <= this. m experimental
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.verdict.validity_length`
**More**: 'auto' is 2 h, the paper's two cells, where h is h_obs, the cell size on the mapped network, raised to 'map.position_accuracy' if that is declared. A length such as '150 m' is used as it is. The bound qualifies the result and never penalises the cost.
**Values**:
- `"auto"`
**Accepted**: "auto" or number or "<n> m" (a bare number is read in the canonical unit)
**Unit**: m
**Was**: `calibration.outputs.validity_length`

`# on_invalid = "warn"` : What a violation of Eq. 4 does: D_optim above 'validity_length'. experimental
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.verdict.on_invalid`
**More**: The bound is read once, on the trial the search returns, as the paper reads it at the optimum, and on each bound in the cost of the two-bound mode; every trial still records 'r_optim', 'r_optim_valid' and 'validity_length_m'. 'warn' logs it and returns the value, because a calibration is asked for a number. 'error' raises after the session is saved, so a staged calibration freezes nothing and runs no phase that depends on this one.
**Values**:
- `"warn"`
- `"error"`
**Accepted**: "warn" | "error"
**Was**: `calibration.outputs.on_roptim_violation`

`# max_catchment_mismatch = 0.05` : Largest gap allowed between the scored catchment and the delineated one, as a share of the delineated area: 'catchment_mismatch', the area of their symmetric difference over the area of the outline the mesh followed. >= 0 experimental
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.verdict.max_catchment_mismatch`
**More**: It depends on the geometry alone, so it is read once, before the first solve, and a gap above it refuses the search. A large gap means an outlet on another branch, or a mesh too coarse for the catchment. false never refuses, and the gap is still published on every trial. A synthetic domain has no delineated catchment and is never refused.
**Values**:
- `false`no explanation
**Accepted**: number or false
**Valid range**: >= 0 (refused outside)

`# alpha_warning_threshold = 0.9` : Below this value of 'alpha_obs_closure_catchment' the run warns that its distances carry a top-versus-map disagreement on top of the hydrogeology. alpha is the share of the downstream closure of the mapped network the network itself covers, measured on the MODEL TOP and on the catchment. ]0, 1] expert experimental
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.verdict.alpha_warning_threshold`
**More**: It changes nothing that is computed: the criterion is scored the same way above and below it.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: ]0, 1] (refused outside)
**Was**: `calibration.outputs.alpha_warning_threshold`

[calibration]

`# method_options = {}` : Options of the method, named as that method names them: points_per_dim for 'grid', sampler for 'optuna', sweep_points for 'bisection'. experimental
**Path**: `calibration.method_options`
**More**: They belong to one method, so a calibration that gives them writes method beside them. A key the method does not take is refused when the file loads.
**Accepted**: table { key = any value }
**Was**: `calibration.optimizer_kwargs`

[geographic]

`# dem_correc_type = "fill"` : How the DEM is conditioned before the catchment is delineated.
**Path**: `geographic.dem_correc_type`
**More**: 'fill' (default) only raises cells: each closed depression is raised to its spill level, then a small gradient on the flats lets every cell drain. 'breach' mostly lowers cells: it carves a path through the barrier that closes a depression, after raising single-cell pits to their lowest neighbour, with no limit on length or depth and no fill afterwards (least-cost breaching, Lindsay 2016); it changes far fewer cells than 'fill' and can dig deep. 'capped_breach' lowers and raises: it breaches only within the limits of [geographic.capped_breach] (a maximum cumulative lowering and a maximum length, in metres), then fills every depression the limits refused (the hybrid of Lindsay 2016). The depth limit is a sum over the cells of a path, so it does not give the same landscape at every grid resolution. 'fill' is the default because it is the tool of the paper behind the network criterion (FillDepressions, Abherve et al. 2023), and the criterion itself fills the model top on the mesh by a priority flood: one conditioning rule from the DEM to the score. A DEM declared state = "conditioned" on its [[data.dem.sources]] entry is already conditioned, so this key is ignored and the run records 'provided'.
**Values**:
- `"breach"`
- `"fill"`
- `"capped_breach"`
**Accepted**: "breach" | "fill" | "capped_breach"

[solver]

`# drain_bed_thickness_m = 1.0` : Metres. m > 0 expert
**Path**: `solver.drain_bed_thickness_m`
**More**: Thickness of the drain BED in the fallback conductance C = K * cell_area / bed_thickness, used when no drainage conductance is declared. A drain bed is the clogging layer at the bottom of a watercourse, decimetres to a metre; it is NOT the aquifer, and the layer thickness this used to borrow (tens of metres) has no physical relation to it. The value matters because it sets how much head the drain itself imposes to pass the recharge: dh = R * bed_thickness / K, independent of the cell size. For R = 439 mm/yr, 30 m gives 4.17 m of head at K = 1e-7 m/s and makes the drain the limiting resistance over two decades of a [1e-7, 1e-3] search; 1 m gives 13.9 cm and 0.1 m gives 1.4 cm. In this method the drain is a seepage face, so it must never limit: K and the recharge decide where water surfaces, not the boundary condition. Proportionality to K is preserved either way, so the K/R invariance the network criterion rests on is untouched. The value 1.0 is a convention with no measured source: no measurement and no document gives it, and it is kept as it is so that no earlier result moves. It stays in [solver], whatever the layer of the other drain keys. Write your own value when you have a measure.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: > 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: m
**Example**: `1.0`, `0.5`, `0.1`

Lines generated from the models, as in the reference. Open one for its card.

The keys of a calibration on a network are in [calibration.outputs].

# How water leaves the aquifer

Water enters the saturated zone as recharge and leaves it through a few exits. Each exit is a boundary package of the solver: a drain where the water table reaches the ground, a fixed head at the sea, a stream that routes what it receives, a lake that stores it. The laws are those of MODFLOW. These pages give the way HydroModPy builds each exit, and how the cells where the water table reaches the surface become a simulated network. The keys of a routed network and of a lake are in [flow.sinks_sources.sfr] and [flow.sinks_sources.lakes].

Note

Scope. MODFLOW 6 builds every exit below. MODFLOW-NWT builds the drains, the sea, the side heads and the evapotranspiration package, and no stream, lake or water mover: a file that declares a stream network or a lake with another solver in `solver.backend` is refused when it is read, with the solvers that honor it. The Boussinesq solver has its own surface exchange, on Boussinesq theory.

## The exits in one table

| Exit | Law | MODFLOW 6 | MODFLOW-NWT | Switched on by | Page |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Drain at the ground surface | one-sided, head dependent | DRN | DRN | a `[flow.bc.drainage]` table | Drains and evapotranspiration at the top of the model |
| Evapotranspiration from the water table | linear in depth | EVTA | EVT | a `[flow.sinks_sources.etp]` table, or a negative recharge | Drains and evapotranspiration at the top of the model |
| Sea | fixed head | CHD | BAS and CHD | a `[flow.bc.ocean]` table | Fixed heads: the sea, the rivers and the sides |
| River head, lateral heads | fixed head | CHD | lateral heads only | a `[flow.bc.stream]` table, `[flow.bc.west_side]` and the other sides | Fixed heads: the sea, the rivers and the sides |
| Lake or reservoir | storage, head dependent bed and banks | LAK | none | a `[flow.sinks_sources.lakes.<id>]` table | Lakes and reservoirs |
| Stream network | routed flow, head dependent streambed | SFR | none | a `[flow.sinks_sources.sfr.<id>]` table | Streams and the water mover |
| Transfer between exits | a rule on a provider flow | MVR | none | a mover key of an exit | Streams and the water mover |

Wells are a prescribed flux and not an exit. Recharge is not an exit either, but the evapotranspiration is drawn by an exit package, so both are on Drains and evapotranspiration at the top of the model.

Fig. 53 One cross-section, five columns, each with the exit the build gives it. A fixed head holds every layer of its column. A drain sits at the top of its cell, or half a band lower. A reach replaces the drain of its cell and keeps its bed inside the cell. A lake makes its top layer inactive and exchanges with the cells below and beside it.

Where the water goes once a drain has released it, and why a mesh needs a routing surface of its own, is on Routing on the mesh: the descent D. Which cells count as flowing streams is on Where the water table reaches the surface.

## The order the build assembles them

The order matters, because each exit masks the others.

1. The lake cells are made inactive in their top layers, so that every other exit sees the aquifer without them.
1. The fixed heads are placed: sea, river, sides.
1. The descent \(D\) is built from the model top, the fixed-head cells and the lakes.
1. The recharge and the evapotranspiration are written, with no recharge on a lake cell.
1. The drains are written on every cell, minus the cells that host a reach or a lake bed.
1. The lake, then the stream network, then the water mover, which names the packages above.

In the code: `run_pre_processing`.

## The budget closes

The budget is the one of MODFLOW: each package reports its flow into the cells, \(\Phi_{n,p}\), positive into the aquifer, and the terms close against the change of storage. The solver prints the percent discrepancy of the sum, and the options that bound it are on The solvers of the aquifer. The budget terms are those of Langevin et al. [2017]. The input of each package is in the MODFLOW 6 input and output guide.

HydroModPy stores the terms as `recharge`, `evapotranspiration`, `drain`, `drain_to_mover`, `stream`, `lake`, `constant_head`, `well` and `storage`. The part of the drain handed to the mover leaves the aquifer through its own record and enters the stream or the lake as water from the mover, so the package budgets of SFR and LAK close the rest.

## Assumptions common to every exit

- A drain acts on the top layer. A fixed head acts on every layer of its column. A reach and a lake exchange with the cells that hold them.
- The recharge, the rain and the ETP are constant over a stress period.
- Water routed by the mover reaches its receiver in the same period.
- No overland flow is solved. A drain that is not routed discharges where it is, and the water leaves the model there. The water balance counts it, and no surface routing carries it on.
- Fixed heads: the sea, the rivers and the sides
- Routing on the mesh: the descent D
- Drains and evapotranspiration at the top of the model
- Lakes and reservoirs
- Streams and the water mover
- Where the water table reaches the surface
