# The mesh

The solver does not see the DEM. It sees cells, each with one top, one bottom and one center. This page explains how the code builds these cells from the DEM and how it checks them.

Note

MODFLOW 6 reads every grid as a DISV grid, and this page follows it. MODFLOW-NWT and Boussinesq read one engine each (Mesh engines), and Boussinesq ignores the top sampling of 6. The top of a cell. The use of the cells by the solvers is on The solvers of the aquifer, the XT3D terms on XT3D on irregular meshes and the keys on [mesh].

## The chain in one list

The code builds the cells in this order.

1. The top from the DEM \(Z\), the bottom from the depth model.
1. A planar mesh from the engine of `mesh.engine`: squares (1. The regular engine), triangles (3. The triangle engine) or Voronoi cells (4. The Voronoi engine). The planner first cleans the lines the mesh follows and smooths the outline of the catchment (Cleaning the lines), and the last two engines follow a size field (2. The lines and the size field).
1. One top (6. The top of a cell) and one bottom per cell.
1. A check of the thickness (9. The checks the code applies), then the layers (7. Thickness and layers).
1. The export to MODFLOW 6 as a DISV grid. A cell with no valid top or bottom is inactive.

| Engine | Cells | Center | Connections | Lines it follows |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `regular` | squares, one per DEM pixel or larger | cell center | orthogonal | rivers as chains of cells, contacts and shores as staircases |
| `triangle` | triangles | mean of the vertices | not orthogonal, XT3D set by `solver.modflow6.runtime.mf6_enable_xt3d` | rivers, contacts and shores as edges |
| `voronoi` | polygons | the generator | orthogonal | rivers as chains of cells, contacts and shores as faces |

## 1. The regular engine

With no `[mesh]` section, or with `engine = "regular"` and no `mesh.cell_size`, the cells are the pixels of the top raster and take their values with no interpolation:

\[z_{\mathrm{top},ij} = Z_{ij}, \qquad N_S = n_{\mathrm{row}}\, n_{\mathrm{col}}, \qquad a_{ij} = \Delta_x \Delta_y .\]

A nodata pixel makes its cell inactive, and \(N_S\) counts that cell too. A coarser `mesh.cell_size` gives \(\operatorname{round}(L_x/\ell_g)\) cells along an extent \(L_x\). The code resamples the top and the bottom with a bilinear rule. In the zonal mode of 6. The top of a cell, a cell that covers two DEM pixels or more takes the zonal top instead. The engine refuses a finer size with `the regular engine cannot mesh finer than the DEM`. The developer key `mesh.regular.shape` gives the rows and columns instead.

The engine ignores `mesh.river_cell_size` and `mesh.river_band`, so a mesh finer along the rivers needs the `triangle` or the `voronoi` engine. A river is the chain of cells its line crosses. A contact or a shore becomes a staircase of faces, whose distance to the line is in the quality report. A barrier takes the faces whose two centers its line separates. MODFLOW-NWT reads this grid as a DIS grid.

## 2. The lines and the size field

### Cleaning the lines

Rivers, lake shores and geology contacts come from different sources, so they often miss each other by a few meters or carry tiny holes and repeated vertices. Before it computes any size, the planner cleans the domain and the families of `mesh.families`, at a tolerance of a tenth of a DEM pixel. It leaves a triangulation read from a file as it is. It drops the holes smaller than the square of the local cell size, and an island counts as a hole of its lake. It merges close vertices but keeps those another line holds, so a barrier laid on a shore stays on it. It cuts back a river or contact end that runs along another line, and it snaps a line end onto a line it almost touches. A barrier is never cut back, because its length is physical. The log and the mesh QA count each change.

The delineated catchment is the outline of a pixel mask, so it is a staircase. The planner smooths it once, before the size field and the families read it. It does so for the `triangle` and `voronoi` engines, and only where the mesh follows the outline. That is the case with `mesh.families.watershed_boundary` at `face`, or when `geographic.domain_extent` makes the domain the catchment or its buffer. The planner cuts each corner of a step at half a pixel, then simplifies the line with a tolerance of half a pixel (Douglas-Peucker). No point of the new outline lies more than one pixel from the staircase, and the area moves by a few thousandths. A corner between two edges longer than two pixels belongs to the shape and stays. The end of a river, the end of a barrier and a vertex of a lake shore that touch the outline stay on it, so the outlet keeps its place. A box, the `regular` engine, a triangulation read from a file and a catchment that the mesh does not follow keep their outline. If the smoothed polygon is not valid, the outline stays a staircase and the notes say so. The declared outlet counts as a contact of the outline, like a river end, so it stays on the outline when it lies within a tenth of a pixel of it.

The smoothed outline travels with the cell mesh (`PlanarCellMesh.smoothed_catchment`). Where a step needs the catchment, it reads the cells against this outline: the polygon fallback of the discharge support, the catchment area fraction, the outlet search of the build and the polygon mask of the network criterion. Without a smoothed outline these steps read the delineated polygon.

On example 04 (DEM of 75 m, catchment of 64.6 km²), the outline goes from 421 to 160 vertices. The area moves by -0.05 % and no point moves by more than 0.81 pixel. With the catchment as the domain, a `cell_size` of 100 m and no river in the mesh, the Voronoi cells with an isoperimetric quotient under 0.6 (4π times the area over the squared perimeter) go from 114 to 6 out of about 6500. On the `triangle` engine the gain shows with the buffer as the domain. The mesh goes from 8815 to 8027 cells, and the triangles with a corner under 20 degrees from 61 to 0. With the catchment as the domain the count falls from 7263 to 6673 cells, with a box it does not move, and neither has a corner under 20 degrees. A cell that touches the outline can change side on a band of 0.8 pixel at most.

### The size field

The `triangle` and `voronoi` engines mesh under one size field \(\ell(\mathbf{x})\), the wanted cell size on the DEM grid. For every engine, a size is the side of the square that has the mean area of a cell (Three sizes, read in order). The background size \(\ell_g\) is `mesh.cell_size`, or the DEM pixel when unset. Each refined line or zone adds a term. For the rivers, the size is \(\ell_s\) = `mesh.river_cell_size` on the line and grows back to \(\ell_g\) over the distance \(\xi_s\) = `mesh.river_band`. Lake shores and the zones of `mesh.refinement_zone.cell_size` (Refinement zones drawn by a field) are other terms. The field reads

(29)\[\ell(\mathbf{x}) = \min\Bigl(\ell_b(\mathbf{x}),\ \min_k\bigl[\ell_{s,k} + \sigma_k\, \xi_k(\mathbf{x})\bigr]\Bigr),\]

where \(\xi_k\) is the distance to line \(k\) and \(\sigma_k = \min\bigl((\ell_g - \ell_{s,k}) / \xi_{s,k},\ \sigma_{\max}\bigr)\) its growth per meter. The field never goes below the DEM pixel \(\Delta\). The background \(\ell_b\) is \(\ell_g\) in the catchment and grows outside to \(\kappa\,\ell_g\), with \(\kappa\) = `mesh.outside_factor`, over at least `mesh.transition_distance`. Since \(\sigma_{\max}\) = `mesh.max_slope` bounds every term, two neighboring cells differ in size by a ratio of at most about \((1 + \sigma_{\max}/2)/(1 - \sigma_{\max}/2)\), which is 1.67 for the default 0.5. A smaller slope gives a smoother mesh and more cells. A triangulation read from a file ignores the field.

Fig. 29 Left: the field around a river (white) in a catchment (dashed). Right: the size against the distance to the river. A band of 20 m asks for a slope of 2, and `build_size_field` holds it at 0.5.

### Refinement zones drawn by a field

A refinement zone is a vector layer, or the pixels of the DEM where a field passes a threshold. The user writes the field in `mesh.refinement_zone.where` and the threshold in `mesh.refinement_zone.below` or `mesh.refinement_zone.above`. The zone is a term of the size field, like a polygon. The cells inside it have the size `mesh.refinement_zone.cell_size`, and the size grows back to the background over `mesh.refinement_zone.buffer`, at \(\sigma_{\max}\) at most. The `triangle` and `voronoi` engines follow these zones. The `regular` engine does not grade its cells, so it ignores them, and the mesh QA says so.

The field `height_above_stream` is the height of a pixel above the first stream pixel it drains to (HAND, [Nobre et al., 2011]). The code fills the depressions of a copy of the DEM by a priority flood [Barnes et al., 2014], seeded on the streams and on the edge of the grid. Then each pixel follows the steepest descent of that copy to the first stream pixel, and takes its height on the raw DEM. The streams are the stream network traced from the DEM with the threshold of `[geographic.river_network]`. A mapped network never enters. A pixel below its stream gets 0, and a pixel whose path leaves the grid with no stream gets no height. On a grid of 464 by 420 pixels the computation takes less than a second.

The fields `watertable_depth` and `seepage` come from an earlier run of the project, named in `mesh.refinement_zone.run`. A first run on a coarse mesh gives the depth of the water table or the seepage, which is the drain outflow per cell area in mm/d. The second mesh refines where that field passed the threshold at any time step. The minimum over time is compared to `below` and the maximum to `above`, so the seepage front of a wet winter counts even when the run ends in summer. The first run is named as `restart_from` names a run, and it must be sealed. Its `sim_id` enters the mesh request and the product key, so another first run gives another mesh. The frozen `config.toml` of the new run writes that `sim_id` in place of the name, so a replay reads the same run even after a later version of it exists. A replay needs that run to be still in the project, and it stops with a message when the run is gone.

On the Nançon catchment (64.6 km², DEM of 25 m, network threshold 0.05 km²), the zone where the ground is less than 2 m above the stream covers 20 % of the catchment. A Voronoi mesh of 75 m with this zone at 25 m holds 40 043 cells, against 14 897 at 75 m and 134 074 at 25 m. The ramp around the zone also costs cells, because the size is below 75 m on 58 % of the catchment. The size ratio between two neighboring cells exceeds 1.5 on 2 % of the faces, against 0.3 % on the uniform mesh of 75 m.

### The gap between face lines

A cell larger than the space between two lines it has to follow cannot follow both. So the face lines (lake shores, barriers, contacts, the catchment boundary) and the domain outline add a term. At each point of a line, the gap \(e\) is the distance to the nearest point of another line. The same line counts as another when the way along it is more than twice the straight distance. So a narrow lake arm makes a gap, and so does a corner sharper than 53 degrees, but a right-angle junction makes none. The planner sizes the chord of a gap inside the domain as

(30)\[\ell_e = \max\bigl(e / n_e,\ \Delta\bigr),\]

where \(n_e\) = `mesh.gap_cells` is the number of cells across, 2 by default and 0 to switch the term off. After rounding, a gap holds \(n_e\) to \(1.19\,n_e\) cells. The rivers stay out, because a river is a chain of cells. On a generated Voronoi mesh with lakes, only the shores the faces follow count.

## 3. The triangle engine

The `triangle` engine builds a constrained Delaunay triangulation of \(\Omega\) with Gmsh [Geuzaine and Remacle, 2009] under the size field. Rivers, contacts, shores and barriers are edges, so no triangle holds two zones, and the cells of a river are the triangles on one bank. The center of a triangle is the mean of its vertices, so a connection has an angle (5. Flow between two cells, and the angle), and MODFLOW 6 turns XT3D on by default. An explicit `solver.modflow6.runtime.mf6_enable_xt3d` wins. Gmsh cannot promise the same triangulation twice for one input, so the workflow stores the mesh in `<project>/.hmp/products/`, keyed by the request, the engine version, the builds of Gmsh and of the geometry libraries and the code of the mesh package, and reuses it while the key is the same. On one thread gmsh redraws the same mesh. `mesh.triangle.path` reads an existing triangulation instead.

Gmsh reads a size as the length of an edge, so the engine multiplies each size it gives to Gmsh by a factor measured for the algorithm: 1.62 for `delaunay`, 1.58 for `meshadapt` and 1.52 for `frontal`. A triangle then has an edge about 1.5 times longer than `mesh.cell_size`, and the count follows \(A_\Omega/\ell^2\) (Three sizes, read in order). When the request has a size field, the engine also resamples the lines at this edge length, because Gmsh keeps every vertex it receives. The corners of the barriers stay fixed vertices. With lines in the request, Gmsh still adds cells around them, at the bends and at the confluences. So the count stays above the integral of the size field, by 11 % with one river and by 35 % on the dense network of the Flume. Without lines, the field of the Flume gives 1.05.

## 4. The Voronoi engine

A cell of the `voronoi` engine is the Voronoi (PEBI) cell of a generator \(\mathbf{s}_i\), the points closer to \(\mathbf{s}_i\) than to any other generator, clipped to the outline \(\Omega\). The generator is the cell center. The engine puts one generator on each vertex of a river line, so the river runs through a chain of centers. It puts a pair of mirror generators across each segment of a contact, a shore, a barrier or the catchment boundary, after Berge et al. [2019], so the segment is a face. Other generators sit on the domain boundary. Free generators fill the rest with the density \(\ell^{-2}\), and a Lloyd relaxation weighted by \(\ell^{-4}\) moves them. So the engine draws about \(\int_\Omega \ell^{-2}\,\mathrm{d}A\) generators, one per cell of area \(\ell^2\) (Three sizes, read in order).

So each cell lies in one zone, and the cells of a lake are those inside its shore. Where a river crosses a contact, the contact yields on a short segment, and the river cell there takes the minimum of its pixels as top (6. The top of a cell). A flow barrier never yields, and the river chain crosses it through a barrier face. Every face is the perpendicular bisector of two generators, so \(\varphi_{nm} = 0\) where both cells kept their generator as center. As a check, 36 generators on a \(6 \times 6\) lattice, the 16 inner ones moved at random, give 36 cells at \(0^\circ\) on every connection. The construction and its gates are on Mesh engines.

## 5. Flow between two cells, and the angle

MODFLOW 6 writes the flow between two cells as \(G_{nm}\,(h_m - h_n)\), the two-point term of (25) [Harbaugh, 2005, Langevin et al., 2017]. It is exact only when the conductivity is isotropic in the plane and the line between the centers is perpendicular to the shared face. The code measures the departure as an angle. With \(\mathbf{d}_{nm}\) the vector between the centers and \(\mathbf{n}_{nm}\) the unit normal of the shared edge, it reads

(31)\[\varphi_{nm} = \arccos\!\left(\frac{\lvert \mathbf{d}_{nm} \cdot \mathbf{n}_{nm} \rvert} {\lVert \mathbf{d}_{nm} \rVert}\right).\]

Over the edges shared by two cells, the code keeps the median, the 95th and 99th percentiles, the maximum and the share of angles above 30 degrees. The effect on the flux and the XT3D trigger are on XT3D on irregular meshes. For example, the two triangles of a \(2 \times 1\) rectangle cut along its diagonal have their centers at \((2/3, 1/3)\) and \((4/3, 2/3)\), so \(\cos\varphi = 4/5\) and \(\varphi \approx 36.9^\circ\). The four corners of the same rectangle, taken as seeds, give four Voronoi cells of \(1 \times 0.5\), all at \(0^\circ\).

Fig. 31 Left: the two triangles above. Right: the 36 seeds of the check of 4. The Voronoi engine, their 50 triangles (dotted) and their Voronoi cells (blue).

The two-point term also assumes that the line of the centers crosses the face in its middle. On a face of length \(L\) crossed at a distance \(s\) from one end, the bisection offset is

(32)\[\beta = \frac{\lvert s - L/2 \rvert}{L},\]

which is 0 for a bisected face and 0.5 when the line passes through a face end. A cell takes the largest \(\beta\) of its faces. A Voronoi face is bisected only when its two generators sit at the same distance from its two ends, so the offset can be large where the angle is zero.

Fig. 33 Left: two Voronoi cells whose generators sit 0.6 above the middle of their face (square). Right: the two triangles above. Both measures come from `planar/quality.py`.

## 6. The top of a cell

The top of a cell is one number read from the DEM \(Z\) by the rule that `solver.modflow6.sgrid.top_sampling.mode` picks, `centroid` by default. The bottom always takes the centroid rule.

### Centroid

The code interpolates the DEM at the cell center between the four pixel centers around it, with a zero weight on a nodata pixel:

\[\tilde z_c = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{4} w_k\, Z_k\, \mathbf{1}[Z_k \text{ valid}]} {\sum_{k=1}^{4} w_k\, \mathbf{1}[Z_k \text{ valid}]} .\]

The cell is inactive when its center is outside the raster or the four pixels are nodata. On an incised channel the center often falls on a bank, so the cell is too high. On a `voronoi` mesh, a river cell whose center lies off the river line takes the minimum of its pixels in this mode too. This happens where a contact crosses the river, where two thalwegs share a cell and at a river end near the boundary.

### Zonal

The zonal rule reduces the pixels whose center falls in the cell. A pixel is a channel pixel when the stream raster of the delineation marks it, with the mask widened by `solver.modflow6.sgrid.top_sampling.channel_buffer_px` pixels. The code reads that raster only when `solver.modflow6.sgrid.top_sampling.channel_source` asks for it, and without it every pixel is a hillslope pixel. With the statistic of `solver.modflow6.sgrid.top_sampling.channel_stat` on the channel pixels and of `solver.modflow6.sgrid.top_sampling.hillslope_stat` on the others, the top reads

(33)\[\begin{split}z_{\mathrm{top},c} = \begin{cases} \operatorname{stat}_{\mathrm{ch}}\{Z_p : p \in P_c^{\mathrm{ch}}\} & P_c^{\mathrm{ch}} \neq \emptyset, \\[0.5ex] \operatorname{stat}_{\mathrm{hill}}\{Z_p : p \in P_c\} & P_c^{\mathrm{ch}} = \emptyset \text{ and } \lvert P_c \rvert \ge n_{\min}, \\[0.5ex] \tilde z_c & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}\end{split}\]

Then a hillslope top more than \(\varepsilon_z\) away from \(\tilde z_c\) goes back to it, which guards against a nodata edge. Channel cells are exempt, and \(\varepsilon_z = 0\) switches the guard off. A lowered top must also stay above the bottom. On the regular grid the code raises the top to at least \(z_{\mathrm{bot},c} + b_{\min}\). On a triangle or Voronoi mesh the top stays. The bottom follows it down when the column left is thinner than \(b_{\min}\) or than a tenth of the column of the center sample:

\[z_{\mathrm{bot},c} \leftarrow z_{\mathrm{top},c} - \max\bigl(\tilde z_c - z_{\mathrm{bot},c},\ b_{\min}\bigr).\]

The cell then keeps the thickness of its center sample, because MODFLOW 6 cannot solve under Newton a column of a few decimeters next to neighbors of tens of meters. Elsewhere the bottom stays, so a lowered top thins every layer of the column. The log counts these changes once per build.

Fig. 35 A cell of 32 m radius over 5 m pixels, its center on a bank 18 m from a channel incised 2 m (blue). The centroid sample and the hillslope median sit about 4 m above the channel minimum of `zonal_top`.

The zonal rule falls back to the centroid value, with a message in the log, in three cases. The surface has no georeferencing, the channel source has no stream raster, or the cells of a structured grid cover fewer than two DEM pixels.

## 7. Thickness and layers

One table, `[domain.layers]`, cuts each column into layers for MODFLOW 6 and MODFLOW-NWT alike, and the code moves the older `[modflow6.sgrid.vertical]` or `[modflownwt.sgrid.vertical]` to it. With `domain.layers.genmtd_lay` at `constant`, `decay` or `list`, the layers are the same shares of the thickness in every cell ((22), The solver grid and its layers). Every layer shares the cells of the plan. A cell is inactive in every layer when its top or its bottom is nodata, not finite, or at or below the nodata value.

### Layers by surfaces

With `genmtd_lay = "surfaces"`, each `[[domain.layers.layer]]` table gives the base of its layer with one key: a `thickness` below the layer above (below the terrain for the first layer), a `depth` below the terrain, an `elevation`, or a `surface`, the name of a raster of `[[data.layer_base.sources]]`. The last layer ends on the base of the aquifer of `[domain.depth_model]` (The domain). A raster that leaves a cell without a value is refused. Each base stays between the base of the aquifer and the base of the layer above, so bases never cross. Where a layer is thinner than its `min_thickness`, the code pinches it out as `domain.layers.pinch_out` says:

| `pinch_out` | What the cell becomes |
| --- | --- |
| `pass_through` | a vertical pass-through cell, `idomain = -1`. Its thickness goes to the active cell below it, or above it at the base of the column, so the column keeps its top, its base and its transmissivity |
| `keep_min_thickness` | a cell of the minimum thickness. Its base moves down, and so do the bases of the layers below it and the base of the aquifer |

Fig. 37 The base of the middle layer comes from a raster (dotted) that rises to the layer above, with a `min_thickness` of 4 m. Left: the thin cells pass their thickness to the layer below. Right: they keep 4 m and the base below them moves down.

With `pass_through`, a column whose layers are all too thin keeps its thickest layer active. `idomain` is 1 for an active cell, 0 for an inactive one and -1 for a pass-through cell. MODFLOW 6 connects the cells above and below a pass-through cell. A lake over such a column reads the active cells under it (The connections). MODFLOW-NWT has no such cell, so it refuses `pass_through` in the file and in the grid. The build refuses an active cell whose top is at or below its bottom. The code stores the layering with `vertical_layout = "surfaces"` on `mesh/` (Storage layout).

### The top active layer

With pass-through cells, the first layer is not always the top of the column. One function gives the top active layer of each column. A point, a well or an observation without a layer goes to that cell. The drains, the imposed heads, the evapotranspiration surface, the computational top, the filling of closed depressions and the saturated thickness of a calibration read the same cell (The solvers of the aquifer).

## Three sizes, read in order

Three keys speak of a size, and each one reads the one before it.

1. `resolution_m` asks a provider for a pixel. With a DEM file, the file has its own pixel and this key does not apply.
1. `dem_resolution` aggregates that pixel before anything is delineated. It cannot be finer than the pixel of the DEM: the run refuses it. The routing surface, the catchment, the mesh and the model top take the result. Unset, the pixel stays.
1. `cell_size` sizes the cells of the model. Unset, it is the pixel from step 2. A triangle or a voronoi mesh never grades finer than this pixel, whatever a size says.

So the same run can route on 25 m, and solve on 50 m cells. A cell size changes the cells, and never the surface that was delineated.

## 8. How many cells a size costs

The cost of a run grows with the number of cells, so this section counts them. For the three engines, `mesh.cell_size` is the side \(\ell\) of the square that has the mean area of a cell. Over an area \(A_\Omega\), a mesh then holds about \(A_\Omega/\ell^2\) cells. The grid of pixel side \(\Delta\) is the case \(N_S = A_\Omega/\Delta^2\). With a size field, \(A_\Omega/\ell^2\) becomes \(\int_\Omega \ell(\mathbf{x})^{-2}\,\mathrm{d}A\).

The same count does not give the same edge. An equilateral triangle of side \(\ell_T\) has the area \(\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\ell_T^2\), and a Voronoi hexagon has \(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\ell_V^2\) when neighboring seeds are \(\ell_V\) apart, so

(34)\[N_T = \frac{4}{\sqrt3}\,\frac{A_\Omega}{\ell_T^2} \approx 2.31\,\frac{A_\Omega}{\ell_T^2}, \qquad N_V = \frac{2}{\sqrt3}\,\frac{A_\Omega}{\ell_V^2} \approx 1.15\,\frac{A_\Omega}{\ell_V^2}.\]

Setting \(N_T = N_V = A_\Omega/\ell^2\) gives \(\ell_T = \sqrt{4/\sqrt3}\,\ell \approx 1.52\,\ell\) and \(\ell_V = \sqrt{2/\sqrt3}\,\ell \approx 1.07\,\ell\). So at the cell count of a grid of pixel \(\Delta\), the Voronoi generators are \(1.07\,\Delta\) apart and the triangles have a side of \(1.52\,\Delta\).

A square of 4 km at a `cell_size` of 100 m expects 1600 cells. The `regular` and `voronoi` engines give 1600, and the `triangle` engine gives 1652, which is 3 % more. The engine contract holds every engine to 10 % of the expected count on a uniform size. With lines to follow, the `triangle` engine stays above the integral (3. The triangle engine). On the Flume, with cells of 25 m along the rivers in a background of 150 m, the count over the integral is 1.00 for `voronoi` and 1.35 for `triangle`.

Example 04 declares no `[mesh]` section. Its box holds 172 by 157 cells of 75 m, 27004 cells and about \(152\ \mathrm{km^2}\), inactive cells included. The same count means a `mesh.cell_size` of 75 m for each engine, with Voronoi generators about 81 m apart and triangles of about 114 m. A real mesh refines near the interfaces, so the count of a run is the \(\mathrm{ncpl}\) of its DISV file. Also, \(N_S\) counts the whole raster box, while a mesh lies in \(\Omega\).

Fig. 39 (34) for \(A_\Omega\) = 120 km². Each dot holds 21406 cells. The Voronoi dot sits at 1.07 times the pixel side and the triangle dot at 1.52 times.

## 9. The checks the code applies

The code refuses a mesh when its inputs are wrong, and it stops a run when the grid it solves is not the stored mesh. Apart from the `voronoi` build, it refuses no mesh for its shape. The table lists the checks that the sections above do not give.

| What is checked | Rule | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Solver and mesh | the solver reads the engine of `[mesh]` | refused when the file is read: `reads the meshes of the engines` |
| River size | `mesh.river_cell_size` at most `mesh.cell_size` | refused when the file is read |
| Voronoi build | each cell covers its generator, conformal faces lie on their lines, river chains are connected, the areas add up to the domain, no repeated vertex, no face under a micrometer | the build stops with `MeshGenerationError` |
| Solved grid | the DISV or DIS grid of the solver is the stored mesh | the run stops with `IncompatibleMeshError` |
| Top and bottom | one valid cell at least, and the bottom strictly below the top on every valid cell | refused: `No finite overlapping valid cells found between top and bottom surfaces.` or `Bottom surface must be strictly below top surface on valid cells` |
| Thick cells | thickness above the larger of 10 times the median and 500 m | warning on triangle and Voronoi meshes: `Aquifer thickness outliers:` |
| Cell shape | no triangle corner under 20 degrees, no face crossed more than 0.25 of its length from its middle, no concave cell | warning at build |
| Imported triangulation | no vertex inside an edge that does not hold it, no two vertices closer than 1e-9 of the extent | a T-junction is refused with its coordinates, duplicates warn |
| Active cells | one group, counted on the grid the solver reads after the lake mask. Faces join cells, so do vertical connections (a pass-through cell joins the layers above and below it), and so does a lake, for the active cells it touches | warning with the number and sizes of the groups |
| Point on the mesh | a point outside the mesh lies within one cell size (the square root of the area) of a cell | no cell for the point, and a warning that names it, on every solver |

Eight fields measure the cells one by one, computed on read: `mesh_cell_area`, `mesh_neighbour_ratio` (size ratio between neighbors), `mesh_center_offset` (offset of a center from its cell centroid), `mesh_nonorthogonality`, `mesh_bisection_offset`, `mesh_min_angle`, `mesh_max_angle` and `mesh_concavity`, how far the largest angle exceeds 180°. A corner within 0.1° of 180° counts as straight. The layer `mesh_cells` of `hmp export` carries the eight, and it names the two angle columns `min_angle_deg` and `max_angle_deg`. The quality report `MeshQA` is stored as the attribute `qa` of `mesh/`. It holds their quantiles, the number of concave cells and, for each line family, how much of the line the faces follow. A mesh with a poor report still runs.

## 10. The catchment of a cell

The delineated catchment is a polygon, and its outline can cross a cell. The solver build stores for each face the share of its area that lies inside the polygon, from 0 to 1, as `catchment_fraction`. A cell inside has 1 and a cell outside has 0. The share is exact in between, because the code intersects the polygon with the cells that the outline cuts, and with no other. The basin of the descent D, the cells whose descent passes through the outlet, does not change (Routing the hillslope drainage). It stays all or nothing, and it still gives the `catchment` line of the budget and the discharge at the outlet, which are hydraulic quantities.

A total over the catchment of a quantity that varies in space sums the cell values with the shares. `budget_over` does it for a term of the budget stored per cell, such as the recharge or the seepage, over the catchment or over any polygon. `catchment_mean` averages a variable with the share times the area of the cell, so a small cell counts less than a large one. A run with no stored share counts the whole cells of the basin of D and logs it. The shares also cover the cells outside the basin that the polygon touches. A distorted disc over a grid of 75 m shows why. A mask by cell center gives the area of the polygon within -0.03 % (standard deviation 0.13 %) for a radius of 3 km, and within -0.06 % (0.45 %) for 1 km. Weights limited to the basin lose the part of the polygon that falls in the neighboring cells, and give -0.67 % and -2.0 %.

On example 04 the polygon is the staircase of the DEM, so it cuts no cell of the grid and every share is 0 or 1. The totals still differ a little from the budget line, because the basin of D and the polygon disagree on whole cells. The basin holds 13 cells outside the polygon (0.073 km²), and the polygon holds 12 cells outside the basin (0.068 km²). The recharge over the catchment is 0.01 % below the line of the budget, and the seepage is equal to it within 0.01 %. A cut cell needs a triangle or a Voronoi mesh, or a grid coarser than the DEM.

A synthetic domain has no catchment polygon and no outlet. It stores no share, its basin of D is the largest basin of the domain, and `budget_over` without a polygon and `catchment_mean` refuse it.

## Assumptions

- A cell has one top and one bottom, so the surface inside the cell is flat.
- A mesh is fixed for the run. It does not move with the water table.
- The conductivity is isotropic in the plane unless the flow sets `K22` or the angles of the tensor, which MODFLOW 6 alone reads (The conductivity tensor).
- The coordinates are in a projected CRS in meters. The size field, the 1 mm merge of the Voronoi vertices and every distance of the engines rely on it.
- The zonal rule takes the channel pixels from the stream raster of the delineation. It does not read the observed network.

## Limits

- Boussinesq cannot run on Voronoi cells, nor MODFLOW-NWT on a refined mesh. The zonal top of MODFLOW-NWT needs `solver.modflow_nwt.sgrid.top_sampling.channel_source` at `"none"`.
- Deleting `.hmp/products/` makes a resumed triangle run mesh again. On one thread gmsh redraws the same mesh, and the log warns that a rebuilt mesh may differ from the one the results were computed on.
- One request and one seed give one Voronoi mesh on one machine, GEOS and scipy build. Another build can give the same quality with another connectivity.
- Where the size field grows at its largest slope, a Voronoi center sits off its cell centroid by about a quarter of the slope times the cell size.
- A lake arm narrower than the local cell cannot hold a pair of generators. The faces then follow part of the shore, and the cells of the lake are those its polygon overlaps.
- A head imposed on a side applies at the centers of the cells with a face on it: half a cell from the side on a regular grid, a third of the height on triangles, on the side for Voronoi cells.
- The tenth of the column that moves a bottom under a lowered top is empirical. It keeps the cells next to a quarry solvable.
- The layers are an extrusion of the plan, so the footprint and the size of the cells never change with depth.
- Two face lines that meet at less than 53 degrees make a gap that closes at the corner, so the cells at its tip take the size of the DEM pixel. Lines closer than a tenth of a pixel count as one.
- A nodata value read as an elevation gives a cell kilometers deep with a clean top, and the run converges. The thickness warning is the only sign, and a structured grid does not emit it.
- Under Newton, XT3D can fail to converge on triangle cells, and the run stops with E401. The cause and the two ways out are on XT3D on irregular meshes.
- A refinement zone that reads an earlier run needs that run in the project. A run copied to another project stops with a message when it replays.

## Parameters of this page

The keys that choose the engine, the size and the top. The keys of the layers are in [domain], those of the top in [solver] and those of the mesh in [mesh]. The cards show the defaults and the allowed values, and the developer keys are behind the developer button.

[mesh]

`# engine = "regular"` : Mesh engine: 'regular' (one quadrilateral cell per DEM pixel, or per cell_size), 'triangle' (triangles that follow the lines), 'voronoi' (polygons around generators) or 'catchment' (the catchment as one polygon cell, for a global model, read only by a solver that names it).
**Path**: `mesh.engine`
**More**: A string and not a closed choice, since an installed third-party engine is named the same way.
**Accepted**: string
**Example**: `"regular"`, `"triangle"`, `"voronoi"`

`# cell_size = ‹number›` : Cell size in metres, the side of the square of the same mean area as the cells, whatever the engine: a domain of area A gets about A / cell_size^2 cells, and a regular, a triangle and a voronoi cell of this size have about the same area. m > 0
**Path**: `mesh.cell_size`
**More**: It is the side of the regular grid cells and the background size of the triangle and voronoi engines. Unset, the DEM pixel size, which is the pixel of geographic.catchment.dem_resolution when that key is set, else the pixel of the DEM file. It is the last of the three sizes and reads none of them back: it changes the cells and not the surface that was delineated.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: > 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: m

`# river_cell_size = ‹number›` : Cell size in metres along the rivers, the side of the square of the same mean area as the cells, as cell_size. m > 0 only if engine = "triangle" | "voronoi"
**Path**: `mesh.river_cell_size`
**More**: Unset, the DEM pixel size; never finer than the DEM pixel.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: > 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: m
**Only if**: engine = "triangle" | "voronoi"

`# river_band = ‹number›` : Distance in metres from a river over which the cell size grows back to cell_size. m > 0 only if engine = "triangle" | "voronoi"
**Path**: `mesh.river_band`
**More**: Unset, twice cell_size.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: > 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: m
**Only if**: engine = "triangle" | "voronoi"

`# max_slope = 0.5` : Largest growth of the cell size per meter of distance, which bounds the size ratio of two neighbors. m/m ]0, 1] dev
**Path**: `mesh.max_slope`
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: ]0, 1] (refused outside)
**Unit**: m/m

`# gap_cells = 2.0` : Cells across the gap between two face lines (lake shores, barriers, geology contacts, catchment boundary) or between one and the domain outline: the cell size there, with the meaning of cell_size, is the gap divided by this number, never finer than the DEM pixel. cells >= 0 only if engine = "triangle" | "voronoi" dev
**Path**: `mesh.gap_cells`
**More**: 0 switches it off.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: >= 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: cells
**Only if**: engine = "triangle" | "voronoi"

`# outside_factor = 2.0` : Cell size outside the catchment, as a multiple of cell_size; the cells there have about outside_factor^2 times the area of a cell_size cell. - >= 1 dev
**Path**: `mesh.outside_factor`
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: >= 1 (refused outside)
**Unit**: -

`# transition_distance = 500.0` : Distance in meters outside the catchment over which the cell size grows to its outside value. m >= 0 dev
**Path**: `mesh.transition_distance`
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: >= 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: m

`# seed = 0` : Seed of the random draws of an engine; one seed gives one mesh. - >= 0 dev
**Path**: `mesh.seed`
**Accepted**: integer
**Valid range**: >= 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: -

[mesh.regular]

`shape = [60, 60]` : Number of rows and columns [nrow, ncol] of the grid over the DEM extent; the cells are rectangular when the extent is not square. required cells dev example value
**Path**: `mesh.regular.shape`
**Accepted**: list of integer
**Unit**: cells
**Example**: `[60, 60]`

[mesh.families]

`# rivers = "cell"` : How the mesh follows the river network traced from the DEM.
**Path**: `mesh.families.rivers`
**Values**:
- `"cell"` : The cells along each river form an ordered chain, from upstream to downstream; the river size applies along it.
- `"none"` : The mesh ignores the rivers.
**Accepted**: "cell" | "none"

`# geology = "face"` : How the mesh follows the contacts between the zones of the vector geology map that a flow parameter reads.
**Path**: `mesh.families.geology`
**Values**:
- `"face"` : Cell faces lie on the contacts between geology zones.
- `"none"` : The mesh ignores the geology contacts.
**Accepted**: "face" | "none"

`# lakes = "face"` : How the mesh follows the shore of each lake of the flow model.
**Path**: `mesh.families.lakes`
**Values**:
- `"face"` : Cell faces lie on the lake shores.
- `"none"` : The mesh ignores the lake shores.
**Accepted**: "face" | "none"

`# barriers = "face"` : How the mesh follows the flow barriers: the cutoff wall of each lake that declares one, and the lines of [flow.sinks_sources.flow_barriers].
**Path**: `mesh.families.barriers`
**See**: flow.sinks_sources.flow_barriers
**Values**:
- `"face"` : Cell faces lie on each barrier line, wings and free ends included, and the HFB rows go on them. The regular engine takes the staircase of faces the line crosses.
- `"none"` : The mesh ignores the barriers; the HFB rows go on the faces each line crosses.
**Accepted**: "face" | "none"

`# watershed_boundary = "none"` : How the mesh follows the boundary of the catchment inside the domain.
**Path**: `mesh.families.watershed_boundary`
**Values**:
- `"face"` : Cell faces lie on the catchment boundary.
- `"none"` : The mesh ignores the catchment boundary.
**Accepted**: "face" | "none"

[[mesh.refinement_zone]]

`# where = "height_above_stream"` : The field whose threshold draws the zone, on the pixels of the DEM, instead of a vector layer. example value
**Path**: `mesh.refinement_zone.where`
**More**: The zone is the set of pixels where the field is below the value of below, or above the value of above. Give path or where, not both.
**Values**:
- `"height_above_stream"` : Height in metres of the ground above the stream it drains to, computed from the DEM and the river network traced from it ([geographic.river_network]). The mapped network never enters. Takes below.
- `"watertable_depth"` : Depth in metres of the water table below the ground in the run named by run, at any of its time steps: its minimum over time is compared to below, its maximum to above.
- `"seepage"` : Drain outflow per cell area, in mm/d, in the run named by run, at any of its time steps: its maximum over time is compared to above, its minimum to below.
**Accepted**: "height_above_stream" | "watertable_depth" | "seepage"
**Example**: `"height_above_stream"`, `"watertable_depth"`, `"seepage"`

`# below = 2.0` : The zone holds the pixels where the field of where is below this value: metres for height_above_stream and watertable_depth, mm/d for seepage. m, or mm/d for seepage > 0 example value
**Path**: `mesh.refinement_zone.below`
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: > 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: m, or mm/d for seepage
**Example**: `2.0`

`# above = 0.5` : The zone holds the pixels where the field of where is above this value: metres for watertable_depth, mm/d for seepage. m, or mm/d for seepage >= 0 example value
**Path**: `mesh.refinement_zone.above`
**More**: Not read for height_above_stream.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: >= 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: m, or mm/d for seepage
**Example**: `0.5`

`# run = "nancon_coarse"` : The earlier run of this project whose field draws the zone, for watertable_depth and seepage: its name, with or without its _vN (the latest version without), or its full sim_id. example value
**Path**: `mesh.refinement_zone.run`
**More**: The run must be sealed and hold the field. The mesh then depends on that run: its sim_id enters the mesh request and the product key.
**Accepted**: string
**Example**: `"nancon_coarse"`

[mesh.triangle]

`# path = "mesh/catchment.msh"` : Existing gmsh .msh file (format 2.2) to read instead of generating a triangulation, relative to the project root (the folder of project.toml). example value
**Path**: `mesh.triangle.path`
**More**: The line families are derived on the mesh read.
**Accepted**: path
**Example**: `"mesh/catchment.msh"`

`# algorithm = "delaunay"` : Two-dimensional gmsh algorithm that generates the triangles of the triangle engine. dev
**Path**: `mesh.triangle.algorithm`
**More**: The voronoi engine does not triangulate and ignores it.
**Values**:
- `"delaunay"` : Gmsh Delaunay (algorithm 5): fast and robust.
- `"frontal"` : Gmsh frontal-Delaunay (algorithm 6): better shaped triangles.
- `"meshadapt"` : Gmsh MeshAdapt (algorithm 1): for complex curved boundaries.
**Accepted**: "delaunay" | "frontal" | "meshadapt"

[mesh.voronoi]

`# seeds = ‹"generated" | "triangulation"›` : Where the generators of the Voronoi cells come from. dev
**Path**: `mesh.voronoi.seeds`
**More**: Unset, they are the vertices of the triangulation read from [mesh.triangle] path when a path is given, and generated by the engine otherwise.
**Values**:
- `"generated"` : The engine places the generators itself: along the rivers, in mirror pairs on the face lines, on the boundary, and freely from the size field.
- `"triangulation"` : The vertices of the triangulation read from [mesh.triangle] path are the generators.
**Accepted**: "generated" | "triangulation"

`# lloyd_tolerance = 0.01` : Stop of the Lloyd relaxation of the generated generators: the root mean square of the displacements of the free generators in one iteration, as a share of their local cell size. - > 0 dev
**Path**: `mesh.voronoi.lloyd_tolerance`
**More**: The relaxation also stops after 25 iterations, and the mesh QA reports whether the tolerance was reached and the largest displacement.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: > 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: -

[solver.modflow6.sgrid.top_sampling]

`# mode = "centroid"` : Top-sampling strategy.
**Path**: `solver.modflow6.sgrid.top_sampling.mode`
**More**: 'centroid' samples the DEM at each cell generator, or resamples it to a structured grid (fast, the default). On a mesh that publishes a lateral offset for a river cell (the river runs through the cell but beside its centre, as where a contact line crosses it or two thalwegs share it), that cell takes the lowest DEM pixel it covers. 'zonal' reduces every DEM pixel inside a cell with per-class stats.
**Values**:
- `"centroid"`
- `"zonal"`
**Accepted**: "centroid" | "zonal"

`# hillslope_stat = "median"` : Zonal statistic over non-channel (hillslope) pixels inside a cell.
**Path**: `solver.modflow6.sgrid.top_sampling.hillslope_stat`
**Values**:
- `"mean"` : Averages every hillslope pixel in the cell to set its top elevation.
- `"median"` : Uses the median hillslope pixel elevation, robust to outlier pixels.
- `"min"` : Uses the lowest hillslope pixel elevation found inside the cell.
- `"max"` : Uses the highest hillslope pixel elevation found inside the cell.
- `"p10"` : Uses the 10th percentile of hillslope pixel elevations inside the cell.
- `"p25"` : Uses the 25th percentile of hillslope pixel elevations inside the cell.
**Accepted**: "mean" | "median" | "min" | "max" | "p10" | "p25"

`# channel_stat = "min"` : Zonal statistic over channel pixels inside a cell (thalweg-preserving; 'min' keeps the incised low).
**Path**: `solver.modflow6.sgrid.top_sampling.channel_stat`
**Values**:
- `"min"` : Uses the lowest channel pixel elevation, keeping the incised thalweg low.
- `"p10"` : Uses the 10th percentile of channel pixel elevations, near the thalweg low.
- `"p25"` : Uses the 25th percentile of channel pixel elevations, above the thalweg low.
- `"median"` : Uses the median channel pixel elevation, less aggressive than the thalweg low.
- `"mean"` : Averages channel pixel elevations, smoothing over the incised thalweg.
**Accepted**: "min" | "p10" | "p25" | "median" | "mean"

`# channel_source = "streams_raster"` : Where channel pixels come from when mode='zonal'.
**Path**: `solver.modflow6.sgrid.top_sampling.channel_source`
**More**: 'streams_raster' uses the delineated river-network raster reprojected onto the DEM grid; 'none' disables the channel class (every pixel is hillslope).
**Values**:
- `"none"`
- `"streams_raster"`
**Accepted**: "none" | "streams_raster"

`# channel_buffer_px = 0` : Dilate the channel pixel mask by this many pixels before reducing, to capture a channel that grazes a cell without a pixel centre on it. pixel >= 0 dev
**Path**: `solver.modflow6.sgrid.top_sampling.channel_buffer_px`
**Accepted**: integer
**Valid range**: >= 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: pixel

`# spike_guard_tol_m = 2.0` : Revert a hillslope cell's zonal value to the centroid sample when it deviates more than this many metres (guards nodata/edge spikes); channel cells are exempt since they are lowered on purpose. m >= 0 dev
**Path**: `solver.modflow6.sgrid.top_sampling.spike_guard_tol_m`
**More**: 0 disables the guard.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: >= 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: m

`# min_pixels = 3` : Minimum DEM pixels inside a cell to trust a hillslope zonal statistic; below this the cell falls back to the centroid sample. - > 0 dev
**Path**: `solver.modflow6.sgrid.top_sampling.min_pixels`
**More**: A channel cell uses its channel stat from a single thalweg pixel.
**Accepted**: integer
**Valid range**: > 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: -

`# min_thickness_m = 0.1` : Minimum column thickness (m) kept under a zonal top lowered by a channel or a crossing. m >= 0 dev
**Path**: `solver.modflow6.sgrid.top_sampling.min_thickness_m`
**More**: On a mesh of polygons the bottom of a cell whose lowered top leaves less than this, or less than a tenth of the column its centre sample gave, moves down with it and keeps the thickness of the cell-centre sample; on a regular grid the top is raised back instead.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: >= 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: m

[domain.layers]

`# genmtd_lay = "constant"` : How the aquifer thickness is split into layers: equal layers, layers that thicken with depth, the fractions you list, or one base per layer.
**Path**: `domain.layers.genmtd_lay`
**Values**:
- `"constant"` : Splits local thickness into nlay equal-fraction layers at every cell.
- `"decay"` : Grows layer thickness geometrically with depth when lay_decay is above one.
- `"list"` : Uses the explicit per-layer thickness fractions given in lay_proportions.
- `"surfaces"` : Gives each layer its own base in the [[domain.layers.layer]] tables.
**Accepted**: "constant" | "decay" | "list" | "surfaces"

`# nlay = 1` : Number of layers for 'constant' and 'decay'. -
**Path**: `domain.layers.nlay`
**More**: With 'list', the number of fractions sets it, with 'surfaces' the number of layer tables.
**Accepted**: integer
**Unit**: -

`# lay_decay = 2.0` : Ratio of each layer's thickness to the thickness of the layer above it, above 1. - only if genmtd_lay = "decay" example value
**Path**: `domain.layers.lay_decay`
**More**: With 2, each layer is twice as thick as the one above.
**Accepted**: number
**Unit**: -
**Example**: `2.0`
**Only if**: genmtd_lay = "decay"

`# lay_proportions = [0.2, 0.3, 0.5]` : Share of the thickness each layer takes, from the top. only if genmtd_lay = "list" example value
**Path**: `domain.layers.lay_proportions`
**More**: The shares must sum to 1.
**Accepted**: list of number
**Example**: `[0.2, 0.3, 0.5]`
**Only if**: genmtd_lay = "list"

`# pinch_out = "pass_through"` : What a layer thinner than its min_thickness becomes, for 'surfaces'. only if genmtd_lay = "surfaces"
**Path**: `domain.layers.pinch_out`
**More**: Read only with that value of genmtd_lay.
**Values**:
- `"pass_through"` : The cell becomes a vertical pass-through (idomain -1, MODFLOW 6 only) and the active cell below it, or above it at the base, takes its thickness.
- `"keep_min_thickness"` : The base of the layer moves down to keep min_thickness, and the layers below and the base of the aquifer with it. MODFLOW-NWT reads only this value.
**Accepted**: "pass_through" | "keep_min_thickness"
**Only if**: genmtd_lay = "surfaces"

[[domain.layers.layer]]

`# thickness = 30.0` : Base this far below the base of the layer above, or below the terrain for the first layer (canonical metres). m > 0 example value
**Path**: `domain.layers.layer.thickness`
**Accepted**: number or "<n> m" (a bare number is read in the canonical unit)
**Valid range**: > 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: m
**Example**: `30.0`

`# min_thickness = 0.1` : Thinnest the layer may be (canonical metres). m > 0
**Path**: `domain.layers.layer.min_thickness`
**More**: Where it is thinner, [domain.layers] pinch_out says what happens.
**Accepted**: number or "<n> m" (a bare number is read in the canonical unit)
**Valid range**: > 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: m

[solver.modflow6.runtime]

`# mf6_enable_xt3d = ‹true | false›` : Enable MF6 NPF XT3D terms. expert
**Path**: `solver.modflow6.runtime.mf6_enable_xt3d`
**More**: When left to None, XT3D turns on where a consistent result needs it, with a RuntimeWarning: a tilted K tensor (a non-zero flow parameter angle2 or angle3, which MF6 reads only under XT3D), and a K22 different from K on a cell whose angle1 is not a multiple of 90 degrees, or anywhere on an unstructured mesh. Without XT3D the two-point flux drops the cross terms of such a tensor, and the head error does not shrink with refinement. XT3D also turns on, with an INFO log, on triangle cells and on a significantly non-orthogonal mesh. A structured grid with K along its axes, or an orthogonal mesh with K22 equal to K, keeps it off. XT3D costs from about 1.5 times the MF6 run time on one layer to about 10 times on ten layers. true turns it on without a warning; false turns it off, with a RuntimeWarning when a consistent result needs it.
**Accepted**: true | false

Lines generated from the models, as in the reference. Open one for its card.

# Notation

Every symbol of the theory pages, with its unit and the key that sets it. The tables are generated from one registry, `docs/source/theory/symbols.yaml`, and each theory page renders its own table from the same file.

The units are the ones the code stores: lengths in meters, hydraulic conductivity in m/s, rates in m/s. The soil reservoir is the exception, because it works in mm and days. A name that exists in the code or in an output file is given in `code font` in the meaning column, so a symbol can be matched with a column of a result file.

## Conventions

- Lengths are in meters, and elevation is positive up.
- A flux into the aquifer is positive. The residual of the Boussinesq solver is the one exception: it counts a loss as positive, and its page says so.
- Cells are \(n\) and \(m\) on the pages of the two MODFLOW solvers and of the mesh, and \(i\) on the Boussinesq page, which runs on triangles.
- A symbol with an overbar, such as \(\bar B\), is an average over the catchment. It is by area, unless the page says otherwise.
- A TOML value can carry its unit, such as `"500 m"` or `"1 month"`. The unit of a key is on its card.

## Space, time and heads

| Symbol | Meaning | Unit | Set by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| \(x, y\) | horizontal coordinates | m | the grid, The mesh |
| \(z\) | elevation, positive up | m | - |
| \(d\) | depth below the model top, the variable of the depth factor of a property | m | - |
| \(t\) | time; on the soil page, the day | s | `start_datetime` and `end_datetime` bound the run |
| \(\Delta t\) | length of a stress period, the stretch of time that gets one forcing value | s | `step_value` |
| \(\delta t\) | solver time step, \(\delta t = \Delta t / n_\mathrm{sub}\) | s | derived |
| \(n_\mathrm{sub}\) | number of solver time steps in a stress period |
-
 | `substeps_per_period` |
| \(h\) | hydraulic head, measured from a fixed datum | m | solved, not set |
| \(h_0\) | head at the start of the run | m | `kind` |
| \(z_\mathrm{top}\) | model top, the land surface | m | `data.dem` |
| \(z'_\mathrm{top}\) | computational top MODFLOW 6 reads, \(z'_\mathrm{top} = z_\mathrm{top} + \max H_1 - H_1\) | m | derived |
| \(z_\mathrm{bot}\) | bottom of the aquifer | m | `kind` |
| \(H\) | aquifer thickness, \(H = z_\mathrm{top} - z_\mathrm{bot}\) | m | `kind` |
| \(H_1\) | thickness of the top layer under the ground | m | `nlay` |
| \(B\) | saturated thickness, \(B(h) = \min\bigl(\max(h - z_\mathrm{bot}, 0), H\bigr)\) | m | state, not a field |
| \(\bar B\) | saturated thickness averaged by area over the catchment (`d_sat_m`) | m | derived |
| \(A\) | catchment area | m² | `geographic.catchment` |
| \(L_h\) | horizontal length of a flow path, from a divide to the stream that drains it | m | derived |

## Fluxes

| Symbol | Meaning | Unit | Set by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| \(\mathbf{q}\) | specific discharge (Darcy flux) | m/s | derived |
| \(\Phi\) | volumetric discharge, for example at the outlet | m³/s | derived |
| \(N\) | recharge rate, positive into the aquifer | m/s | `flow.sinks_sources.recharge` |
| \(\bar N\) | recharge averaged over the catchment and a period of time (`R_mean_m_s` on the stream-network page) | m/s | derived |
| \(\Phi_{n,p}\) | flow into cell \(n\) from the stress package \(p\), positive into the aquifer | m³/s | `flow.sinks_sources`, `flow.bc` |

A recharge series is read in the unit of `flow.sinks_sources.recharge.units` and converted to m/s. When the soil reservoir computes it, \(N = (1 - f)\,O_t\) (see The daily soil reservoir).

## The descent and the distance between networks

The descent \(D\) is where water goes on the model top: from each cell, the path to a lower neighbor, down to the outlet or to a cell where water leaves the model. It is a computation on a copy of the top and is never given back to the solver. The distances below are not measured on \(D\), but on their own copy (Downslope distance between two networks).

# Recharge estimated from the data

A `[recharge_estimates]` section asks for a range of recharge on the catchment, computed from the loaded weather, gauge and piezometers before the solver runs. None of these numbers enters the model. They bound the answer the way the ESPERE tool of the BRGM does (report RP-69538-FR, Lanini et al. 2016), and the run’s own recharge is set beside them, so one look says whether the run sits inside what the data allow.

## What each method reads and gives

| Method | Reads | Gives, per calendar year |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `turc` | rain and mean temperature | effective rainfall, Turc (1954) |
| `guttman_zuckerman` | rain | recharge, Guttman and Zuckerman (1995) |
| `kessler` | monthly rain | recharge, Kessler (1967) |
| `wallingford` | gauge | baseflow and baseflow index, Gustard et al. (1992) |
| `chapman_maxwell` | gauge | baseflow, Chapman and Maxwell (1996) |
| `eckhardt` | gauge | baseflow, Eckhardt (2005) |
| `wtf` | each piezometer, specific yield | recharge, Healy and Cook (2002) |
| `closing_factor` | gauge, the run’s recharge and runoff | one factor, Abherve (2022), eq. 12 |

The weather is reduced to one basin series, the mean of the grid cells or of the stations. The gauge is turned into mm/day over the catchment area. A gap of 3 days or less in the gauge, 5 days or less in a piezometer, is filled by a straight line, and a longer gap cuts the series. A year counts when its series covers 90 % of its days. A method whose data is missing is skipped with a sentence that says why.

## The formulas

Turc gives an effective rainfall \(P_e = P\,(1 - 1/\sqrt{0.9 + (P/L)^2})\) with \(L = 300 + 25T + 0.05T^3\). The cube is the one of the method and of ESPERE 2.44, and the manual of ESPERE prints a square by mistake. It is a rainfall that has not yet infiltrated, and the table says so.

Guttman and Zuckerman give three straight lines of the yearly rain, \(0.45(P - 180)\) under 600 mm, \(0.88(P - 410)\) under 1000 mm, and \(0.97(P - 463)\) from 1000 mm. ESPERE leaves a year of exactly 1000 mm on no line. Under 180 mm the recharge is zero.

Kessler reads the share of the yearly rain that falls from January to April, corrected by how wet the previous autumn was against the mean autumn, and turns it into a rate of infiltration by the cubic of his abacus. The correction goes by steps of \(|CPR|\) up to 0.70, then 15. ESPERE leaves a gap between 0.70 and 0.71. The first year has no value.

The three filters split the daily discharge into a quick part and a baseflow, read as the recharge that leaves the aquifer. Wallingford joins the smoothed minima of blocks of 5 days. Chapman and Maxwell use one recession constant \(k\), Eckhardt adds the largest share of baseflow \(\mathrm{BFI}_{max}\),

(21)\[Q_b(t) = \min\!\left(Q(t),\ \frac{(1 - \mathrm{BFI}_{max})\,k\,Q_b(t-1) + (1 - k)\,\mathrm{BFI}_{max}\,Q(t)}{1 - k\,\mathrm{BFI}_{max}}\right).\]

Unset, \(k\) is read on the falling limbs of the gauge of 5 days or more, their first 2 days dropped, and \(\mathrm{BFI}_{max}\) is the largest yearly index of Wallingford, as ESPERE does.

The water table fluctuation multiplies the rises of the water table by the specific yield. With `correction = "recession"` it adds to each rise the decline the rain interrupted: the daily declines of the recession before it are fitted as an exponential of time and extended to the start of the next one. ESPERE fits the logarithm of the raw elevation, so its answer moves with the datum. Fitting the declines does not. The estimate is proportional to \(S_y\), which the section asks for.

Wallingford also gives the infiltration ratio ESPERE v2 proposes for its soil budgets, the lowest yearly baseflow index of the record. The table writes it as a row `infiltration_ratio`, and the user copies it into `infiltration_ratio` when the soil should send the rest of its excess to the streams.

The same Wallingford filter also judges a run. The run metric `bfi_gap` is the baseflow index of the simulated discharge minus the one of the gauge, both filtered on the same days of the metrics window, and the calibration criterion `bfi_error` is its absolute value. It is the index of the whole window, not the lowest yearly index above. It asks whether the simulated stream is fed by its aquifer in the share the gauge shows: a slower aquifer, or drains that rarely overflow, raise it. It is blind to the volume and to the timing, since a simulated series twice the observed one scores zero, so it goes beside a fit such as `nse`, never alone. The filter reads blocks of five days, so it needs a daily discharge: a monthly run leaves `bfi_gap` empty, and the criterion is refused outside a transient run with a daily step.

The closing factor is the number that would scale the run’s recharge and runoff onto the gauged volume over their common days. Abherve (2022) multiplies the SURFEX recharge by it before he calibrates on that same gauge. Here it is only printed, so a user who wants it copies it into `factor` knowing what it does.

## The storage loop

With a soil reservoir and a gauge, the section also writes, month by month, the rain minus the soil’s ETR beside the gauged discharge. The figure `water_balance_loop` draws them: above the 1:1 line the catchment stores water, below it the aquifer drains, and the shape of the loop reads the size of the store (Abherve 2022, section 2.2.3, after Schmidt et al. 2020).

## The soil laws and a loaded product, month by month

`recharge_estimates.soil_methods` runs each soil law of the soil reservoir on the same rain, ETP, ru, crop coefficient, snow and sealed share as the run. Only the storage law changes. A run without a soil section of its own gives the laws `recharge_estimates.soil`, with its ru written, and never reads it. In a run whose soil computes the recharge, `recharge_estimates.compare_loaded` loads `data.recharge` and `data.runoff`, SIM2 DRAINC and RUNC for instance, and sets them aside before the model is bound, so the model never receives them. Each law and the product give yearly recharge rows, which join the range above, and monthly rows of recharge and runoff beside the run’s own and beside the rain and the ETP. The figure `recharge_signals` draws them month by month and `recharge_regime` draws their mean year. One ru is not one soil, because the ru that closes the budget differs from law to law: on the Nancon over 2015-2020 it is 187 mm with `fao56` and 376 mm with `dingman`.

These figures need no solve. `hmp run <file> --until prepare_solver` writes the run and its tables in a minute or two, then `hmp show <run> --figure recharge_signals --to signals.png` draws one.

## A steady run on a yearly formula

Turc, Guttman and Zuckerman and Kessler give one value a year, so they never force a transient run. A steady run may take one as its rate with `data.recharge.formula`. The data step runs the formula on each complete calendar year of the run, on the basin mean of the rain (and of the temperature for Turc), and lays the mean over the years on the grid of the rain. Turc gives an effective rainfall, which the run takes whole, so the drains do the share a RIPE would do. A transient run, a soil section and a scenario beside the formula are refused.

## Where the results go

The run prints one block at the end of the data step, one line per method with its mean, its range and its years. It writes the table `recharge_estimates`, one row per method, year and quantity, and the figures `recharge_estimates` and `water_balance_loop` read it.

## Parameters of this page

[recharge_estimates]

`# methods = "all"` : Methods to run, or "all". experimental
**Path**: `recharge_estimates.methods`
**More**: "all" skips wtf when no specific yield is given. Weather: turc (an effective rainfall), guttman_zuckerman, kessler. Gauge: wallingford, chapman_maxwell, eckhardt, closing_factor. Piezometer: wtf.
**Values**:
- `"all"`
**Accepted**: list of string or "all"
**Example**: `"all"`, `["turc", "eckhardt"]`

`# soil_methods = []` : Soil laws to run on the same weather and the same ru, or "all". experimental
**Path**: `recharge_estimates.soil_methods`
**More**: Each gives a daily recharge and runoff, written as monthly rows and as yearly recharge, to set beside the run's own and beside a loaded product. The laws read the soil section of the run, else [recharge_estimates.soil]. One ru is not one soil: the ru that closes the budget differs from law to law.
**Values**:
- `"all"`
**Accepted**: list of string or "all"
**Example**: `"all"`, `["fao56", "dingman"]`

`# compare_loaded = false` : In a run whose soil section computes the recharge, load [data.recharge] and [data.runoff] for the comparison only, such as SIM2 DRAINC and RUNC: they are written beside the soil laws and never reach the model. experimental
**Path**: `recharge_estimates.compare_loaded`
**More**: List recharge, and runoff if it has one, in data.types.
**See**: data.recharge, data.runoff
**Accepted**: true | false

[recharge_estimates.soil]

`ru = "150 mm"` : Available water capacity of the soil, in mm of water: what the roots can draw between field capacity and wilting point. required mm [0, 1000] calibrable experimental example value
**Path**: `recharge_estimates.soil.ru`
**More**: A bare number is in mm; "120 mm" and "12 cm" also read. Between 0 and 1000 mm. Required, since it belongs to the site. Start from a soil map, then compare the recharge the soil alone prints for 50 to 250 mm with the gauged discharge (hmp run <file> --until load_data). With [data.soil_capacity], it is the mean capacity over the catchment, and the raster spreads it over classes inside each cell. Calibrate it with [calibration.parameters.ru].
**Accepted**: number or "<n> mm" (a bare number is read in the canonical unit)
**Valid range**: [0, 1000] (refused outside)
**Unit**: mm
**Example**: `"150 mm"`
**Calibration**: yes, search space identity, sampling uniform, bounds belong to the site: write them in `calibration.parameters.<name>.bounds`

`# method = "fao56"` : Storage law of the soil, the one thing that differs between methods. experimental
**Path**: `recharge_estimates.soil.method`
**More**: "fao56" lowers ETR linearly below alpha x ru (Allen et al. 1998). "thornthwaite" meets the full demand while water is left (Thornthwaite 1948). "dingman" empties the soil as an exponential of the deficit on dry days (Dingman 2008). "edijatno_michel" is the production store of GR4J without its percolation (Edijatno and Michel 1989). The sealed share, the curve number, the bypass, the transit and the snow work the same around every law.
**Accepted**: string
**Example**: `"fao56"`, `"thornthwaite"`

`# alpha = 0.45` : Share of ru above which the soil evaporates at the full rate kc x ETP. ]0, 1] calibrable experimental
**Path**: `recharge_estimates.soil.alpha`
**More**: Below alpha x ru, ETR falls linearly with the stored water. It is 1 - p of FAO-56 and LP of HBV. The default 0.45 is a choice: it means p = 0.55, the value of FAO-56 table 22 for cereals and maize (pasture 0.60). Above 0, at most 1. Kept fixed by default: on the discharge alone it trades off with ru, since both move the annual volume.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: ]0, 1] (refused outside)
**Unit**: -
**Calibration**: yes, search space identity, sampling uniform, default bounds [0.3, 1.0]

`# impervious_fraction = 0.0` : Share of the area that is sealed (roofs, roads). [0, 1[ calibrable experimental
**Path**: `recharge_estimates.soil.impervious_fraction`
**More**: The rain that falls on it runs off at once, with no infiltration and no evaporation, and reaches the streams, the lakes and the gauged discharge. The soil reservoir covers the rest of the area. From 0 up to, not including, 1. Calibrate it with [calibration.parameters.impervious_fraction]; the range belongs to the site, so a file has to state it. [data.impervious] gives it cell by cell instead, and then it is not written here.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: [0, 1[ (refused outside)
**Unit**: -
**Calibration**: yes, search space identity, sampling uniform, bounds belong to the site: write them in `calibration.parameters.<name>.bounds`

`# bypass_fraction = 0.0` : Share of the rain on the unsealed area that skips the soil through macropores and joins the recharge the same day, even when the soil is dry. [0, 1[ calibrable experimental
**Path**: `recharge_estimates.soil.bypass_fraction`
**More**: From 0 up to, not including, 1. Keep it at 0 while K and Sy are calibrated: a bypass can rebuild the summer recharge the soil reservoir removes.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: [0, 1[ (refused outside)
**Unit**: -
**Calibration**: yes, search space identity, sampling uniform, default bounds [0.0, 0.3]

`# transit_time = 0.0` : Mean time the water leaving the soil takes to cross the unsaturated zone down to the water table, in days. day [0, 30] calibrable experimental
**Path**: `recharge_estimates.soil.transit_time`
**More**: A linear reservoir with this time constant delays and smooths the recharge; 0 sends it the same day. A bare number is in days; "5 days" also reads. At most 30 days: a longer delay would rebuild the slow groundwater memory MODFLOW computes itself.
**Accepted**: number or "<n> day" (a bare number is read in the canonical unit)
**Valid range**: [0, 30] (refused outside)
**Unit**: day
**Calibration**: yes, search space identity, sampling uniform, default bounds [0.0, 30.0]

`# curve_number = ‹number›` : SCS curve number (AMC II), dimensionless, of a HELP-style surface runoff (Schroeder et al. 1994): the unsealed share of the rain above a daily retention loses some to a fast runoff, more as the soil is wetter. [30, 98] calibrable experimental
**Path**: `recharge_estimates.soil.curve_number`
**More**: None turns the term off, bit for bit as before. Between 30 and 98. It reads the soil and never the water table, so it renders saturation runoff badly: leave it off where the drains already give that runoff. To calibrate it, state a range under [calibration.parameters.curve_number]: it belongs to the soil group and the land use of the site. [data.curve_number] gives it cell by cell instead, and then it is not written here.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: [30, 98] (refused outside)
**Unit**: -
**Calibration**: yes, search space identity, sampling uniform, bounds belong to the site: write them in `calibration.parameters.<name>.bounds`

`# infiltration_ratio = 1.0` : Share of the water leaving the soil that goes on to the aquifer, the RIPE of ESPERE (BRGM): the rest runs off on the same day, beside the sealed share and the curve number, and reaches the streams through the runoff of the run. - [0, 1] experimental
**Path**: `recharge_estimates.soil.infiltration_ratio`
**More**: 1, the default, sends it all to the aquifer, bit for bit as before, and the drains give back what saturates. Between 0 and 1. ESPERE proposes the lowest yearly baseflow index of the gauge, which the soil budget of `hmp run --until load_data` prints when a gauge is loaded: copy it here, the gauge never sets it on its own. [data.infiltration_ratio] gives it cell by cell instead, and then it is not written here.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: [0, 1] (refused outside)
**Unit**: -

`# runoff_time = 1.0` : Time constant of the linear reservoir that routes the curve-number runoff to the outlet, in days. day [0, 10] calibrable experimental
**Path**: `recharge_estimates.soil.runoff_time`
**More**: No effect without a curve number, here or in [data.curve_number]. 0 sends it the same day; "2 days" also reads. Between 0 and 10 days: a longer delay would smooth away the fast surface peak the term exists for.
**Accepted**: number or "<n> day" (a bare number is read in the canonical unit)
**Valid range**: [0, 10] (refused outside)
**Unit**: day
**Calibration**: yes, search space identity, sampling uniform, default bounds [0.0, 10.0]

`# runoff_lag = 0.0` : Pure delay applied to the routed curve-number runoff, after runoff_time, before it reaches the gauged discharge: the travel time to the outlet plus any lag between the forcing's daily step and the gauge's. day [0, 5] calibrable experimental
**Path**: `recharge_estimates.soil.runoff_lag`
**More**: No effect without a curve number, here or in [data.curve_number]. 0 adds no delay, bit for bit as before; "0.75 days" also reads, interpolated linearly between the neighbouring whole-day shifts. Between 0 and 5 days: a longer shift belongs to runoff_time's reservoir, not to a fixed travel time. Calibrate it with [calibration.parameters.runoff_lag].
**Accepted**: number or "<n> day" (a bare number is read in the canonical unit)
**Valid range**: [0, 5] (refused outside)
**Unit**: day
**Calibration**: yes, search space identity, sampling uniform, default bounds [0.0, 5.0]

`# spinup = "first_year"` : State of the soil on the first day. experimental
**Path**: `recharge_estimates.soil.spinup`
**More**: "first_year" repeats the first 365 days of the run until the storage at the end of that year moves by less than 0.1 mm, 20 times at most; the run must last 364 days (52 weeks) at least, and a 364-day run repeats those 364 days. "none" starts from a full soil, the state of a soil in a wet winter. Beside a cyclic spin-up of the aquifer (flow.ic.kind = "spinup_cyclic"), the two starts are computed over two windows: the soil settles on the first year, the heads on the whole run. That pair is allowed without a warning, because it is sometimes what the study wants.
**Values**:
- `"first_year"` : Repeat the first year until the soil storage settles.
- `"none"` : Start from a full soil and an empty transit store.
**Accepted**: "first_year" | "none"

[data.recharge]

`# formula = "turc"` : Compute a steady recharge from the yearly weather instead of loading a series: the formula runs on each complete calendar year of the run on the basin mean of [data.precipitation] (and of [data.temperature] for turc), and the run takes the mean over the years as its one rate. experimental example value
**Path**: `data.recharge.formula`
**More**: Only a run with [flow] flow_regime = "steady" reads it. "turc" gives an effective rainfall, which the run takes whole as recharge, so the drains do the share a RIPE would do. Guttman and Zuckerman and Kessler were fitted on karsts.
**See**: data.precipitation, data.temperature
**Accepted**: string
**Example**: `"turc"`

Lines generated from the models, as in the reference. Open one for its card.

```
1# not checked: the section alone, without the data it reads
2[recharge_estimates]
3methods = "all"
4
5[recharge_estimates.eckhardt]
6bfi_max = 0.80
7
8[recharge_estimates.wtf]
9specific_yield = 0.05
```
